Intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, while energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam. The reflected light and incident light are in the same medium, with equal cross-sectional areas, while the refracted light and incident light are in different media, with different cross-sectional areas, which is noteworthy.

1. According to Fresnel's equations, the amplitude reflectance $r_{s}$ and amplitude transmittance $t_{s}$ for the $S$ component are

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{s}=\frac{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}-n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}=-\frac{\sin \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\
t_{s}=\frac{2 n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{2 \sin \theta_{2} \cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

The amplitude reflectance $r_{P}$ and amplitude transmittance $t_{P}$ for the $P$ component are

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{P}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}-n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{\tan \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}{\tan \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

where $n_{1}=1$, $n_{2}=n=1.50$, $\theta_{1}$ is the angle of incidence, and $\theta_{2}$ is the angle of refraction. Since the angle of incidence is the Brewster's angle, we have

$$
\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}=\arctan n=\arctan 1.50=56.3^{\circ}
$$

Additionally,

$$
\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}
$$

Substituting into the formulas for $r_{s}$ and $r_{p}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{s}=-\frac{\sin \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}{\sin \left(56.3^{\circ}+33.7^{\circ}\right)}=-0.384 \\
r_{p}=0
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the reflected light and incident light are in the same medium with equal cross-sectional areas, the intensity reflectance $R_{S}$ and $R_{P}$, as well as the energy flow reflectance $\bar{R}_{S}$ and $\bar{R}_{P}$ for the $S$ and $P$ components respectively, are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& R_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad R_{P}=0 \\
& \bar{R}_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad \bar{R}_{P}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

For the refracted light, substituting $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ into $t_{s}$ and $t_{P}$, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
t_{s}=\frac{2 \sin \theta_{2} \cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \sin 33.7^{\circ} \cos 56.3^{\circ}}{\sin \frac{\pi}{2}}=0.616 \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \cos 56.3^{\circ} \sin 33.7^{\circ}}{\cos \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}=0.667
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the refracted light and incident light are in different media with different cross-sectional areas, the intensity transmittance and energy flow transmittance are not simply equal to the square of the amplitude transmittance. The intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, given by

$$
\widetilde{S}=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_{0} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}{\mu_{0} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}}} E^{2}
$$

where $E$ is the amplitude of the electric vector. Since $\mu_{\mathrm{r}} \approx 1$, and the speed of light in vacuum $c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{0}} \mu_{0}}$, and the refractive index $n=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}} \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}$, this can be rewritten as

$$
\bar{S}=\frac{1}{2 c \mu_{0}} n E^{2}
$$

Thus, the intensity is proportional to $n E^{2}$, and the intensity transmittance is

$$
T=\frac{\bar{S}_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1}}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t^{2}
$$

The intensity transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& T_{S}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{S}^{2}=n t_{S}^{2}=0.569 \\
& T_{P}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{P}^{2}=n t_{P}^{2}=0.667
\end{aligned}
$$

The energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam, and the ratio of the cross-sectional areas of the refracted beam to the incident beam is $\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}}$, so the energy flow transmittance is

$$
\bar{T}=\frac{\bar{S}_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}} t^{2}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T
$$

Substituting the values, the energy flow transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{gathered}
\bar{T}_{S}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{S}=0.853 \\
\bar{T}_{P}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{P}=1
\end{gathered}
$$

The fact that the energy flow transmittance $\bar{T}_{P}=1$ for the $P$ component is expected because, when light is incident at the Brewster's angle $\left(\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}\right)$, the reflected light does not contain any $P$ component, meaning the entire energy of the incident $P$ component is transmitted.

subject: Wave Optics
problem:
Suppose the complex amplitude transmittance function of a grating is

$$
t(x) = t_{0} + t_{1} \cos(2 \pi f x) + t_{1} \cos \left(2 \pi f x + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)
$$

How many diffraction spots will appear in the Fraunhofer diffraction pattern of this grating?
solution: Excluding the DC component term $t_{0}$, the complex amplitude transmittance function of this grating includes two terms with the same spatial frequency $f$. It can be determined that this grating will still produce only three Fraunhofer diffraction spots.

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: A snowplow is traveling on a horizontal road at a speed of $15 \, \text{km/h}$, throwing snow with a mass of $30 \, \text{t}$ per minute to the roadside. The velocity of the snow relative to the snowplow is $12 \, \text{m/s}$. Find the traction force needed to drive the snowplow's machinery.
solution:
In a stationary reference frame, the snowplow machinery and the snow being shoveled form a system. Let the traction force required to drive the snowplow machinery be $f$. During a time interval from $t$ to $t+\mathrm{d} t$, using the principle of momentum conservation in the direction of the snowplow's motion:

$$
M v + \mathrm{d} m \cdot v - M v = f \mathrm{d} t
$$

where $M$ is the mass of the snowplow machinery, $\mathrm{d} m$ is the mass of the snow shoveled during this period, and $v$ is the speed of the snowplow.

Therefore,

$$
f = \frac{\mathrm{d} m}{\mathrm{d} t} \cdot v = \frac{30 \times 10^3}{60} \times \frac{15 \times 10^3}{3600} = 2.08 \times 10^{3} \, \text{N}
$$

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: Light with a wavelength of 200 nm shines on an aluminum surface. The energy required to remove an electron is known to be 4.2 eV. If the intensity of the incident light is \(2.0 \, \mathrm{W/m^2}\), what is the average number of photons hitting the unit area per unit time?
solution:
The relationship between light intensity and the average photon flux \(N\) is given by:

\[
I = N h \nu
\]

\[
N = \frac{I}{h \nu} = \frac{I \lambda}{h c} = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{-19}}{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}} = 2 \times 10^{8} \, \text{m}^{-2} \cdot \text{s}^{-1}
\]

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem:
Consider the one-dimensional motion of three particles, each with mass $m$. The force between the particles is a harmonic oscillator force, with the potential given by

$$
V=\frac{1}{2} k\left[(x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}+(x_{2}-x_{3})^{2}+(x_{3}-x_{1})^{2}\right]
$$

If the three particles are spin $\frac{1}{2}$ fermions, what is the ground state energy?
solution:
For three spin $\frac{1}{2}$ fermions, since there is no spin term in the Hamiltonian, the eigenstate wave function can be separated into a product of a spin wave function and a spatial wave function.

Note the coordinate transformation in the center of mass coordinates. We can also use the following coordinate transformations:

$$
\left\{
\begin{array}{l}
y_{1}^{\prime}=x_{2}-x_{3} \\
y_{2}^{\prime}=\frac{x_{2}+x_{3}}{2}-x_{1} \\
y_{3}^{\prime}=\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}}{3}
\end{array}
\right.
$$

Clearly, the result is the same as that in the center of mass coordinates. The eigen wave function (spatial part) and energy are respectively

$$
\left\{
\begin{array}{l}
\psi\left(y_{1}^{\prime}, y_{2}^{\prime}, y_{3}^{\prime}\right)=\phi_{1 n}\left(y_{1}^{\prime}\right) \phi_{2 l}\left(y_{2}^{\prime}\right) Y\left(y_{3}^{\prime}\right) \\
E=(n+l+1) \hbar \sqrt{\frac{3 k}{m}}
\end{array}
\right.
$$

It is easy to see that $\phi_{10}\left(y_{1}\right) \phi_{20}\left(y_{2}\right)=\phi_{10}\left(y_{1}^{\prime}\right) \phi_{20}\left(y_{2}^{\prime}\right)$, so the spatial wave function is necessarily symmetric with respect to particle exchange, while the three spin $1/2$ fermions cannot form a spin wave function that is antisymmetric with respect to particle exchange. Hence, the three spin $\frac{1}{2}$ fermions cannot form this state.

Noting the characteristics of the harmonic oscillator wave function, we know that the exponential part of $\phi_{1 n}\left(y_{1}\right) \phi_{2 l}\left(y_{2}\right)$ is identical to that of $\phi_{10}\left(y_{1}\right) \phi_{20}\left(y_{2}\right)$ and is symmetric, let

$$
\Phi_{1}=\phi_{11}\left(y_{1}\right) \phi_{20}\left(y_{2}\right)=C(x_{1}-x_{2})
$$

$$
\Phi_{2}=\phi_{11}\left(y_{1}^{\prime}\right) \phi_{20}\left(y_{2}^{\prime}\right)=C(x_{2}-x_{3})
$$

$C$ is symmetric with respect to particle exchange. Construct the wave function $\left(\Phi_{2}+\Phi_{1}=C(x_{1}-x_{3})\right)$

$$
\Phi=\Phi_{1}\binom{1}{0}_{1}\binom{1}{0}_{2}\binom{0}{1}_{3}+\Phi_{2}\binom{0}{1}_{1}\binom{1}{0}_{2}\binom{1}{0}_{3}-\left(\Phi_{2}+\Phi_{1}\right)\binom{1}{0}_{1}\binom{0}{1}_{2}\binom{1}{0}_{3}
$$

It is easy to verify that $\Phi$ is antisymmetric with respect to particle exchange. Therefore, the ground state energy of the three spin $\frac{1}{2}$ fermions is (excluding the translational energy of the center of mass)

$$
E_{0}=2 \hbar \sqrt{\frac{3 k}{m}}
$$

subject: Wave Optics
problem: Dip a metal frame into a soap solution and then remove it, keeping it vertical, thus forming a wedge-shaped film. Illuminate it approximately vertically with argon ion laser light (\(\lambda=514.53 \mathrm{~nm}\)), and 12 fringes can be observed per centimeter. Find the apex angle of this wedge-shaped film if the refractive index of the soap solution is \(n=1.33\).
solution:
Solution

$$
\theta=\frac{\lambda}{2 n \Delta x}, \quad \Delta x=\frac{1}{12} \mathrm{~cm}
$$

Substituting the values of \(\lambda\) and \(n\), we get

$$
\theta=2.3 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{rad}
$$

subject: Classical Electromagnetism
problem: The charge $Q$ is uniformly distributed on a spherical surface with a radius of $r_0$, and both the inside and outside of the sphere are vacuum. Calculate the electric force per unit area on the spherical surface. For $Q=1 \mathrm{C}$, $r_0=1 \mathrm{cm}$, provide a numerical answer.
solution:
The surface charge density $\sigma = \frac{Q}{4 \pi r_0^2}$. The electric field outside the sphere is

$$
\boldsymbol{E} = \frac{Q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 r^2} \boldsymbol{e}_r.
$$

The electric force per unit area on the external surface of the sphere is

$$
\boldsymbol{f} = \left.\frac{\sigma \boldsymbol{E}}{2}\right|_{r=r_0} = \frac{Q^2}{32 \pi^2 \varepsilon_0 r_0^4} \boldsymbol{e}_r.
$$

Substituting the values gives

$$
f = 3.6 \times 10^{16} \, \mathrm{N/m^2}.
$$

subject: Statistical Mechanics
problem: In a cubic copper structure with a side length of \( 100 \, \text{} \), the valence electrons form a Fermi gas. Calculate the difference in energy \( \Delta \varepsilon \) between the ground state energy and the first excited state energy of this Fermi gas. Given that the density and atomic mass of copper are \( \rho=8.93 \mathrm{~g/cm}^{3} \) and \( A=63.5 \), respectively.
solution:
When the gas is in equilibrium at temperature \(T\), it follows the Maxwell velocity distribution law. The number of molecules within a unit volume with velocities between \(\boldsymbol{v}\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}+\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}\) is given by:

\[
f(v) \mathrm{d} v=n\left(\frac{m}{2 \pi k T}\right)^{3 / 2} \exp \left(-\frac{m v^{2}}{2 k T}\right) \mathrm{d} v \tag{1}
\]

To calculate the number of collisions, consider the two types of molecules as elastic hard spheres with diameters \(d_{1}\) and \(d_{2}\). Using the center of a molecule of the first type as the sphere's center and a radius of \(d_{12}=(d_{1}+d_{2})/2\), the sphere surface is conceptualized. When two molecules collide, the center of the second type must be on this imaginary sphere, with \(v_{r}=v_{2}-v_{1}\) being the relative velocity of molecule 2 concerning molecule 1. In a time \(\mathrm{d} t\), for the second type of molecule to collide with the first within the solid angle element \(\mathrm{d} \Omega\) along the axis direction \(\boldsymbol{n}\), it must be located within a cylinder with base \(d_{12}^{2} \mathrm{d} \Omega\) and height \(v_{r} \cos \theta \mathrm{d} t\). The volume of this cylinder is:

\[
\mathrm{d} \tau=d_{12}^{2} v_{r} \cos \theta \mathrm{d} \Omega \mathrm{d} t \tag{2}
\]

Therefore, in time \(\mathrm{d} t\), the number of collisions within the solid angle element \(\mathrm{d} \Omega\) along the axis \(\boldsymbol{n}\) between a molecule 1 with speed \(\boldsymbol{v}_{1}\) and molecule 2 with speeds in the range \(\boldsymbol{v}_{2}\) to \(\boldsymbol{v}_{2}+\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{2}\) is:

\[
f_{2}\left(\boldsymbol{v}_{2}\right) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{2} \mathrm{d} \tau = d_{12}^{2} v_{r} \cos \theta f_{2}\left(\boldsymbol{v}_{2}\right) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{2} \mathrm{d} \Omega \mathrm{d} t \tag{3}
\]

Thus, the average number of collisions in unit time between one molecule of the first type and all molecules of the second type is:

\[
\overline{\Theta_{12}} = \frac{1}{n_{1}} \iiint d_{12}^{2} v_{r} \cos \theta \cdot f_{1}\left(\boldsymbol{v}_{1}\right) f_{2}\left(\boldsymbol{v}_{2}\right) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{1} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{2} \mathrm{d} \Omega \tag{5}
\]

Completing the angular integration:

\[
\int \cos \theta \mathrm{d} \Omega = \int_{0}^{2 \pi} \mathrm{d} \varphi \cdot \int_{0}^{\pi} \cos \theta \sin \theta \mathrm{d} \theta = \pi \tag{6}
\]

We find:

\[
\overline{\Theta_{12}} = \pi n_{2} d_{12}^{2}\left(\frac{m_{1}}{2 \pi k T}\right)^{3/2}\left(\frac{m_{2}}{2 \pi k T}\right)^{3/2} \iint v_{r} \exp \left(-\frac{m_{1} v_{1}^{2}+m_{2} v_{2}^{2}}{2 k T}\right) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{1} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{2} \tag{7}
\]

Introducing the velocity of the center of mass:

\[
\boldsymbol{v}_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{1}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\left(m_{1} \boldsymbol{v}_{1}+m_{2} \boldsymbol{v}_{2}\right) \tag{8}
\]

We have:

\[
\frac{1}{2} m_{1} v_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} m_{2} v_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2} M v_{\mathrm{c}}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \mu v_{r}^{2} \tag{9}
\]

And

\[
\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{\mathrm{c}} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{r}=|J| \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{1} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{2} \tag{10}
\]

where \(M=m_{1}+m_{2}\) is the total mass of the two molecules, and \(\mu=m_{1} m_{2} /(m_{1}+m_{2})\) is the reduced mass of the two molecules. The absolute value of the Jacobian determinant is:

\[
|J|= \left|\frac{\partial(\boldsymbol{v}_{\mathrm{c}}, \boldsymbol{v}_{r})}{\partial(\boldsymbol{v}_{1}, \boldsymbol{v}_{2})}\right|=1 \tag{11}
\]

Substituting these results into equation (7), we finally obtain the average frequency of collisions between a molecule of the first type and those of the second type:

\[
\overline{\Theta_{12}} = \pi n_{2} d_{12}^{2}\left(\frac{m_{1}}{2 \pi k T}\right)^{3/2}\left(\frac{m_{2}}{2 \pi k T}\right)^{3/2} \int \exp \left(-\frac{M v_{c}^{2}}{2 k T}\right) \mathrm{d} v_{\mathrm{c}} \cdot \int v_{r} \exp \left(-\frac{\mu v_{r}^{2}}{2 k T}\right) \mathrm{d} v_{r} = \pi n_{2} d_{12}^{2} \sqrt{\frac{8 k T}{\pi \mu}} = \pi n_{2} d_{12}^{2}\left(1+\frac{m_{1}}{m_{2}}\right)^{1/2} \overline{v_{1}} \tag{12}
\]

where \(\overline{v_{1}}=\sqrt{8 k T / \pi m_{1}}\) is the average speed of the first type of molecule, and \(n_{1}\) and \(n_{2}\) are the molecular number densities of the first and second types of gas molecules, respectively. For identical molecules, the average collision frequency is \(\Theta=\sqrt{2} n \pi d^{2} v\).

subject: Semiconductor Physics
problem: Within an error range of 10, use estimation, rough calculation, or memorization to answer the following question: What is the de Broglie wavelength of the Earth? Please explain in detail how you arrived at your answer.
solution:
The Earth's orbital speed is \(3 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{~m/s}\), and its mass is \(6 \times 10^{24} \mathrm{~kg}\), so its momentum is

\[
p = m v = 1.8 \times 10^{29} \mathrm{~Ns}
\]

Thus,

\[
\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{1.8 \times 10^{29}} = 3.7 \times 10^{-63} \mathrm{~m}
\]

subject: Classical Electromagnetism
problem: There are $n$ batteries, each with an internal resistance $R_{\mathrm{i}}$ and an output voltage $V$. These batteries are divided into several groups, each consisting of $k$ cells connected in series. The $n / k$ groups are then connected in parallel to the load $R$. What value of $k$ results in the maximum power on the load $R$?
solution: The total voltage of each group is $kV$, and the internal resistance is $kR_{\mathrm{i}}$. After parallel connection, the total voltage of the $n / k$ groups remains $kV$, and the total internal resistance is $\frac{kR_{\mathrm{i}}}{n/k} = \frac{k^2 R_{\mathrm{i}}}{n}$. The power on the load is maximized when the internal resistance matches the load. At this point, $R = \frac{k^2 R_{\mathrm{i}}}{n}$, hence $k = \sqrt{\frac{nR}{R_{\mathrm{i}}}}$.

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem:
A particle with charge \( e \) is confined within a cubic box with side length \( 2b \). The given electric field is defined as:

\[
\boldsymbol{E} = \begin{cases} 
0, & t < 0 \\ 
\boldsymbol{E}_{0} e^{-\alpha t}, & t > 0 
\end{cases}
\]

where \( \alpha \) is a constant, and \( E_{0} \) is perpendicular to one face of the box. Assume that at \( t = 0 \), the charged particle is in the ground state. The ground state is known as \(|111\rangle\), and the first excited states include \(|211\rangle, |121\rangle, |112\rangle\). Verify through the following calculations that the transition probabilities of the particle to the states \(|121\rangle\) and \(|112\rangle\) are zero.
solution:
Let \( E_{0} = E_{0} \hat{e}_{x} \), then \( H^{\prime} = -e E_{0} x e^{-\alpha t} \). Calculate the matrix elements:

\[
\langle 111| x |121 \rangle = \langle 111| x |112 \rangle = 0
\]

Since the transition matrix elements are zero, the transition probabilities of the particle to the states \(|121\rangle\) and \(|112\rangle\) are both zero.

subject: Atomic Physics
problem:
The ground state of a sodium atom \((Z=11)\) is \(3s\). It is known that the wavenumber of its resonance line is \(1.6952 \times 10^{6} \ \mathrm{m}^{-1}\), the first line of the diffuse series has a wavenumber of \(1.2218 \times 10^{6} \ \mathrm{m}^{-1}\), the first line of the principal series has a wavenumber of \(5.4158 \times 10^{5} \ \mathrm{m}^{-1}\), and the series limit wavenumber of the sharp series is \(2.4492 \times 10^{6} \ \mathrm{m}^{-1}\).

(3) Calculate the effective nuclear charge on the atomic nucleus for the electrons in \(3s, 3p, 3d\) states, retaining two significant figures, and briefly explain the physical significance of this result.
solution:
(3) \(Z^{*}=\left(\frac{T n^{2}}{R}\right)^{1 / 2}=\left(\frac{T n^{2} h c}{R h c}\right)^{1 / 2}\). Using \(n=3, R h c=13.6 \ \mathrm{eV}, h c=1240 \ \mathrm{eV} \cdot \mathrm{nm}\), the effective charges for electrons in the \(3s, 3p, 3d\) states are calculated as follows:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& Z_{3s}^{*}=1.8, \quad Z_{3p}^{*}=1.4, \quad Z_{3d}^{*}=1.0 \\
& Z_{3s}^{*} > Z_{3p}^{*} > Z_{3d}^{*} \geqslant 1
\end{aligned}
\]

This indicates that valence electrons have a certain probability of penetrating the atomic core and approaching the nucleus. For states with the same \(n\) but different \(l\), the smaller the \(l\), the greater the probability of the electron appearing closer to the nucleus, resulting in a higher effective nuclear charge it experiences. When \(l\) is larger, the electron is further away from the nucleus and the \((Z-1)\) electrons, experiencing a more fully shielded nucleus, such as in the case of the 3d electron, leading to \(Z_{3d}^{*} \rightarrow 1\).

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: At the edge of the Earth's atmosphere, the solar radiance value is $B = 2.0 \times 10^{7} \, \mathrm{W} \cdot \mathrm{m}^{-2} \cdot \mathrm{sr}^{-1}$. Determine the power of the light on a unit area directly facing the Sun at that location. The diameter of the Sun is given as $D = 1.4 \times 10^{6} \, \mathrm{km}$, and the Earth-Sun distance is $z = 1.5 \times 10^{8} \, \mathrm{km}$. ($\mathrm{sr}$ is the unit of solid angle).
solution:
$B$ represents the radiative power per unit area and per unit solid angle on the Sun (considered as a Lambertian emitter, a luminous disk with an equivalent diameter $D$). The solid angle subtended by the Sun from a unit area on Earth is $\Omega = \frac{1 \, \mathrm{m}^{2}}{z^{2}} = \frac{1}{(1.5 \times 10^{11})^{2}}$. Therefore, the solar constant, which is the solar power received by a unit area above the Earth's atmosphere, is calculated as

$$
S = B \cdot \frac{\pi D^{2}}{4} \cdot \Omega = \frac{B \pi}{4} \left(\frac{D}{z}\right)^{2} = \frac{2.0 \pi \times 10^{7}}{4} \left(\frac{1.4 \times 10^{9}}{1.5 \times 10^{11}}\right)^{2} = 1.4 \times 10^{3} \, \mathrm{W} \cdot \mathrm{m}^{-2}
$$

subject: Thermodynamics
problem: The wall of a house is made of cement, with a thickness of \(2 \, \text{cm}\) and a thermal conductivity of \(0.29 \, \text{W/m} \cdot {^\circ} \text{C}\). If the indoor air temperature is \(20^\circ \text{C}\) and the outdoor atmospheric temperature is \(-5^\circ \text{C}\), find the heat flux density per square meter.
solution:
Let the temperature at the interface between the cement and the brick be \(\theta\), with the indoor temperature \(t_{2}=20^\circ \text{C}\) and the atmospheric temperature \(t_{1}=-5^\circ \text{C}\).

According to the continuity of heat transfer, the heat flux \(q\) through the wall (i.e., the amount of heat passing vertically through the wall per unit time) is equal everywhere. From Fourier's law of heat conduction, we have

\[
q = \kappa_{1} \frac{\theta - t_{1}}{d_{1}}
\]

and

\[
\theta - t_{1} = q \frac{d_{1}}{\kappa_{1}}
\]

For the cement layer, the final heat flux density \(q\) is calculated as:

\[
q = \left(t_{2} - t_{1}\right)\left( \frac{d_{1}}{\kappa_{1}} \right)^{-1}
\]

Therefore, the heat flux density through the wall per square meter is \(q = 114 \, \text{W/m}^2\).

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: A certain atom's ${}^{3} \mathrm{P}_{2}$ energy level is found to split into five sublevels, with the ratio of the intervals between adjacent sublevels being $9: 7: 5: 3$. Using the interval rule, determine the nuclear spin quantum number $I$ of this atom and the total atomic angular momentum quantum number $F$ corresponding to each sublevel. Find the nuclear spin quantum number $I$.
solution:
The rule for hyperfine level intervals is: for a given $J$ value, the interval between two adjacent hyperfine sublevels is proportional to the larger of the quantum numbers $F$ of the two sublevels.  
Since the total atomic angular momentum quantum numbers are $F = I + J, I + J - 1, \ldots, |I - J|$,  
When $I \geqslant J$, there are $2J+1$ sublevels; when $I < J$, there are $2I+1$ sublevels.  
There are 5 sublevels, and since $J = 2$, we have $2J+1 = 5$.  
This implies $I \geqslant 2$, so the quantum numbers $F = I+2, I+1, I, I-1, I-2$.  
According to the interval rule, $(I+2):(I+1): I:(I-1)=9: 7: 5: 3$.  

Therefore, $I = \frac{5}{2}$.

subject: Wave Optics
problem: Observe the Michelson interference fringes using sodium light at \(5893 \, \text{}\). Initially, there are 12 bright rings with the center being bright. After moving the plane mirror \(M_{1}\), the center has absorbed (or emitted) 10 rings, and at this point, there are 5 bright rings left in the interference field. Determine the displacement of \(M_{1}\).
solution:
Typically, when natural light is reflected at the interface of two media, the reflected light is partially polarized. However, when the angle of incidence satisfies

$$
\theta_{B}=\arctan \frac{n_{1}}{n_{0}}
$$

where $n_{0}$ and $n_{1}$ are the refractive indices of the incident medium and the refractive medium respectively, the reflected light is linearly polarized with vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence. This angle $\theta_{B}$ is called the Brewster's angle or the polarization angle.

The calculations for $r, R, \bar{R}$, and $t, T, \bar{T}$ for the $S$ and $P$ components are based on Fresnel's equations. Because the angle of incidence is Brewster's angle, the sum of the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction is $\frac{\pi}{2}$. Intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, while energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam. The reflected light and incident light are in the same medium, with equal cross-sectional areas, while the refracted light and incident light are in different media, with different cross-sectional areas, which is noteworthy.

1. According to Fresnel's equations, the amplitude reflectance $r_{s}$ and amplitude transmittance $t_{s}$ for the $S$ component are

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{s}=\frac{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}-n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}=-\frac{\sin \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\
t_{s}=\frac{2 n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{2 \sin \theta_{2} \cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

The amplitude reflectance $r_{P}$ and amplitude transmittance $t_{P}$ for the $P$ component are

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{P}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}-n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{\tan \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}{\tan \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

where $n_{1}=1$, $n_{2}=n=1.50$, $\theta_{1}$ is the angle of incidence, and $\theta_{2}$ is the angle of refraction. Since the angle of incidence is the Brewster's angle, we have

$$
\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}=\arctan n=\arctan 1.50=56.3^{\circ}
$$

Additionally,

$$
\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}
$$

Substituting into the formulas for $r_{s}$ and $r_{p}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{s}=-\frac{\sin \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}{\sin \left(56.3^{\circ}+33.7^{\circ}\right)}=-0.384 \\
r_{p}=0
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the reflected light and incident light are in the same medium with equal cross-sectional areas, the intensity reflectance $R_{S}$ and $R_{P}$, as well as the energy flow reflectance $\bar{R}_{S}$ and $\bar{R}_{P}$ for the $S$ and $P$ components respectively, are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& R_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad R_{P}=0 \\
& \bar{R}_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad \bar{R}_{P}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

For the refracted light, substituting $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ into $t_{s}$ and $t_{P}$, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
t_{s}=\frac{2 \sin \theta_{2} \cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \sin 33.7^{\circ} \cos 56.3^{\circ}}{\sin \frac{\pi}{2}}=0.616 \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \cos 56.3^{\circ} \sin 33.7^{\circ}}{\cos \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}=0.667
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the refracted light and incident light are in different media with different cross-sectional areas, the intensity transmittance and energy flow transmittance are not simply equal to the square of the amplitude transmittance. The intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, given by

$$
\widetilde{S}=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_{0} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}{\mu_{0} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}}} E^{2}
$$

where $E$ is the amplitude of the electric vector. Since $\mu_{\mathrm{r}} \approx 1$, and the speed of light in vacuum $c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{0}} \mu_{0}}$, and the refractive index $n=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}} \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}$, this can be rewritten as

$$
\bar{S}=\frac{1}{2 c \mu_{0}} n E^{2}
$$

Thus, the intensity is proportional to $n E^{2}$, and the intensity transmittance is

$$
T=\frac{\bar{S}_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1}}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t^{2}
$$

The intensity transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& T_{S}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{S}^{2}=n t_{S}^{2}=0.569 \\
& T_{P}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{P}^{2}=n t_{P}^{2}=0.667
\end{aligned}
$$

The energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam, and the ratio of the cross-sectional areas of the refracted beam to the incident beam is $\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}}$, so the energy flow transmittance is

$$
\bar{T}=\frac{\bar{S}_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}} t^{2}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T
$$

Substituting the values, the energy flow transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{gathered}
\bar{T}_{S}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{S}=0.853 \\
\bar{T}_{P}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{P}=1
\end{gathered}
$$

The fact that the energy flow transmittance $\bar{T}_{P}=1$ for the $P$ component is expected because, when light is incident at the Brewster's angle $\left(\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}\right)$, the reflected light does not contain any $P$ component, meaning the entire energy of the incident $P$ component is transmitted.

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: There are two flywheels with radii \( R_{1} \) and \( R_{2} \), respectively, satisfying \( R_{1}=2R_{2} \). The two flywheels can rotate frictionlessly around symmetrical parallel axes. Their moments of inertia are \( I_{1} \) and \( I_{2} \), satisfying \( I_{1}=16I_{2} \). Initially, the flywheels are not in contact, and the large flywheel is rotating at a speed of \( n_{0}=2000 \text{ r/min} \), while the small flywheel is stationary. If the parallel axes are moved so that the two flywheels make contact, find the angular velocity of the small flywheel when they reach a stable state where there is no slipping at the point of contact and the rotational speeds no longer change.
solution: From the time of contact to the point of reaching a stable state, apply the angular momentum conservation theorem about a fixed axis to each flywheel. Consider the direction of the flywheels' angular velocity and the direction of the interaction force \( f \), along with the initial conditions and geometric relationships. Solving the equations yields the angular velocity of the small flywheel \(\Omega_{2} = \frac{16}{5} \pi \cdot \frac{2000}{60} = 335.1 \text{ rad/s}\).

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: A homogeneous cube is freely rotating around its diagonal. Given that the cube has a side length of $a$, a mass of $m$, and an angular velocity of $\omega_{0}$ about the diagonal, determine the new angular velocity $\omega$ of the system when one edge is suddenly fixed, causing it to rotate around that edge.
solution:
When an edge is suddenly fixed, the impulse moment about a point on this edge is zero. The rotation abruptly transitions from around the diagonal to the fixed edge, without change to the impulse moment about this edge. Therefore, the component of the system's angular momentum in the direction of this edge remains unchanged between the two rotations.

While rotating around the diagonal,
$$
J_{0}=I_{\mathrm{C}} \omega_{0}
$$

The component of angular momentum along the edge is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} I_{\mathrm{C}} \omega_{0}$.

When rotating around an edge, let the angular velocity be $\omega$. The angular momentum about the axis, i.e., the component of the angular momentum at a point on this axis in the direction of the edge, is $I \omega$.

Hence,

$$
\begin{gathered}
I \omega=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} I_{\mathrm{C}} \omega_{0} \\
\omega=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \frac{I_{\mathrm{C}}}{I} \omega_{0}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \frac{\frac{1}{6} m a^{2}}{\frac{2}{3} m a^{2}} \omega_{0}=\frac{1}{4 \sqrt{3}} \omega_{0}
\end{gathered}
$$

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: The rotational period of a binary star system with unequal masses \((M_{1} \neq M_{2})\) that are a distance \(L\) apart.
solution:
The distances from the center of mass to the stars \(l_{1}, l_{2}\) for the binary star system are as shown in Figure 6.11,

\[
l_{1}=\frac{M_{2}}{M_{1}+M_{2}} L, \quad l_{2}=\frac{M_{1}}{M_{1}+M_{2}} L
\]

Using the reference frame of the center of mass,

\[
\begin{gathered}
\frac{M_{1} v_{1}^{2}}{l_{1}}=G \frac{M_{1} M_{2}}{L^{2}} \\
v_{1}^{2}=\frac{G M_{2}}{L^{2}} l_{1}=\frac{G M_{2}}{L^{2}} \cdot \frac{M_{2}}{M_{1}+M_{2}} L=\frac{G M_{2}^{2}}{\left(M_{1}+M_{2}\right) L} \\
T=\frac{2 \pi l_{1}}{v_{1}}=2 \pi \frac{M_{2}}{M_{1}+M_{2}} L \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\left(M_{1}+M_{2}\right) L}{G M_{2}^{2}}}=2 \pi L \sqrt{\frac{L}{G\left(M_{1}+M_{2}\right)}}
\end{gathered}
\]

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: Find the threshold energy for a gamma ray to produce an electron-positron pair in interaction with a stationary electron.
solution:
According to problem 14.25 (1), the threshold energy for a gamma ray to produce an electron-positron pair in interaction with a stationary electron is

$$
E_{\gamma}^{\text{th}} = 2\left(1+\frac{m_{\mathrm{e}}}{m_{\mathrm{e}}}\right)m_{\mathrm{e}} = 4m_{\mathrm{e}} = 2.044 \, \mathrm{MeV}
$$

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: Consider the scenario where, as \( k \rightarrow 0 \), the wavelength of a neutron is much larger than the distance between nucleons in a hydrogen molecule. Neglecting the recoil effect, denote the coherent scattering amplitude caused by the two protons in the molecule as \( A_{2} \). Determine the ratio of the scattering cross-sections \(\sigma\) for orthohydrogen \((S=1)\) and parahydrogen \((S=0)\).
solution:
The coherent scattering amplitude \( A_{2} \) is given by

\[
A_{2} = -\frac{(3a_{\mathrm{t}} + a_{\mathrm{s}})}{2} - \frac{(a_{\mathrm{t}} - a_{\mathrm{s}}) \sigma_{\mathrm{n}} \cdot (\sigma_{1} + \sigma_{2})}{4} \tag{1}
\]

The total scattering cross-section is

\[
\frac{\sigma}{4\pi} = \frac{1}{2} \operatorname{Tr} (S_{2}^{+} S_{2}) = \frac{(3a_{\mathrm{t}} + a_{\mathrm{s}})^{2}}{4} + \frac{3(a_{\mathrm{t}} - a_{\mathrm{s}})^{2} S^{2}}{4}
\]

where \( S \) is the nuclear spin of the two protons in the hydrogen molecule, specifically

\[
\boldsymbol{S} = \frac{(\sigma_{1} + \sigma_{2})}{2}
\]

By measuring the scattering cross-sections of orthohydrogen \((S=1)\) and parahydrogen \((S=0)\), their relative signs can be determined. In practice, when ignoring the effect of the reduced mass, the scattering amplitude \( A_{2} \) leads to the ratio

\[
\frac{\sigma_{\text{ortho}}}{\sigma_{\text{para}}} = 1 + \frac{2(a_{\mathrm{t}} - a_{\mathrm{s}})^{2}}{(3a_{\mathrm{t}} + a_{\mathrm{s}})^{2}}
\]

subject: Quantum Mechanics
topic: Orbital and Spin Angular Momentum Problems
problem: Consider an electron in a uniform magnetic field along the $z$ direction. At time $t_0$, the electron's spin is measured to be along the positive $y$ axis. Find the expectation value of the polarization $2 S_z$ in the $z$ direction for $t > t_0$.
solution:
The Schrödinger equation for the spin state vector is

$$
\mathrm{i} \hbar \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t}\begin{pmatrix} a(t) \\ b(t) \end{pmatrix} = -\mu_e \boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \boldsymbol{B} \begin{pmatrix} a(t) \\ b(t) \end{pmatrix}
$$

where $\mu_e = \frac{|e| \hbar}{2 m_e c}$ is the electron's magnetic moment. The magnetic field $B$ is along the $z$ direction, so the equation becomes

$$
\mathrm{i} \hbar \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \begin{pmatrix} a(t) \\ b(t) \end{pmatrix} = -\mu_e B \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a(t) \\ b(t) \end{pmatrix}
$$

yielding the set of equations

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{i} \hbar \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} a(t) = -\mu_e B a(t), \\
& \mathrm{i} \hbar \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} b(t) = \mu_e B b(t).
\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& a(t) = a(t_{0}) \mathrm{e}^{\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\hbar} \mu_e B(t-t_0)}, \\
& b(t) = b(t_{0}) \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\hbar} \mu_e B(t-t_0)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the time $t_{0}$, the spin of the electron is along the positive $y$ direction, therefore

$$
S_y \begin{pmatrix} a(t_0) \\ b(t_0) \end{pmatrix} = \frac{\hbar}{2} \begin{pmatrix} a(t_0) \\ b(t_0) \end{pmatrix}.
$$

We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
-\mathrm{i} b(t_0) & = a(t_0), \\
\mathrm{i} a(t_0) & = b(t_0).
\end{aligned}
$$

By the normalization condition,

$$
|a(t_0)|^2 + |b(t_0)|^2 = 1.
$$

Solving gives

$$
a(t_0) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \quad b(t_0) = \frac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

For $t > t_0$, the polarization along the $z$ direction (actually the expectation value $\langle 2 S_z \rangle$) is

$$
\langle 2 S_z \rangle = \hbar \begin{pmatrix} a^*, b^* \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix} = \hbar (a^* a - b^* b) = 0.
$$

subject: Wave Optics
problem: A hologram is recorded using a planar reference wave with a wavelength of $\lambda_1$ incident normally. The object is located at a distance of $z_{1} = 10 \, \text{cm}$ from the film. The reconstructed wave has a wavelength of $\lambda_{2} = 10 \lambda_{1}$ and propagates along the $z$-axis. Find the transverse magnification during reconstruction. The scale of the hologram remains unchanged during both recording and reconstruction.
solution:
Using the conclusion from the previous problem. In this problem, the object point coordinates are $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1}\right)$, where $z_{1} = 10 \, \text{cm}$; the reference light source coordinates are $\left(x_{2}, y_{2}, z_{2}\right)$, where $z_{2} = \infty$; the reconstruction light source coordinates are $\left(x_{3}, y_{3}, z_{3}\right)$, where $z_{3} = \infty$. Substituting into equations (9), (10), and (11) from the previous problem, where $\zeta_{2} = \infty, \zeta_{3} = \infty$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
& z_{p} = \frac{1}{10} z_{1} \\
& x_{p} = x_{1}, \, y_{p} = y_{1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the transverse magnification is

$$
N = \frac{x_{p}}{x_{1}} = \frac{y_{p}}{y_{1}} = 1
$$

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: Consider the non-leptonic weak decays of hyperons $\Sigma^{+} \rightarrow \pi^{+} \mathrm{n}$, $\Sigma^{-} \rightarrow \pi^{-} \mathrm{n}$, and $\Sigma^{+} \rightarrow \pi^{0} \mathrm{p}$, which satisfy the $\Delta S=1$ condition and obey the $\Delta I=\frac{1}{2}$ rule. Determine the amplitude ratio $y$, where $y=\frac{A\left(\Sigma^{+} \rightarrow \pi^{+} \mathrm{n}\right)-A\left(\Sigma^{-} \rightarrow \pi^{-} \mathrm{n}\right)}{A\left(\Sigma^{+} \rightarrow \pi^{0} \mathrm{p}\right)}$.
solution:
For the non-leptonic decay of hyperons with $\Delta I=\frac{1}{2}$, introduce a "pseudo-particle" with $\left(I=\frac{1}{2}, I_{3}=\frac{1}{2}\right)$. In the isospin coupling representation, the hyperon and pseudo-particle couple together, and using the orthogonality of isospin wave functions, we determine the transition amplitude $A$. The coupling of the hyperon and pseudo-particle is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \left|\Sigma^{-} \mathrm{a}\right\rangle=\left|1,-1, \frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}\right\rangle=\left|\frac{3}{2},-\frac{3}{2}\right\rangle \\
& \left|\Sigma^{+} \mathrm{a}\right\rangle=\left|1,1, \frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}\right\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\left|\frac{3}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right\rangle+\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\left|\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right\rangle 
\end{aligned}
\]

Similarly, the wave function of the final state in the isospin representation is written as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
& \left|\pi^{+} \mathrm{n}\right\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\left|\frac{3}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right\rangle+\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\left|\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right\rangle \\
& \left|\pi^{-} \mathrm{n}\right\rangle=\left|\frac{3}{2},-\frac{3}{2}\right\rangle \\
& \left|\pi^{0} \mathrm{p}\right\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\left|\frac{3}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right\rangle-\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\left|\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right\rangle 
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus, we can derive that:
\[ A_{3}\left(\Sigma^{-} \rightarrow \pi^{-} \mathrm{n}\right)=M_{3/2} \quad \text{where } M_{3/2}=\left\langle\frac{3}{2}\right| H_{\omega}\left|\frac{3}{2}\right\rangle \]

\[ A_{4}\left(\Sigma^{+} \rightarrow \pi^{0} \mathrm{p}\right)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\left(M_{3/2}-M_{1/2}\right) \]

\[ A_{5}\left(\Sigma^{+} \rightarrow \pi^{+} \mathrm{n}\right)=\frac{1}{3}\left(M_{3/2}+2 M_{1/2}\right) \]

We obtain the value of $y$:

\[ y=\frac{A_{5}-A_{3}}{A_{4}}=\frac{M_{3/2}+2 M_{1/2}-3 M_{3/2}}{\sqrt{2}\left(M_{3/2}-M_{1/2}\right)}=-\sqrt{2} \]

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: A particle with mass \( m \), charge \( e \), and momentum \( P \) is scattered in an electrostatic potential field produced by a spherically symmetric charge distribution, where \(\rho(r) \mathrm{d}^{3} x\) is the charge within the volume element \(\mathrm{d}^{3} x\). Assume that \(\rho\) quickly approaches zero as \(r \rightarrow \infty\), and that \(\int \mathrm{d}^{3} x \rho=0\) and \(\int \mathrm{d}^{3} x r^{2} \rho(r)=A\), where \( A \) is a known constant. Calculate the differential scattering cross-section for forward scattering \(\left.\frac{\mathrm{d} \sigma}{\mathrm{d} \Omega}\right|_{\theta=0}\) using the first-order Born approximation, where \(\theta\) is the scattering angle.
solution:
Using the Born approximation, we have

\[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \sigma}{\mathrm{~d} \Omega}=\frac{m^{2} e^{2}}{4 \pi^{2} \hbar^{4}}\left|\int U(r) \exp (\mathrm{i} q \cdot r) \mathrm{d}^{3} x\right|^{2}
\]

where \( q=k-k^{\prime}, q=2 k \sin \frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{2 P}{\hbar} \sin \frac{\theta}{2} \).

\(U(r)\) is the electrostatic Coulomb potential, satisfying Poisson's equation

\[
\Delta U=-4 \pi \rho(r)
\]

Taking the Fourier transform

\[
F(q) \equiv \int \rho(r) \exp (\mathrm{i} \boldsymbol{q} \cdot \boldsymbol{r}) \mathrm{d}^{3} x
\]

we have

\[
\int U(r) \exp (\mathrm{i} q \cdot r) \mathrm{d}^{3} x=\frac{4 \pi}{q^{2}} F(q)
\]

thus

\[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \sigma}{\mathrm{~d} \Omega}=\frac{m^{2} e^{2}}{4 \pi^{2} \hbar^{4}} \cdot \frac{(4 \pi)^{2}}{q^{4}}|F(q)|^{2}=\frac{4 m^{2} e^{2}}{\hbar^{4} q^{4}}|F(q)|^{2}
\]

For forward scattering, \( \theta \) is very small, \( q \) is very small, thus

\[
\begin{aligned}
F(q) & =\int \rho(r) \exp (\mathrm{i} q \cdot r) \mathrm{d}^{3} x=\int \rho(r)\left[1+\mathrm{i} q \cdot \boldsymbol{r}+\frac{1}{2!}(\mathrm{i} q \cdot r)^{2}+\cdots\right] \mathrm{d}^{3} x \\
& =\int \rho(r) \mathrm{d}^{3} x-\frac{1}{2!} \int \rho(r)(\boldsymbol{q} \cdot \boldsymbol{r})^{2} \mathrm{~d}^{3} x \\
& =-\frac{1}{6} q^{2} \int \rho(r) r^{2} \mathrm{~d}^{3} x=-\frac{A q^{2}}{6} \\
\left.\frac{\mathrm{~d} \sigma}{\mathrm{~d} \Omega}\right|_{\theta=0} & =\frac{A^{2} m^{2} e^{2}}{9 \hbar^{4}}
\end{aligned}
\]

subject: Solid-State Physics
problem: (2) Derive the expression for the packing density of the hexagonal close-packed structure.
solution:
(2) The packing density of a crystal is defined as the ratio of the maximum volume occupied by rigid atomic spheres in a unit cell to the volume of the unit cell. Figure 1.1.15 depicts a unit cell of a hexagonal close-packed crystal, composed of \(A, B, C, D, A', B', C', D'\) (where \(A, B, C, D\) and \(A', B', C', D'\) are the atoms in the first and third layers, respectively). The three primitive vectors of the unit cell are \(DA, DC\), and \(DD'\), labeled as \(a, b\), and \(c\). They are given by

\[
a = ai, \quad b = -\frac{1}{2} ai + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} aj, \quad c = ck
\]

where \(\boldsymbol{i}, \boldsymbol{j}, \boldsymbol{k}\) are the unit vectors in the \(x, y, z\) directions, respectively. The volume of the unit cell is

\[
\Omega = |a \cdot (b \times c)| = |b \cdot (a \times c)| = \left\lvert \left(-\frac{1}{2} ai + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} aj\right) \cdot acj \right\rvert = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} a^2 c
\]

There are two atoms in a unit cell of the hexagonal close-packed structure. Assuming the radius of the atomic sphere is \(a / 2\), the packing density of the hexagonal close-packed crystal is

\[
D = \frac{2 \times \frac{4}{3} \pi \left(\frac{a}{2}\right)^{3}}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} a^2 c} = \frac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{6}
\]

subject: Wave Optics
problem: Optical apodization is a method of enhancing the resolution capability of an optical system by altering the diffraction aperture function of the system, thereby changing the energy distribution of the diffraction pattern of the image spot. If the amplitude transmittance across the slit from $-\frac{b}{2}$ to $+\frac{b}{2}$ is modulated by the cosine function $\cos \pi \frac{x}{b}$, where $b$ is the width of the slit, determine the intensity of light at the midpoint between the ($n-1$)-th and the $n$-th minima in the diffraction pattern (close to the $n$-th secondary maximum). Normalize the calculation result to the central maximum.
solution:
After apodization, the angular position of the ($n-1$)-th minimum is given by $\sin \theta_{n-1} = \frac{\lambda}{2b}(2n - 1)$. The angular position of the $n$-th minimum is $\sin \theta_{n} = \frac{\lambda}{2b}(2n + 1)$. The midpoint between these positions is at $\sin \theta = \frac{n \lambda}{b}$, and its light intensity is

$$
I = A^{2} = \frac{4}{\left(\frac{\pi}{b}\right)^{2}\left(1 - 4n^{2}\right)^{2}}.
$$

The position of the central maximum is at $\sin \theta = 0$, therefore,

$$
I_{0} = \frac{4}{\left(\frac{\pi}{b}\right)^{2}}.
$$

Thus,

$$
\frac{I}{I_{0}} = \left(\frac{1}{1 - 4n^{2}}\right)^{2}.
$$

The above result indicates that apodization (see Figure 2) fundamentally reduces the value of the secondary maxima relative to the central maximum. In other words, apodization suppresses higher spatial frequencies. Using the above principle, it may be possible to apodize the aperture diaphragm of a telescope, thereby significantly reducing the relative intensity of the diffraction rings surrounding the images of multiple stars. This, in turn, will enhance the telescope's ability to resolve the image of a faint star close to a bright star.

subject: Semiconductor Physics
problem: At room temperature, \(\frac{k_{\mathrm{B}} T}{e} = 26 \, \mathrm{mV}\). A cadmium sulfide sample has a mobile carrier density of \(10^{16} \, \mathrm{cm}^{-3}\) and a mobility of \(\mu = 10^{2} \, \mathrm{cm}^{2} / \mathrm{V} \cdot \mathrm{s}\). The carriers continuously get trapped in immobile states and are then thermally excited back to mobile states. If the average free time in the mobile state is \(t = 10^{-5} \, \mathrm{s}\), what is the root mean square distance of diffusion of the carriers between two successive traps?
solution:
According to the equipartition theorem

\[
\frac{1}{2} m v_{x}^{2} = \frac{1}{2} m v_{y}^{2} = \frac{1}{2} m v_{z}^{2} = \frac{1}{2} k_{\mathrm{B}} T
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} = \frac{3}{2} k_{\mathrm{B}} T, \quad v^{2} = \frac{3 k_{\mathrm{B}} T}{m}
\]

Hence, the root mean square distance of diffusion of the carriers between two successive traps is

\[
\begin{aligned}
l &= \sqrt{v^{2}} \cdot t = \sqrt{\frac{3 k_{\mathrm{B}} T}{m}} \cdot t = \sqrt{3 \left(\frac{k_{\mathrm{B}} T}{e}\right) \frac{e}{m}} \cdot t \\
&= \sqrt{3 \times 26 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.76 \times 10^{11}} \times 10^{-5} \\
&= 1.17 \, (\mathrm{m}) = 117 \, (\mathrm{cm})
\end{aligned}
\]

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: A neutral $\pi^0$ meson decays into two $\gamma$ photons. Assume the energy of the $\pi^0$ meson is $E = 1000 \ \mathrm{MeV}$, and its mass $m_\pi = 135 \ \mathrm{MeV}$. If the two $\gamma$ photons are emitted at the same angle relative to the original direction, find the energy of the $\gamma$ rays.
solution:
Assume the angles between the two $\gamma$ photons and the $\pi^0$ are $\theta$ and $-\theta$, respectively. From conservation laws, we have:

$$
E = 2E_{\gamma}, \quad p_\pi = 2p_{\gamma} \cos \theta
$$

Noting the symmetry, the two $\gamma$ photons have the same momentum and energy $E_{\gamma}, p_{\gamma}$. By combining the two equations, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_\pi^2 &= 4E_{\gamma}^2(1 - \cos^2 \theta) = E^2 \sin^2 \theta, \\
\theta &= \pm \arcsin\left(\frac{m_\pi}{E}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the angle between the two photons is:

$$
\theta_{2\gamma} = 2\theta = 2 \arcsin\left(\frac{135}{1000}\right) \approx 15.5^\circ
$$

subject: Statistical Mechanics
problem: Electrons in the energy band of an ideal crystal. The relationship between the electron's energy and momentum is isotropic, but not parabolic, and is given by $\varepsilon(k)=\sqrt{a+b k^{2}}$, where $\varepsilon$ and $k$ are the electron's energy and wave number, respectively, and $a$ and $b$ are two numerical factors. At $T \approx 0 \mathrm{~K}$, the conduction band and valence band are separated at $k=0$ by an energy gap $E_{\mathrm{g}}=2 \sqrt{a}$. Assuming the conduction and valence bands have mirror symmetric dispersion relations, photons with energy $2 E_{\mathrm{g}}$ can induce direct optical transitions between bands. Calculate the $k$ value corresponding to this transition.
solution:
The wave number corresponding to the optical transition is $k_{\mathrm{p}}$. The bottom of the conduction band and the top of the valence band are both located at wave number $k=0$, with an energy gap $E_{\mathrm{g}}=2 \sqrt{a}$ between them. The energy of the photon inducing the interband optical transition is $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{p}}=2 E_{\mathrm{g}}=4 \sqrt{a}$. The electron energy is given by $\varepsilon=\sqrt{a+b k^{2}}$. By equating the photon energy to twice the electron energy $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{p}}=2 \varepsilon$, we can find the wave number $k_{\mathrm{p}}$ as:

\[
k_{\mathrm{p}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 a}{b}} 
\]

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: In the momentum representation, find the bound state energy levels of the delta potential well \( V(x) = -V_{0} \delta(x) \).
solution:
For the delta potential well in the momentum representation, the energy level equation is

\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{p^{2} - 2mE} = \frac{\pi \hbar}{m V_{0}}
\]

Combined with

\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{p^{2} + \hbar^{2} k^{2}} = \frac{\pi}{\hbar k}
\]

we substitute \( k = \frac{m V_{0}}{\hbar^{2}} \) into the equation, which gives

\[
E = -\frac{\hbar^{2} k^{2}}{2m} = -\frac{m V_{0}^{2}}{2 \hbar^{2}}
\]

subject: Quantum Mechanics
topic: Orbital and Spin Angular Momentum Problems
problem:
A spinless particle has a wave function given by

$$
\psi=K(x+y+2z) \mathrm{e}^{-ar}
$$

where $r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}$ and $K, a$ are real constants. What is the expectation value of the z-component of the angular momentum?
solution:
Express the wave function in spherical coordinates

$$
\psi=K r(\cos \phi \sin \theta+\sin \phi \sin \theta+2 \cos \theta) \mathrm{e}^{-ar}
$$

After normalization, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
K^{\prime}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{8 \pi}} \\
\psi(\theta, \phi)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{8 \pi}}\left[-\frac{1}{2}(1-\mathrm{i}) \sqrt{\frac{8 \pi}{3}} Y_{11}+\frac{1}{2}(1+\mathrm{i}) \sqrt{\frac{8 \pi}{3}} Y_{1-1}+2 \sqrt{\frac{4 \pi}{3}} Y_{10}\right]
\end{gathered}
$$

The expectation value of the z-component of the angular momentum is $\left\langle L_{z}\right\rangle=\frac{1}{8 \pi}\left[\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{8 \pi}{3}(+\hbar)+\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{8 \pi}{3}(-\hbar)\right]=0$.

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: Protons with energy of 60 MeV are used to bombard a ${ }^{54}\mathrm{Fe}$ target in an inelastic scattering experiment. If the differential inelastic scattering cross-section is given by \(\frac{\mathrm{d} \sigma}{\mathrm{d} \Omega} = 1.3 \times 10^{-31} \, \text{m}^2 \cdot \text{sr}^{-1}\), and the current intensity of the incident proton beam is \(10^{-7} \, \mathrm{A}\), determine the number of recorded events per second.
solution:
The number of particles recorded per second is given by

\[
\Delta N = N \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d} \sigma}{\mathrm{d} \Omega} \cdot \Delta \Omega \cdot I
\]

Substituting the given values, we obtain

\[
\Delta N = \frac{6.02}{54 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \times 10^{25} \times 1.3 \times 10^{-31} \times 10^{-3} \times 10^{-7} = 90.6 \, (\text{s}^{-1})
\]

Thus, 90.6 events can be detected per second.

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated by a voltage of \(10000 \ \text{V}\).
solution: \(\lambda_{e} = \frac{h}{p_{e}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m_{e} E}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m_{e} e V}} \approx 0.12 \times 10^{-10} \ \text{m} = 0.12 \ \text{Å}\). This indicates that the de Broglie wavelength of the electron is comparable to the atomic spacing in a crystal, thus allowing the electron diffraction experiment with crystals to reveal the electron's wavelength.

subject: Solid-State Physics
problem: Given that the bulk modulus of NaCl crystal is \(2.4 \times 10^{10} \, \mathrm{Pa}\), by what percentage will the distance between adjacent ions in the crystal decrease under a pressure of 20,000 atmospheres? It is known that \(1 \, \mathrm{atm} = 10^{5} \, \mathrm{Pa}\).
solution:
From problem solution 1.1.35, we know that under a pressure \(P\), the volume of the NaCl crystal will change to \(V\), which is related to the original equilibrium volume \(V_{0}\) by the equation

\[
P = -K \ln \frac{V}{V_{0}}
\]

where \(K\) is the elastic modulus of the NaCl crystal.

\[
\frac{V}{V_{0}} = \left(\frac{r}{r_{0}}\right)^{3}
\]

Here, \(r\) is the distance between adjacent ions, and \(r_{0}\) is the equilibrium distance. Therefore, we have

\[
P = -K \ln \frac{V}{V_{0}} = -K \ln \left(\frac{r}{r_{0}}\right)^{3}
\]

Thus,

\[
\frac{r}{r_{0}} = \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{P}{3K}} = \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{2 \times 10^{4} \times 10^{5}}{3 \times 2.4 \times 10^{10}}} = 0.9726
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{r_{0} - r}{r_{0}} = 1 - \frac{r}{r_{0}} = 1 - 0.9726 = 0.0274 = 2.74\%
\]

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: Fast neutrons can be detected by observing the fluorescence produced by recoil protons in a scintillator. Suppose there is a scintillator with a thickness of 5 cm, where the number density of carbon atoms and hydrogen atoms are the same, each being $4 \times 10^{22}$ atoms/cm$^{3}$. Assume $\sigma_{\text{H}}=1.5$ b, $\sigma_{\text{C}}=1.0$ b, and $1$ b $=10^{-24}$ cm$^{2}$. What portion of incident neutrons with an energy of about 5 MeV will produce recoil protons?
solution:
The fraction of neutrons interacting with the material is $\eta^{\prime}=1-\eta=39.5 \%$, where only interactions with hydrogen result in recoil protons. Therefore, the fraction of neutrons producing recoil protons is

$$
\eta^{\prime \prime}=\eta^{\prime} \frac{\sigma_{\text{H}}}{\sigma_{\text{H}}+\sigma_{\text{C}}}=\eta^{\prime} \cdot \frac{1.5}{1.5+1.0}=\frac{3}{5} \eta^{\prime}=23.7 \%
$$

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: There is a very simple "bag" model concerning elementary particles, which describes mesons as quark-antiquark states confined within an elastic bag. The bag is spherical with a variable radius $R$, and a surface tension coefficient $\sigma = 50 \, \mathrm{MeV} / (\mathrm{fm})^{2}$. Both quark and antiquark are treated as non-relativistic particles, with a rest mass of $200 \, \mathrm{MeV} / \mathrm{c}^{2}$, and their interactions are neglected. Allow $R$ to vary and calculate the ground state "bag" radius, then compare it with the accepted size of mesons.
solution:
When $R$ can vary, the surface energy of the elastic bag should also be considered:

$$
E_{\sigma}(R) = 4 \sigma \pi R^{2}
$$

The value of $R$ should make $E_{0}(R) + E_{\sigma}(R)$ minimal. From the condition of extremum:

$$
\frac{\partial \left(E_{0}(R) + E_{\sigma}(R)\right)}{\partial R} = 0
$$

we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}
R & = \left(\frac{\pi \hbar^{2}}{4 m \sigma}\right)^{1/4} = \left(\frac{\pi \hbar^{2} c^{2}}{4 m c^{2} \sigma}\right)^{1/4} \\
& = \left(\frac{\pi}{4} \cdot \frac{(197 \, \mathrm{MeV} \cdot \mathrm{fm})^{2}}{200 \, \mathrm{MeV} \times 50 \, \mathrm{MeV} \cdot (\mathrm{fm})^{-2}}\right)^{1/4} = 1.3 \, \mathrm{fm}
\end{aligned}
$$

This is precisely the order of magnitude of the accepted size of elementary particles.

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: Calculate the relative change in kinetic energy of an \(\alpha\) particle during a \(180^{\circ}\) scattering by a \({ }^{16} \mathrm{O}\) nucleus under non-relativistic conditions.
solution:
Let the kinetic energy and momentum of the \(\alpha\) particle before and after scattering be \(E, p\) and \(E^{\prime}, p^{\prime}\), respectively. Let the masses of the \(\alpha\) particle and \({ }^{16} \mathrm{O}\) be \(m_{\alpha}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{O}}\), respectively. Under non-relativistic conditions, we have

\[
p=\sqrt{2 m_{\alpha} E}, \quad p^{\prime}=\sqrt{2 m_{\alpha} E^{\prime}}
\]

Let the recoil momentum of \({ }^{16} \mathrm{O}\) be \(p_{\mathrm{O}}\). From the conservation of momentum and energy, we get

\[
\begin{aligned}
p_{\mathrm{O}} & = p + p^{\prime} = \sqrt{2 m_{\alpha} E} + \sqrt{2 m_{\alpha} E^{\prime}} \\
E & = E^{\prime} + \frac{\left(\sqrt{2 m_{\alpha} E} + \sqrt{2 m_{\alpha} E^{\prime}}\right)^{2}}{2 M_{\mathrm{O}}}
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(M_{\mathrm{O}} \approx 4 m_{\alpha}\), we obtain

\[
E = E^{\prime} + \frac{1}{4}\left(\sqrt{E} + \sqrt{E^{\prime}}\right)^{2}=\frac{5}{4} E^{\prime} + \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{E E^{\prime}} + \frac{1}{4} E
\]

\[
\left(5 \sqrt{E^{\prime}} - 3 \sqrt{E}\right)\left(\sqrt{E^{\prime}} + \sqrt{E}\right) = 0
\]

Thus,

\[
5 \sqrt{E^{\prime}} - 3 \sqrt{E} = 0
\]

which gives

\[
E^{\prime} = \frac{9}{25} E
\]

The relative change in kinetic energy of the \(\alpha\) particle is

\[
\frac{E^{\prime} - E}{E} = -\frac{16}{25}
\]

subject: Classical Electromagnetism
problem: There is a closely wound detection coil with a cross-sectional area of \(4 \ \mathrm{cm}^{2}\), 160 turns, and a resistance of \(50 \ \Omega\). The coil is connected to a ballistic galvanometer with an internal resistance of \(30 \ \Omega\). When the coil is quickly rotated from a position parallel to (the normal to the section) a uniform magnetic field to a perpendicular position, the galvanometer reads \(4 \times 10^{-5} \ \mathrm{C}\). What is the magnetic flux of the magnetic field?
solution:
During a short time \(\Delta t\), the coil moves from a position parallel to the magnetic field to a perpendicular one, and because \(\Delta t\) is very short, we have:

\[
\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta \phi}{\Delta t} = i(R+r)
\]

Since \(q = i \Delta t\), the total change in magnetic flux is:

\[
\Delta \phi = q(R+r) = B A N
\]

Thus, the magnetic flux density is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
B & = \frac{(R+r) q}{A N} = \frac{(50+30) \times \left(4 \times 10^{-5}\right)}{4 \times 10^{-4} \times 160} \\
& = 0.05 \ (\mathrm{T})
\end{aligned}
\]

subject: Theoretical Mechanics
problem: Two particles with masses \( m_{1} \) and \( m_{2} \) are connected by an inextensible light string of length \( l \) that passes through a smooth small hole on a frictionless horizontal surface. \( m_{1} \) moves on the horizontal surface, while \( m_{2} \) moves vertically. If \( m_{2} \) is slightly displaced from its vertical equilibrium position, it will cause small oscillations. Use Lagrange's equation to find the period of the oscillation.
solution:
Let the polar coordinates \( r, \varphi \) of \( m_{1} \) relative to the small hole (as the origin of the coordinate system) be the generalized coordinates,

\[
L=\frac{1}{2} m_{1}\left(\dot{r}^{2}+r^{2} \dot{\varphi}^{2}\right)+\frac{1}{2} m_{2} \dot{r}^{2}+m_{2} g(l-r)
\]

From \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{r}}\right)-\frac{\partial L}{\partial r}=0\), we obtain

\[
(m_{1}+m_{2}) \ddot{r}-m_{1} r \dot{\varphi}^{2}+m_{2} g=0 \quad \tag{1}
\]

From \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \varphi}=0, \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\varphi}}\right)=0\),

\[
m_{1} r^{2} \dot{\varphi}=m_{1}(l-d) v_{0}=m_{1} \sqrt{\frac{m_{2} g}{m_{1}}}(l-d)^{3/2} \quad \tag{2}
\]

Substituting equation (2) into equation (1),

\[
(m_{1}+m_{2}) \ddot{r}-\frac{m_{2} g(l-d)^{3}}{r^{3}}+m_{2} g=0 \quad \tag{3}
\]

Equilibrium position:

\[
r=r_{0}=l-d
\]

Let

\[
x=r-r_{0}=r-(l-d)
\]

\( m_{2} \) undergoes small oscillations near the equilibrium position, and \( m_{1} \)'s radial movement near \( r=r_{0} \) also executes small oscillations,

\[
\left[\frac{(l-d)}{r}\right]^{3}=\left(\frac{l-d}{l-d+x}\right)^{3}=\left(1+\frac{x}{l-d}\right)^{-3} \approx 1-\frac{3x}{l-d}
\]

Using this approximation, equation (3) approximates to

\[
(m_{1}+m_{2}) \ddot{x}+\frac{3 m_{2} g}{l-d} x=0
\]

The angular frequency \(\omega\) and the period \(T\) of the small oscillations are

\[
\begin{gathered}
\omega=\sqrt{\frac{3 m_{2} g}{(m_{1}+m_{2})(l-d)}} \\
T=\frac{2 \pi}{\omega}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{(m_{1}+m_{2})(l-d)}{3 m_{2} g}}
\end{gathered}
\]

subject: Classical Electromagnetism
problem:
A pulse generator with negligible internal resistance emits a pulse

\[ v_{\mathrm{in}} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1, & 0 \leq t < 5 \, \mu \mathrm{s} \\ 0, & t < 0, \, t > 5 \, \mu \mathrm{s} \end{array} \right. \]

through a coaxial cable with a characteristic impedance of \(20 \, \Omega\) (lossless). The cable length is equivalent to a delay of \(1 \, \mu \mathrm{s}\), and the other end of the cable is open-circuited. Calculate the terminal reflection coefficient \(K_{\text{terminal}}\).
solution:
The cable's internal resistance \(Z_{\mathrm{c}} = 20 \, \Omega\), and the load resistance \(Z_{\mathrm{L}} = \infty\).

The terminal reflection coefficient is given by

\[ K_{\text{terminal}} = \frac{Z_{\mathrm{L}} - Z_{\mathrm{c}}}{Z_{\mathrm{L}} + Z_{\mathrm{c}}} = 1 \]

subject: Semiconductor Physics
problem: A method for measuring the lifetime of multiply ionized atomic states is by using a laser tuned to the resonance wavelength of the ions under study, to excite a given ion beam and measure the change in intensity with distance. When a specific ion beam with a resonance wavelength of \(4885 \, \text{Å}\) is excited by a chlorine-ion laser with a wavelength of \(4880 \, \text{Å}\), the intensity drops to half of the original at a distance of 10 mm from the excitation point. The ion beam velocity is \(v / c = 5 \times 10^{-3}\). Calculate the lifetime of the ion's excited state.
solution:
The radiation intensity decreases exponentially as \(\mathrm{e}^{-t / \tau}\), that is

\[
\frac{1}{2} = \mathrm{e}^{-t / \tau}, \quad \tau = t / \ln 2
\]

\(t\) should be taken in proper time, hence

\[
t = \frac{d / v}{\gamma}
\]

Therefore, the lifetime \(\tau\) of the excited state is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau & = \frac{d}{v \gamma \ln 2} = \frac{\sqrt{1-(5 \times 10^{-3})^{2}} \times 10 \times 10^{-3}}{5 \times 10^{-3} \times 3 \times 10^{8} \times \ln 2} \\
& \approx 9.6 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{s}
\end{aligned}
\]

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: A unit mass object moves in a central force field, and its trajectory is given by $r=a \mathrm{e}^{-b \varphi}$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. At time $t=0$, the object is located at a distance $a$ from the force center, with a radial velocity of $k$. Find the potential energy of the central force.
solution:
Given $r = a \mathrm{e}^{-b \varphi}$, we have $u = \frac{1}{a} \mathrm{e}^{b \varphi}$.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{\mathrm{~d} \varphi} = \frac{b}{a} \mathrm{e}^{b \varphi}, \quad \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 u}{\mathrm{~d} \varphi^2} = \frac{b^2}{a} \mathrm{e}^{b \varphi} = b^2 u
$$

At $t=0$, $\dot{r} = k$, and $\dot{r} = -a b \mathrm{e}^{-b \varphi} \dot{\varphi}$. Substituting $r = a$ into $r = a \mathrm{e}^{-b \varphi}$, we find that $\varphi = 0$ at this moment.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot{r} & = -a b \dot{\varphi} = k, \quad a \dot{\varphi} = -\frac{k}{b} \\
h & = a^2 \dot{\varphi} = -\frac{k a}{b} \\
F & = -m h^2 u^2 \left( \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 u}{\mathrm{~d} \varphi^2} + u \right) \\
& = -1 \cdot \left(-\frac{k a}{b}\right)^2 u^2 \left(b^2 u + u\right) = -\frac{k^2 a^2 (b^2 + 1)}{b^2 r^3} \\
V(r) & = -\int_{\infty}^{r} F(r) \mathrm{d} r = \frac{k^2 a^2 (b^2 + 1)}{b^2} \int_{\infty}^{r} \frac{1}{r^3} \mathrm{~d} r \\
& = -\frac{k^2 a^2 (b^2 + 1)}{2 b^2 r^2} \quad \text{(taking } \infty \text{ as the zero point of potential energy).}
\end{aligned}
$$

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: A neutron with a rest mass of \(940 \mathrm{MeV}/c^{2}\) and a half-life of 13 minutes is 5000 light-years away from Earth. How much energy does this neutron need to reach Earth by the end of its first half-life?
solution:
Let the energy of the neutron be \(E\), the speed be \(\beta\), and the half-life of the stationary neutron be \(T_{1/2}\). In the Earth's reference frame, the half-life is \(\gamma T_{1/2}\). If the neutron is to reach Earth within this period, the distance it must travel is:  
\[ l = \beta \gamma c T_{1/2} = 5000 \times 365 \times 24 \times 60 \times c \]  

Therefore, \(\beta \gamma\) is:  
\[ \beta \gamma = \frac{l}{T_{1/2} c} = 2.02 \times 10^{8} \]  

The corresponding energy of the neutron is:  
\[ E = \sqrt{p^{2} + m_{0}^{2}} = m_{0} \sqrt{1 + \beta^{2} \gamma^{2}} = 1.9 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{MeV} \]

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: A neutral $\pi^{0}$ meson decays into two $\gamma$ photons ($\pi^{0} \rightarrow \gamma+\gamma$), and $\pi^{0}$ can be produced by the reaction $\pi^{-}+p \rightarrow \pi^{0}+n$. The masses of the particles are $m_{\pi^{-}} = 140 \, \mathrm{MeV}$, $m_{\pi^{0}} = 135 \, \mathrm{MeV}$, $m_{\mathrm{p}} = 938 \, \mathrm{MeV}$, and $m_{\mathrm{n}} = 940 \, \mathrm{MeV}$. If both $p$ and $\pi^{-}$ are at rest before the reaction, what is the speed of the outgoing $\pi^{0}$?

subject: Relativity
problem:
A photon collides with a stationary target proton resulting in the following reaction:

$$
\gamma+\mathrm{p} \rightarrow \mathrm{p}+\psi^{\prime}
$$

The rest mass of the particle is approximately $4M_p$, where $M_p$ is the rest mass of the proton. Find the minimum energy $E_{0}$ that the photon must have in the laboratory reference frame to produce the above reaction (expressed in units of $M_{\mathrm{p}} c^{2}$).
solution:
When the photon's energy is precisely the threshold energy $E_{0}$, its momentum $p=\frac{E_{0}}{c}$. In the reaction producing the $\psi^{\prime}$ particle upon collision with a stationary proton, in the center of momentum frame, the proton and the $\psi^{\prime}$ particle are at rest (in the laboratory reference frame, due to the conservation of momentum, they cannot both be at rest).

From the invariant $E^{2}-c^{2} p^{2}$ under Lorentz transformation and the conservation of the isolated system, considering the laboratory reference frame before the reaction, this conserved quantity is $\left(E_{0}+M_{\mathrm{p}} c^{2}\right)^{2}-c^{2} p^{2}=\left(E_{0}+M_{\mathrm{p}} c^{2}\right)^{2}-E_{0}^{2}$ (using the system's momentum $p$ equal to the photon's momentum $\frac{E_{0}}{c}$).

After the reaction, considering the center of momentum frame, this conserved quantity is $\left(4 M_{\mathrm{p}} c^{2}+M_{\mathrm{p}} c^{2}\right)^{2}=25\left(M_{\mathrm{p}} c^{2}\right)^{2}$.

Solve:

$$
\left(E_{0}+M_{\mathrm{p}} c^{2}\right)^{2}-E_{0}^{2}=25\left(M_{\mathrm{p}} c^{2}\right)^{2}
$$

Get:

$$
E_{0}=12 M_{\mathrm{p}} c^{2}
$$

Explanation: In the center of momentum frame, the system's momentum is zero. If the two particles are not at rest, obviously in the center of mass frame, the above conservation quantity would be greater than $25\left(M_{\mathrm{p}} c^{2}\right)^{2}$, thus the incident photon's energy $E$ would be greater than $E_{0}$, so $E_{0}$ is indeed the threshold energy.

subject: Wave Optics
problem: A camera sensitive to visible light (with a focal length of 50 cm) is focused clearly on a star, and then, without refocusing, it photographs an object located at 100 meters. Given that the aperture of this camera is $D$, use the relationship of similar triangles to calculate the diameter $d$ of the light spot formed on the film from a luminous point on the optical axis. What should the aperture $D$ be approximately to ensure the highest resolution for the object? Express $D$ in centimeters.

subject: Electrodynamics
problem: An electron with mass $m$ and charge $e$ is moving in the plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. Ignoring the energy loss due to radiation, the electron's path is a circle with radius $R$. Assume the electron's energy $E \gg m c^{2}$, thus considering relativistic effects. Provide the analytical expression for the required field strength $B$ using the above parameters. Given $R = 30 \mathrm{~m}$, $E = 2.5 \times 10^{9} \mathrm{eV}$, calculate the numerical value of $B$.
solution:
In a uniform magnetic field $\boldsymbol{B}$, the equation of motion for a relativistic electron is

\[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{P}}{\mathrm{~d} t}=e \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{B} \tag{1}
\]

where $\boldsymbol{P}=m \gamma \boldsymbol{v}, \gamma=\left(1-\frac{v^{2}}{c^{2}}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. Since the electron is undergoing circular motion, the speed remains constant, which means $v$ is a constant, and we have

\[
\left|\frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{~d} t}\right|=\frac{v^{2}}{R} \tag{2}
\]

Combining equation (1) and equation (2), we get

\[
B=\frac{P}{e R} \tag{3}
\]

When $E \gg m c^{2}$, $P=\frac{1}{c} \sqrt{E^{2}-m^{2} c^{4}} \approx \frac{E}{c}$, thus

\[
B \approx \frac{1}{c} \cdot \frac{E}{e R} \approx 0.28 (\mathrm{~T}) \tag{4}
\]

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: A ground state hydrogen atom undergoes beta decay and becomes $\mathrm{He}^{+}$. What is the probability of it being in the 2P state?
solution:
By the continuity of the wave function, at the instant of beta decay, it requires:

$$
|1\mathrm{S}\rangle_{\mathrm{H}} = \cdots + a_{3}|2\mathrm{P}\rangle_{\mathrm{He}^{+}} + \cdots 
$$

Where

$$
R_{21} = \left(\frac{Z}{2a}\right)^{3/2} \frac{Z}{\sqrt{3}a} \exp\left(-\frac{Zr}{2a}\right)
$$

Calculate $a_{3}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{3} = & \langle 2\mathrm{P} \mid 1\mathrm{S}\rangle_{\mathrm{H}} = \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{2}{a^{3/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{r}{a}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{6}}\left(\frac{2}{a}\right)^{3/2} \frac{2r}{a} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{r}{a}\right) \cdot r^{2} \mathrm{d}r \int Y_{10} Y_{00} \mathrm{d} \Omega = 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the probability of $\mathrm{He}^{+}$ being in the 2P state is:

$$
W(2\mathrm{P}) = \left|a_{3}\right|^{2} = 0
$$

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: In a one-dimensional infinite deep square potential well containing 3 electrons, at a temperature of $T=0 \mathrm{~K}$ and under the approximation where the Coulomb energy between electrons can be neglected, the average energy of the 3 electrons is $E=12.4 \mathrm{eV}$. Find the value of the energy level $E_1$.
solution:
The energy level $E_{n} = n^{2} E_{1}$. According to the Pauli exclusion principle and the principle of lowest energy, for the 3 electrons in the well, there are 2 electrons at energy level $E_{1}$ and 1 electron at energy level $E_{2}$. Therefore:

$$
12.4 \times 3 = 2 E_{1} + 4 E_{1}, \quad E_{1} = 6.2 \mathrm{eV}
$$

subject: Wave Optics
problem: In a single-wavelength Young's double-slit experiment, a glass plate is placed in one of the optical paths. This glass has a refractive index of $n$ and a thickness of $t$. One slit is twice as wide as the other. When $t$ takes a certain value, the light intensity at the center of the screen is minimized. Find the value of $t$. Assume that when $t=0$, the intensity at the center is $I$. Ignore the absorption of the glass.
solution:
The center intensity $I_{C}$ is minimized when $\delta=(2 k+1) \pi$, and the minimum intensity is $I_{C \text{ min }}=\frac{1}{9} I_{0}$, which implies

$$
t=\frac{(2 k+1) \lambda}{2(n-1)}
$$

subject: Thermodynamics
topic: Second Law of Thermodynamics and Entropy
problem: A resistance wire heats water with a mass of $M=1\ \mathrm{kg}$ from $t_{1}=20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $t_{2}=99^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ (under atmospheric pressure). Determine the factor by which the number of microstates of the water increases.
solution:
According to the Boltzmann relation, $S = k \ln \Omega$,

$$
\frac{\Omega_{2}}{\Omega_{1}} = \mathrm{e}^{\frac{\Delta S}{k}} = \mathrm{e}^{7.24 \times 10^{25}}
$$

subject: Thermodynamics
problem: A cylindrical container is divided into two equal volumes by a fixed piston. The left side is filled with 1 mol of neon gas at a pressure of 4 atm and a temperature of 300 K; the right side is filled with argon gas at a pressure of 1 atm and a temperature of 300 K. The gases can be treated as ideal gases. The entire system is adiabatic in relation to the outside environment, and the specific heat capacity of the container and piston is \(c\) (where \(c\) is a constant). Now the piston is allowed to slide frictionlessly along the cylindrical container. Due to dissipation, the piston eventually comes to rest at an equilibrium position. Calculate the new equilibrium temperature (the piston is thermally conductive).
solution: The internal energy of an ideal gas is only a function of temperature, and the internal energy of the entire system remains unchanged, so the temperature also remains unchanged. The new equilibrium temperature is 300 K.

subject: Geometrical Optics
problem: Calculate the depth of focus of a $10 \times$ magnifying glass or eyepiece.
solution:
The working distance of a magnifying glass (or eyepiece) is such that the object is placed in a small range slightly inside the first focal point, enabling the formation of a virtually magnified image beyond the near point $s_{0}$ for observation by a normal eye. The so-called "depth of focus" refers to the aforementioned small longitudinal interval $\Delta x$, which corresponds to the object distance related to the near point. Let the image distance be $x^{\prime} = -(s_{0} + f)$. According to Newton's formula, we have

$$
x = \frac{f^{2}}{x^{\prime}} = -\frac{f^{2}}{s_{0} + f}
$$

From this, the angular magnification $M = s_{0} / f$, substituting the focal length $f$ into the above expression gives

$$
x = -\frac{s_{0}}{M(M+1)}
$$

The depth of focus is 

$$
\Delta x = |x| = \frac{s_{0}}{M(M+1)}
$$

Thus, we calculate

$$
M=10 \times, \Delta x=0.23 \mathrm{~cm}
$$

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: A low-energy $\pi^{-}$ meson is captured by a nucleus, producing a strong interaction: $\pi^{-} + \mathrm{d} \rightarrow \mathrm{n} + \mathrm{n}$. It is known that the spin of $\pi^{-}$ is zero, and the spin of $\mathrm{d}$ is 1, with parity of $(+1)$. Try to analyze the parity of the system after the reaction and derive the intrinsic parity of the $\pi^{-}$ meson based on parity conservation.
solution:
The parity of the system after the reaction is

$$
P(\mathrm{n})^{2}(-1)^{l^{\prime}} = (+1)^{2}(-1)^{1} = (-1)
$$

In strong interactions, parity is conserved. By comparing the parity of the system before and after the reaction, it can be deduced that $P_{\pi} = (-1)$.
