subject: Thermodynamics
topic: Second Law of Thermodynamics and Entropy
problem: Determine the change in pressure when a mixture of 0.1 mol of helium and 0.2 mol of nitrogen gas, initially at a temperature of \(T = 300 \, \mathrm{K}\) and a volume of 4 L, undergoes an adiabatic process in which the volume decreases by \(1\%\). It is known that the specific heat ratios for helium and nitrogen are \(\gamma_{1} = \frac{5}{3}\) and \(\gamma_{2} = \frac{7}{5}\) respectively.
solution:
Using the ideal gas state equation, we have

$$
p_{f} = p_{i}\left(\frac{V_{i}}{V_{f}}\right)^{\gamma}
$$

where 

$$
\gamma = \frac{n_{1} c_{p1} + n_{2} c_{p2}}{n_{1} c_{V1} + n_{2} c_{V2}}, \quad c_{p j} = c_{V j} + R
$$

Helium is a monoatomic molecule with \(c_{V1} = \frac{3}{2} R, c_{p1} = \frac{5}{2} R\); nitrogen is a diatomic molecule with \(c_{V2} = \frac{5}{2} R, c_{p2} = \frac{7}{2} R\), thus \(\gamma = 1.46\). When \(V_{f} = 0.99 V_{i}\), we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
& p_{f} = 1.015 p_{i} = 1.015 \frac{n R T_{i}}{V_{i}} = 1.9 \times 10^{5} \, \mathrm{N/m}^{2} \\
& \text{where,} \, n = n_{1} + n_{2} = 0.3 \, \mathrm{mol}, \, R = 8.31 \, \mathrm{J/(mol \cdot K)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

subject: Statistical Mechanics
problem: A helium-neon laser produces quasi-monochromatic light with a wavelength of $6328 \, \text{}$, a beam power of $1 \, \text{mW}$, a divergence angle of $10^{-4}$ radians, and a bandwidth of $0.01 \, \text{}$. Please calculate the blackbody temperature.
solution:
When the gas is in equilibrium at temperature \(T\), it follows the Maxwell velocity distribution law. The number of molecules within a unit volume with velocities between \(\boldsymbol{v}\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}+\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}\) is given by:

\[
f(v) \mathrm{d} v=n\left(\frac{m}{2 \pi k T}\right)^{3 / 2} \exp \left(-\frac{m v^{2}}{2 k T}\right) \mathrm{d} v \tag{1}
\]

To calculate the number of collisions, consider the two types of molecules as elastic hard spheres with diameters \(d_{1}\) and \(d_{2}\). Using the center of a molecule of the first type as the sphere's center and a radius of \(d_{12}=(d_{1}+d_{2})/2\), the sphere surface is conceptualized. When two molecules collide, the center of the second type must be on this imaginary sphere, with \(v_{r}=v_{2}-v_{1}\) being the relative velocity of molecule 2 concerning molecule 1. In a time \(\mathrm{d} t\), for the second type of molecule to collide with the first within the solid angle element \(\mathrm{d} \Omega\) along the axis direction \(\boldsymbol{n}\), it must be located within a cylinder with base \(d_{12}^{2} \mathrm{d} \Omega\) and height \(v_{r} \cos \theta \mathrm{d} t\). The volume of this cylinder is:

\[
\mathrm{d} \tau=d_{12}^{2} v_{r} \cos \theta \mathrm{d} \Omega \mathrm{d} t \tag{2}
\]

Therefore, in time \(\mathrm{d} t\), the number of collisions within the solid angle element \(\mathrm{d} \Omega\) along the axis \(\boldsymbol{n}\) between a molecule 1 with speed \(\boldsymbol{v}_{1}\) and molecule 2 with speeds in the range \(\boldsymbol{v}_{2}\) to \(\boldsymbol{v}_{2}+\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{2}\) is:

\[
f_{2}\left(\boldsymbol{v}_{2}\right) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{2} \mathrm{d} \tau = d_{12}^{2} v_{r} \cos \theta f_{2}\left(\boldsymbol{v}_{2}\right) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{2} \mathrm{d} \Omega \mathrm{d} t \tag{3}
\]

Thus, the average number of collisions in unit time between one molecule of the first type and all molecules of the second type is:

\[
\overline{\Theta_{12}} = \frac{1}{n_{1}} \iiint d_{12}^{2} v_{r} \cos \theta \cdot f_{1}\left(\boldsymbol{v}_{1}\right) f_{2}\left(\boldsymbol{v}_{2}\right) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{1} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{2} \mathrm{d} \Omega \tag{5}
\]

Completing the angular integration:

\[
\int \cos \theta \mathrm{d} \Omega = \int_{0}^{2 \pi} \mathrm{d} \varphi \cdot \int_{0}^{\pi} \cos \theta \sin \theta \mathrm{d} \theta = \pi \tag{6}
\]

We find:

\[
\overline{\Theta_{12}} = \pi n_{2} d_{12}^{2}\left(\frac{m_{1}}{2 \pi k T}\right)^{3/2}\left(\frac{m_{2}}{2 \pi k T}\right)^{3/2} \iint v_{r} \exp \left(-\frac{m_{1} v_{1}^{2}+m_{2} v_{2}^{2}}{2 k T}\right) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{1} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{2} \tag{7}
\]

Introducing the velocity of the center of mass:

\[
\boldsymbol{v}_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{1}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\left(m_{1} \boldsymbol{v}_{1}+m_{2} \boldsymbol{v}_{2}\right) \tag{8}
\]

We have:

\[
\frac{1}{2} m_{1} v_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} m_{2} v_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2} M v_{\mathrm{c}}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \mu v_{r}^{2} \tag{9}
\]

And

\[
\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{\mathrm{c}} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{r}=|J| \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{1} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{v}_{2} \tag{10}
\]

where \(M=m_{1}+m_{2}\) is the total mass of the two molecules, and \(\mu=m_{1} m_{2} /(m_{1}+m_{2})\) is the reduced mass of the two molecules. The absolute value of the Jacobian determinant is:

\[
|J|= \left|\frac{\partial(\boldsymbol{v}_{\mathrm{c}}, \boldsymbol{v}_{r})}{\partial(\boldsymbol{v}_{1}, \boldsymbol{v}_{2})}\right|=1 \tag{11}
\]

Substituting these results into equation (7), we finally obtain the average frequency of collisions between a molecule of the first type and those of the second type:

\[
\overline{\Theta_{12}} = \pi n_{2} d_{12}^{2}\left(\frac{m_{1}}{2 \pi k T}\right)^{3/2}\left(\frac{m_{2}}{2 \pi k T}\right)^{3/2} \int \exp \left(-\frac{M v_{c}^{2}}{2 k T}\right) \mathrm{d} v_{\mathrm{c}} \cdot \int v_{r} \exp \left(-\frac{\mu v_{r}^{2}}{2 k T}\right) \mathrm{d} v_{r} = \pi n_{2} d_{12}^{2} \sqrt{\frac{8 k T}{\pi \mu}} = \pi n_{2} d_{12}^{2}\left(1+\frac{m_{1}}{m_{2}}\right)^{1/2} \overline{v_{1}} \tag{12}
\]

where \(\overline{v_{1}}=\sqrt{8 k T / \pi m_{1}}\) is the average speed of the first type of molecule, and \(n_{1}\) and \(n_{2}\) are the molecular number densities of the first and second types of gas molecules, respectively. For identical molecules, the average collision frequency is \(\Theta=\sqrt{2} n \pi d^{2} v\).

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: Based on the results of the first two problems, calculate the total probability, that is, the probability of all $N$ measurement results being +1. What happens when $N \rightarrow \infty$?
solution:

P=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\cos \frac{\pi}{2 N}\right) \frac{1}{2^{N-1}}\left(1+\cos \frac{\pi}{2 N}\right)^{N-1} \rightarrow 0 \quad (\text{when } N \rightarrow \infty).
$$

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: A small marble with mass $m$ and radius $r$ elastically scatters off a large marble with mass $M$ ($m \ll M$) and radius $R$. Find the total scattering cross-section.
solution:
Since $m \ll M$, when $m$ is scattered by $M$, $M$ can be considered stationary. The difference compared to the previous problem is that the radius of the particles was not considered, whereas elastic scattering with radii considered is the same as when $m$ is elastically scattered by a stationary $M$ with radius $R+r$. Therefore, by replacing the previous problem's $a$ with $R+r$, the result for the total scattering cross-section of this problem is obtained.

$$
\sigma = \pi (R+r)^2
$$

topic: Orbital and Spin Angular Momentum Problems
problem: Three matrices \( M_{z}, M_{y}, M_{x} \), each being a 256x256 square matrix, satisfy the commutation relation \([M_{x}, M_{y}] = i M_{z}\) (cyclically for \(x, y, z\)). The eigenvalues of \( M_{z} \) are \(\pm \frac{3}{2}\) each with multiplicity of 8. Determine the eigenvalues of \( M^{2} \equiv M_{x}^{2} + M_{y}^{2} + M_{z}^{2} \) and the corresponding multiplicities for the case where the eigenvalues of \( M_{z} \) are \(\pm \frac{3}{2}\).
solution: For \( m = \frac{3}{2} \), the possible values of \( m_x \) are \(+\frac{3}{2}, \frac{1}{2}, -\frac{1}{2}, -\frac{3}{2}\). The corresponding multiplicity is \(2m + 1 = 4\). There are 8 instances of each \(\pm \frac{3}{2}\), leading to \( M^{2} = \frac{15}{4} \), which has 32 occurrences.

subject: Thermodynamics
topic: Thermodynamic State and First Law of Thermodynamics
problem: How much work is done on the surroundings when 1000 g of nitrogen is heated from $-20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ under constant pressure? It is known that the constant volume specific heat capacity of nitrogen is $c_{\mathrm{v}}=5 \mathrm{cal}/\mathrm{mol}\cdot{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $R=2 \mathrm{cal}/\mathrm{mol}\cdot{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
solution:
The work done on the surroundings is

$$
W = Q - \Delta U = 8.6 \times 10^{3}\, \text{cal}
$$

problem: A quantum mechanical rigid rotor is constrained to rotate within a plane. The rotor has a moment of inertia $I$ and an electric dipole moment $\mu$ located within the plane. The rotor is placed in a weak uniform electric field $\varepsilon$, which lies within the rotational plane. It is known that the electric field can be treated as a perturbation, with the perturbation Hamiltonian given by $H^{\prime} = -\mu \cdot \varepsilon = -\mu \varepsilon \cdot \cos \theta$. Find the first-order correction to the energy $E^{(1)}$.
solution:

$$

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: A neutral meson is produced when a proton hits a thin target, and each meson decays into two $\gamma$ photons. It is known that the photon emitted forward has an energy of 96 MeV, and the photon emitted backward has an energy of 48 MeV. Find the $\beta$ value of the meson.
solution:
The neutral meson decays in the laboratory frame. If one photon is emitted backward, the other photon must be emitted forward. Let their energies and momenta be $E_{2}$, $p_{2}$, $E_{1}$, and $p_{1}$, respectively. Applying the conservation of energy and momentum, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& E=E_{1}+E_{2}=96 + 48 = 144 \, \text{MeV}, \\
& p=p_{1}-p_{2}=96 - 48 = 48 \, \text{MeV}/c.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $\beta$ value of the particle is

$$
\beta = \frac{p}{E} = \frac{48}{144} = \frac{1}{3}.
$$

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: A particle with mass $m$ is launched from infinity with an initial velocity $v_{0}$, and is scattered by a fixed repulsive force center with a magnitude of $\frac{k}{r^{2}}$ (where $k$ is a constant). If the particle were not subject to the repulsive force, it would pass by at a distance $b$ from the force center. Find the angle of deflection that actually occurs.
solution:
Solution (2)

$$
\begin{aligned}
u_{\max} & = \frac{1}{r_{\min}} = \frac{m v_{0}^{2}}{k + \sqrt{k^{2} + m^{2} b^{2} v_{0}^{4}}} = \frac{-k + \sqrt{k^{2} + m^{2} b^{2} v_{0}^{4}}}{m b^{2} v_{0}^{2}} \\
\beta & = \int_{0}^{u_{\max}} \frac{b \, \mathrm{d} u}{\left[1 - \frac{1}{E_{0}} V\left(\frac{1}{u}\right) - b^{2} u^{2}\right]^{1 / 2}} \\
& = \int_{0}^{u_{\max}} \frac{b \, \mathrm{d} u}{\left[1 - \frac{k}{\frac{1}{2} m v_{0}^{2}} u - b^{2} u^{2}\right]^{1 / 2}} \\
& = \int_{0}^{u_{\max}} \frac{b \, \mathrm{d} u}{\left[1 + \left(\frac{k}{m v_{0}^{2} b}\right)^{2} - \left(b u + \frac{k}{m v_{0}^{2} b}\right)^{2}\right]^{1 / 2}} \\
& = \left.\arcsin \left[\left(b u + \frac{k}{m v_{0}^{2} b}\right) / \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{k}{m v_{0}^{2} b}\right)^{2}}\right]\right|_{0}^{u_{\max}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Deflection angle

$$
\begin{aligned}
\theta & = \pi - 2 \beta = \pi - \left[2 \arcsin 1 - 2 \arcsin \left(\frac{k}{\sqrt{k^{2} + m^{2} v_{0}^{4} b^{2}}}\right)\right] \\
& = 2 \arcsin \left(\frac{k}{\sqrt{k^{2} + m^{2} v_{0}^{4} b^{2}}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: A homogeneous cylinder with a mass of 10.0 kg and a radius of 0.070 m is undergoing pure rolling motion on a slope inclined at $30^{\circ}$. A lightweight, inextensible string is wound around the cylinder, passes over a frictionless pulley, and is attached to a 2.0 kg weight on the other end. Find the static friction force acting at the contact point $P$.
solution:
Using the equation

$$
f = (M + 2m) \ddot{x} - m g + M g \sin 30^{\circ}
$$

we can calculate the magnitude of the static friction force as

$$
f = 23 \, \mathrm{N}.
$$

The direction of the static friction force is up the slope.

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: A violin string that has a length of 0.5 m has a fundamental frequency of 200 Hz. What is the speed of transverse pulses on this string?
solution: \(\lambda_{1} = 2L, \quad v = \lambda_{1} \nu_{1} = 2L \nu_{1} = 2 \times 0.5 \times 200 = 200 \, \mathrm{m/s}\).

subject: Thermodynamics
problem: \(1 \, \text{g}\) of water at \(20^{\circ} \text{C}\) and a pressure of \(10^{4} \, \text{atm}\) passes through an adiabatic porous plug into a laboratory with a pressure of \(1 \, \text{atm}\). Assume that the density of water is the same at \(10^{4} \, \text{atm}\) and at \(1 \, \text{atm}\). Find the temperature \(T_f\) of the ejected water.
solution:
The enthalpy of the water remains constant before and after passing through the porous plug, that is:
\[ U_{f} + p_{f} V = U_{i} + p_{i} V \]

If the temperature of the ejected water is \(T_{f}\), then:
\[ \Delta U = U_{f} - U_{i} = mc(T_{f} - T_{i}) = (p_{i} - p_{f}) V \]

This gives:
\[ T_{f} = \frac{(p_{i} - p_{f}) V}{mc} + T_{i} \]

By taking \(p_{i} - p_{f} \approx 10^{4} \, \text{atm} = 1.013 \times 10^{9} \, \text{N/m}^2\), \(V = 10^{-3} \, \text{L} = 10^{-6} \, \text{m}^3\), \(c = 1.0 \, \text{cal/(g} \cdot\text{K}) = 4.187 \, \text{J/g} \cdot \text{K}^{-1}, \, m = 1 \, \text{g}\) and substituting these values, we get:

\[ T_{f} = \frac{(1.013 \times 10^{9} \, \text{N/m}^{2}) (10^{-6} \, \text{m}^{3})}{1 \cdot 4.187} + 293 = 242 + 293 = 535 \, \text{K} \]

\(T_{f} = 535 \, \text{K}\), which is higher than the boiling point of water.

subject: Statistical Mechanics
problem:
Find the chemical potential of a free electron gas with particle number density \( n \) at \( T=0 \, \mathrm{K} \). The conduction electrons in a metal can be considered as a free electron gas.

Given \( n=10^{22} \, \mathrm{cm}^{-3} \), find the chemical potential \( \mu \) of the conduction electrons at \( T=0 \, \mathrm{K} \).
solution:
From the density of states,

\[
D(\varepsilon) \mathrm{d} \varepsilon = \frac{4 \pi}{h^{3}}(2 m)^{3 / 2} \sqrt{\varepsilon} \mathrm{~d} \varepsilon
\]

we obtain the particle number density

\[
n = \int_{0}^{\mu_{0}} \frac{4 \pi}{h^{3}}(2 m)^{3 / 2} \sqrt{\varepsilon} \mathrm{~d} \varepsilon = \frac{8 \pi}{3}\left(\frac{2 m \mu_{0}}{h^{2}}\right)^{3 / 2}
\]

Thus,

\[
\mu_{0} = \frac{h^{2}}{2 m}\left(\frac{3 n}{8 \pi}\right)^{2 / 3}
\]

For \( n=10^{22} \, \mathrm{cm}^{-3} = 10^{28} \, \mathrm{m}^{-3} \), we have

\[
\mu_{0} = 2.7 \times 10^{-19} \, \mathrm{J} = 1.7 \, \mathrm{eV}
\]

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: Given a radioactive parent nucleus with a half-life of $T = 10^4$ years, there are $10^{20}$ nuclei at $t=0$. These parent nuclei undergo a series of cascading decays, ultimately decaying into a stable isotope. Find the activity of the parent at $t=0$.
solution:
The decay constant of the parent nucleus is

$$
\lambda_{1} = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} = 6.93 \times 10^{-5} \text{ year}^{-1} = 2.2 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{s}^{-1}
$$

At $t=0$, the activity of the parent isotope is

$$
A_{1}(0) = \lambda_{1} N_{1}(t=0) = \frac{2.2 \times 10^{-12} \times 10^{20}}{3.7 \times 10^{7}} = 5.95\, \mathrm{mCi}
$$

subject: Electrodynamics
problem: A beam of infinitely long cylindrical relativistic electrons moves at a constant speed \( v \). The electron density is known to be a constant \( n \). Calculate the radial force acting on a single electron, including both electric and magnetic forces.
solution:
Let the electron density be \( n \). Then, the charge density of this electron beam is

$$
\rho = -e n
$$

According to the relevant formula in the problem, in the laboratory reference frame, the force experienced by a single electron is

$$
\boldsymbol{F} = -\frac{e \rho r}{2 \varepsilon_{0} \gamma^{2}} \boldsymbol{e}_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac{e^{2} n r}{2 \varepsilon_{0} \gamma^{2}} \boldsymbol{e}_{\mathrm{r}},
$$

where 

$$
\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^{2} / c^{2}}}
$$ 

is the Lorentz factor.

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: A brick is moving upwards on an inclined plane at an initial speed of $1.5 \mathrm{~m/s}$, where the plane is inclined at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction is $\mu=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{12}$. Determine the distance of the brick from its initial position after 0.5 seconds.

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: A neutral lithium atom under heating ($Z=3$) is placed in a magnetic field. Which energy level, $5^{2} \mathrm{S}_{1/2}$ or $5^{2} \mathrm{P}_{1/2}$, has a lower energy? Please briefly provide the physical reason.
solution:
In an external magnetic field, the atomic energy levels shift:

$$
\Delta E = M_J g \mu_{\mathrm{B}} B
$$

where $g$ is the Landé g-factor, $M_J$ is the magnetic quantum number representing the component of total angular momentum along the direction of the magnetic field, and $B$ is the strength of the external magnetic field. In a magnetic field of 1 T, the splitting is only about $5 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{eV}$.

In the $5^{2} \mathrm{S}_{1/2}$ state, the energy is lowest for $M_J = -1/2$. This is because the energy difference between $^{2} \mathrm{S}$ and $^{2} \mathrm{P}$ is primarily caused by spin-orbit coupling, which can reach the order of eV.

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: Assume there is a spherical celestial body in the solar system, located at a distance from the Sun equal to the Earth's distance from the Sun, \( R = 1.5 \times 10^{11} \, \mathrm{m} \). Assume the Sun is equivalent to a black body with a temperature of \( T_c = 6000 \, \mathrm{K} \) and a radius of \( R_c = 7 \times 10^{8} \, \mathrm{m} \). Determine the temperature of the celestial body based on the following assumption: The celestial body has black body characteristics.
solution:
Assume the diameter of the celestial body is \( d \). Since it is a black body, the absorption coefficient is \( \alpha = 1 \). The absorbed power is

$$
P_1 = \alpha \frac{\pi d^2}{4} \cdot \sigma T_c^4 \left(\frac{R_c}{R}\right)^2.
$$

The total power radiated by the celestial body in all directions is

$$
P_2 = \pi d^2 \cdot \sigma T^4.
$$

In equilibrium, \( P_1 = P_2 \), therefore

$$
T = T_c \sqrt{\frac{R_c}{2R}} = 290 \, \mathrm{K}.
$$

This is approximately equal to the average temperature on the Earth's surface. Note: This conclusion is independent of the size of the celestial body.

subject: Statistical Mechanics
problem: In the high-temperature limit, find the root mean square (rms) value of the noise voltage across the inductor $L$ and capacitor $C$ in an AC circuit.
solution:
In the high-temperature or classical limit $x = \hbar \omega / kT \ll 1$, $\operatorname{coth}(x) \approx 1 / x$, thus

\[
\overline{V^{2}} = \frac{kT}{C}
\]

At this point, the rms value of the noise voltage is $\sqrt{\overline{V^{2}}} = \sqrt{\frac{kT}{C}}$.

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: A particle with mass \( m \) is moving under a central force \( F = -\frac{k}{r^3} \) (where \( k \) is a positive constant). Assuming its orbit is in the form \( r = a \mathrm{e}^{b \varphi} \) (with \( a \) and \( b \) as constants), determine the value of the angular momentum \( J \) using the Binet equation.
solution:
Method Two: Use the Binet equation to find \( h \),

\[
-m h^2 u^2\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 u}{\mathrm{d} \varphi^2} + u\right) = F(u)
\]

Now,

\[
\begin{aligned}
u & = \frac{1}{a} \mathrm{e}^{-b \varphi}, \quad F(u) = -k u^3, \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{\mathrm{d} \varphi} & = -\frac{b}{a} \mathrm{e}^{-b \varphi}, \quad \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 u}{\mathrm{d} \varphi^2} = \frac{b^2}{a} \mathrm{e}^{-b \varphi} = b^2 u.
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
-m h^2 u^2\left(b^2 u + u\right) & = -k u^3 \\
h^2 & = \frac{k}{m(b^2 + 1)}, \quad J = m h = \sqrt{\frac{m k}{b^2 + 1}}
\end{aligned}
\]

The calculation of \( E \) is omitted.

subject: Wave Optics
problem: The specific rotation of a pure sucrose solution is $\alpha = 6.65^{\circ} / (\mathrm{cm} \cdot (\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{cm}^3))$. There is a sucrose solution of unknown purity with a concentration of $c^{\prime} = 0.2 \ \mathrm{g} / \mathrm{cm}^3$. After plane-polarized light passes through this solution with a thickness of $d = 20 \ \mathrm{cm}$, the plane of polarization rotates by $25^{\circ}$. Determine the purity of sucrose in this solution.
solution:
The rotation angle $\varphi$ of the plane of polarization is related to the solution concentration $c$, specific rotation $\alpha$, and thickness $d$ by the equation:

$$
\varphi = \alpha c d
$$

Substituting $\alpha = 6.65^{\circ} / (\mathrm{cm} \cdot (\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{cm}^3))$ and $d = 20 \ \mathrm{cm}$, the pure sucrose concentration $c = 0.188 \ \mathrm{g} / \mathrm{cm}^3$ corresponds to a rotation angle $\varphi = 25^{\circ}$. Given that the concentration of this solution is $c^{\prime} = 0.2 \ \mathrm{g} / \mathrm{cm}^3$, the purity is:

$$
x = \frac{c}{c^{\prime}} = \frac{0.188}{0.20} = 94\%
$$

subject: Quantum Mechanics
topic: Orbital and Spin Angular Momentum Problems
problem: The nucleus is a bound state of protons and neutrons with a total angular momentum \( J = 1 \). It is known to primarily consist of an \( S(l=0) \) state with a small amount of \( D(l=2) \) state involved. Calculate the magnetic moment of the \(\mathrm{n}-\mathrm{p}\) system (total angular momentum \( J = 1 \)) when in a pure \( D \) state; assume that the spins of n and p are coupled to form total spin \( S \), and then this total spin is coupled with orbital angular momentum \( L \) to form total angular momentum \( J \). solution:
For a pure \( D \) state, the total spin \( S = 1 \), and the orbital angular momentum (relative to the \(\mathrm{n}, \mathrm{p}\) center of mass) \( L = 2 \).

The total magnetic moment should be the coupling of the total spin magnetic moment \( \mu_{S} \) and the orbital angular momentum magnetic moment \( \mu_{L} \).

The total spin \( S = S_{\mathrm{p}} + S_{\mathrm{n}} \) results in \( \mu_{S} = \mu_{\mathrm{p}} + \mu_{\mathrm{n}} \) (where \( \mu_{\mathrm{p}}, \mu_{\mathrm{n}} \) are the spin magnetic moments of \( \mathrm{p} \) and \( \mathrm{n} \) respectively). The mean projection of total \( \mu_{S} \) in the direction of total \( S \) is given by

$$
\mu_{S} = \frac{\left(g_{\mathrm{p}} \mu_{N} S_{\mathrm{p}} + g_{N} \mu_{N} S_{\mathrm{n}}\right) \cdot S}{S(S+1)} = \frac{1}{2}\left(g_{\mathrm{p}} + g_{N}\right) \mu_{N} S
$$

where

$$
\mu_{N} = \frac{e \hbar}{2 m_{p} c}; \quad g_{\mathrm{p}} = 5.58, \quad g_{N} = -3.82
$$

As the proton's motion generates a magnetic moment about the center of mass, but the neutron does not, we have

$$
\mu_{L} = \frac{e \hbar}{2 m_{p} c} \cdot \boldsymbol{L}_{\mathrm{p}} = \mu_{N} \cdot \boldsymbol{L}_{\mathrm{p}}
$$

Here, \(\boldsymbol{L}_{\mathrm{p}}\) is the proton's angular momentum about the center of mass. Given \(\boldsymbol{L}_{\mathrm{p}} + \boldsymbol{L}_{\mathrm{n}} = \boldsymbol{L}\) and assuming \( L_{\mathrm{p}} = L_{\mathrm{n}} \), we have \( L_{\mathrm{p}} = \frac{1}{2} L \) (as the center of mass is at the midpoint along the connection line), thus \(\mu_{L} = \frac{1}{2} \mu_{N} L\).

After coupling, the total magnetic moment is

$$
\mu_{r} = \frac{\left[\frac{1}{2} \mu_{N} L \cdot J + \frac{1}{2}\left(g_{\mathrm{p}} + g_{N}\right) \mu_{N} S \cdot J\right] J}{J(J+1)}
$$

Since \( J = L + S \), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu & = \left[\frac{1}{2} \mu_{N} \cdot 3 + \frac{1}{2}\left(g_{\mathrm{p}} + g_{\mathrm{N}}\right) \mu_{N}(-1)\right] J / 2 \\
& = \left[1.5 - \frac{1}{2}\left(g_{\mathrm{p}} + g_{\mathrm{N}}\right)\right] \frac{1}{2} \mu_{N} J = 0.31 \mu_{N} J
\end{aligned}
$$

Projecting in the direction of \( J \) and considering \( J_{x} \) at its maximum value \( J = 1 \), we find

$$
\mu = 0.31 \mu_{N}
$$

subject: Wave Optics
problem: A He-Ne laser operating at 6328  has planar mirrors at the ends of its resonant cavity, spaced 0.5 m apart. Calculate the frequency interval between the longitudinal modes of this laser.
solution:
Typically, when natural light is reflected at the interface of two media, the reflected light is partially polarized. However, when the angle of incidence satisfies

$$
\theta_{B}=\arctan \frac{n_{1}}{n_{0}}
$$

where $n_{0}$ and $n_{1}$ are the refractive indices of the incident medium and the refractive medium respectively, the reflected light is linearly polarized with vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence. This angle $\theta_{B}$ is called the Brewster's angle or the polarization angle.

The calculations for $r, R, \bar{R}$, and $t, T, \bar{T}$ for the $S$ and $P$ components are based on Fresnel's equations. Because the angle of incidence is Brewster's angle, the sum of the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction is $\frac{\pi}{2}$. Intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, while energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam. The reflected light and incident light are in the same medium, with equal cross-sectional areas, while the refracted light and incident light are in different media, with different cross-sectional areas, which is noteworthy.

1. According to Fresnel's equations, the amplitude reflectance $r_{s}$ and amplitude transmittance $t_{s}$ for the $S$ component are

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{s}=\frac{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}-n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}=-\frac{\sin \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\
t_{s}=\frac{2 n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{2 \sin \theta_{2} \cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

The amplitude reflectance $r_{P}$ and amplitude transmittance $t_{P}$ for the $P$ component are

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{P}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}-n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{\tan \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}{\tan \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

where $n_{1}=1$, $n_{2}=n=1.50$, $\theta_{1}$ is the angle of incidence, and $\theta_{2}$ is the angle of refraction. Since the angle of incidence is the Brewster's angle, we have

$$
\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}=\arctan n=\arctan 1.50=56.3^{\circ}
$$

Additionally,

$$
\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}
$$

Substituting into the formulas for $r_{s}$ and $r_{p}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{s}=-\frac{\sin \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}{\sin \left(56.3^{\circ}+33.7^{\circ}\right)}=-0.384 \\
r_{p}=0
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the reflected light and incident light are in the same medium with equal cross-sectional areas, the intensity reflectance $R_{S}$ and $R_{P}$, as well as the energy flow reflectance $\bar{R}_{S}$ and $\bar{R}_{P}$ for the $S$ and $P$ components respectively, are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& R_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad R_{P}=0 \\
& \bar{R}_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad \bar{R}_{P}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

For the refracted light, substituting $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ into $t_{s}$ and $t_{P}$, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
t_{s}=\frac{2 \sin \theta_{2} \cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \sin 33.7^{\circ} \cos 56.3^{\circ}}{\sin \frac{\pi}{2}}=0.616 \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \cos 56.3^{\circ} \sin 33.7^{\circ}}{\cos \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}=0.667
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the refracted light and incident light are in different media with different cross-sectional areas, the intensity transmittance and energy flow transmittance are not simply equal to the square of the amplitude transmittance. The intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, given by

$$
\widetilde{S}=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_{0} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}{\mu_{0} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}}} E^{2}
$$

where $E$ is the amplitude of the electric vector. Since $\mu_{\mathrm{r}} \approx 1$, and the speed of light in vacuum $c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{0}} \mu_{0}}$, and the refractive index $n=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}} \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}$, this can be rewritten as

$$
\bar{S}=\frac{1}{2 c \mu_{0}} n E^{2}
$$

Thus, the intensity is proportional to $n E^{2}$, and the intensity transmittance is

$$
T=\frac{\bar{S}_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1}}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t^{2}
$$

The intensity transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& T_{S}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{S}^{2}=n t_{S}^{2}=0.569 \\
& T_{P}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{P}^{2}=n t_{P}^{2}=0.667
\end{aligned}
$$

The energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam, and the ratio of the cross-sectional areas of the refracted beam to the incident beam is $\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}}$, so the energy flow transmittance is

$$
\bar{T}=\frac{\bar{S}_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}} t^{2}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T
$$

Substituting the values, the energy flow transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{gathered}
\bar{T}_{S}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{S}=0.853 \\
\bar{T}_{P}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{P}=1
\end{gathered}
$$

The fact that the energy flow transmittance $\bar{T}_{P}=1$ for the $P$ component is expected because, when light is incident at the Brewster's angle $\left(\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}\right)$, the reflected light does not contain any $P$ component, meaning the entire energy of the incident $P$ component is transmitted.

problem:
Due to the experimental observation of narrow, long-lived states \( J/\psi, \psi^{\prime} \), a new charm quantum number is introduced. Additionally, states of large mass \((\gamma, \gamma^{\prime}, \cdots)\) with mass \(\sim 10 \mathrm{GeV}\) have been observed. (3) Based on the colored quark model, estimate the relative total cross section for hadron production above the energy region exceeding the threshold for producing b quarks:

\[
R = \frac{\sigma(e^{+} e^{-} \rightarrow h)}{\sigma(e^{+} e^{-} \rightarrow \mu^{+} \mu^{-})}
\]
solution:
(3) After a new quark is produced, its contribution to the \(R\) value is given by

\[
R = \frac{\sigma(e^{+} e^{-} \rightarrow Q \overline{Q})}{\sigma(e^{+} e^{-} \rightarrow \mu^{+} \mu^{-})} = 3 Q^{2}
\]

where \(Q\) is the charge of this new quark. The factor of 3 accounts for the contribution of the three colors. If the total energy in the center-of-mass system is greater than the threshold to produce b quarks, quarks \(u, d, s, c\), and b can all be produced, so we have

\[
R = 3 \sum_{i} Q_{i}^{2} = 3\left[3 \times\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2} + 2 \times \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{2}\right] = \frac{11}{3}
\]

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: A beam of particles with spin $\frac{1}{2}$ and mass $m$ is scattered by a target composed of heavy nuclei, where the nucleus also has a spin of $\frac{1}{2}$. In the experiment, the interaction between the particles and the nuclei is described by $C S_{1} \cdot S_{2} \delta^{(3)}\left(x_{1}-x_{2}\right)$, where $C$ is a small constant, $S_{1} \cdot S_{2}$ represents the spin of the experiment's particles and nuclei, and $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ are their respective positions. If all incoming particles have their spin pointing in the positive $Z$-axis direction, while the orientation of the nucleus spin is arbitrary, what is the probability that the spin of the incident particles still points in the positive $Z$-axis direction after scattering?
solution:
Now, considering the case where the spin of particles remains up after scattering, the two independent spin states of the system after scattering are $\left|\chi_{1}^{1}\right\rangle$ and 

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(|\chi_{1}^{1}\rangle + |\chi_{1}^{0}\rangle \right)
$$

By taking the inner product of these two states with $|\psi\rangle_{f}$, we obtain two corresponding probability amplitudes, which in turn gives the scattering cross-section in this scenario, expressed as

$$
\sigma^{(t)} = \left|c_{1}(t)\right|^{2} \sigma_{1}(\theta) + \frac{1}{4} \left|c_{2}(t)\right|^{2} \left|f_{1}(\theta) + f_{0}(\theta)\right|^{2}
$$

The ensemble average yields

$$
\sigma^{(t)} = \frac{1}{2} \sigma_{1}(\theta) + \frac{1}{8} \left|f_{1}(\theta) + f_{2}(\theta)\right|^{2} = \frac{m^{2}C^{2}}{(8\pi)^{2}}
$$

Finally, the probability sought is

$$
P = \frac{\sigma^{(t)}}{\sigma_{t}} = \frac{1}{3}
$$

subject: Quantum Mechanics
topic: Orbital and Spin Angular Momentum Problems
problem: A certain physical system is composed of two non-identical particles, each with a spin of $\frac{1}{2}$. It is known that particle 1 is in the eigenstate of $S_{1z}=\frac{1}{2}$, and particle 2 is in the eigenstate of $S_{2x}=\frac{1}{2}$. Given that the total spin $S^{2}$ has two eigenvalues: 0 and 2, determine the probability of measuring the total spin state $S^{2}=0$ for the system (take $\hbar=1$).
solution:
The single particle spin states $S_{1z} = \pm \frac{1}{2}$ are denoted as $\alpha(1), \beta(1)$, and in the Pauli representation, $\alpha = \binom{1}{0}, \beta = \binom{0}{1}$. The single spin state for $S_{2x} = \frac{1}{2}$ is

$$
\psi(2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}_{2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\alpha(2) + \beta(2)]
$$

Therefore, the spin state of the system is

$$
\chi(1,2) = \alpha(1) \psi(2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\alpha(1) \alpha(2) + \alpha(1) \beta(2)]
$$

The eigenstate for $S^{2}=0$ is

$$
\chi_{00}(1,2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\alpha(1) \beta(2) - \beta(1) \alpha(2)]
$$

The probability of measuring $S^{2}=0$ in the spin state $\chi$ of the system is $\left|\left\langle \chi_{00} \mid \chi \right\rangle \right|^{2}$. Based on the orthogonality and normalization of $\alpha, \beta$:

$$
\langle \alpha \mid \alpha \rangle = \langle \beta \mid \beta \rangle = 1, \quad \langle \alpha \mid \beta \rangle = \langle \beta \mid \alpha \rangle = 0
$$

It is easy to find that

$$
\left\langle \chi_{00} \mid \chi \right\rangle = \frac{1}{2}
$$

Therefore, the probability of measuring $S^{2}=0$ is $\frac{1}{4}$.

solution:
Using the equation $I = I_{0} \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha l}$, we have $l = \frac{\ln (I_{0} / I)}{\alpha} = \frac{\lg (I_{0} / I)}{0.434 \alpha}$. Given $\alpha = 0.32 \, \mathrm{cm}^{-1}$,\\

problem: A beam of natural light is incident on the surface of water with a refractive index $n=\frac{4}{3}$ such that the reflected light is linearly polarized. Find the Brewster's angle $i$ for the water surface.
solution:
As shown in the figure, when $i$ is the Brewster's angle, $i=90^{\circ}-i_{1}$, and from $n_{1} \sin i=n_{2} \sin i_{1}$, we have

$$
\sin i_{1}=\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}} \sin i=\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}} \cos i_{1}
$$

Therefore,

$$
i_{1}=\arctan \frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}=\arctan \frac{1}{1.33}=36^{\circ} 56^{\prime}
$$

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: The solar constant is $S = 1.35 \, \mathrm{kW/m^2}$. If the sun decreases in mass at this constant rate, how much mass does the sun lose each year? The distance from the Earth to the sun is $1.5 \times 10^{11} \, \mathrm{m}$.
solution:
The total radiation power of the sun is given by $4 \pi r^{2} \cdot S$, where $r$ is the Earth-sun distance. According to $E = mc^2$, the mass decreases per second by

$$
m = \frac{4 \pi r^{2} \cdot S}{c^2} = \frac{3.8 \times 10^{26}}{9 \times 10^{16}} = 4.2 \times 10^9 \, \mathrm{kg/s}
$$

Considering that each year has $3.2 \times 10^{7} \, \mathrm{s}$, the sun loses $1.4 \times 10^{17} \, \mathrm{kg}$ per year.

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: Two piano strings have the same fundamental frequency when maintained at the same tension, assuming this fundamental frequency is 600 Hz. How much percentage increase in tension is required on one of the strings for the beats to occur at a rate of 6 beats per second when both strings are vibrating simultaneously?
solution:
Assume the initial vibration frequency of the two strings is $\nu_1 = \frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T_0}{\eta}}$.

The new vibration frequency is $\nu_1' = \frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T_0'}{\eta}}$.

From the formula for beat frequency, we have:
\[
\nu_{\text{beat}} = \nu_1' - \nu_1
\]

The beat frequency $\nu_{\text{beat}}$ is 6 Hz, thus obtaining the frequency change:

\[
\nu_1' = 600 \, \text{Hz} + 6 \, \text{Hz} = 606 \, \text{Hz}
\]

Using the relationship between tension and frequency, we get:

\[
\frac{T_0'}{T_0} = \left(\frac{\nu_1'}{\nu_1}\right)^2
\]

Substituting the frequency change into the formula:

\[
\frac{T_0'}{T_0} = \left(\frac{606}{600}\right)^2
\]

Calculating the tension increment:

\[
\frac{T_0' - T_0}{T_0} = \frac{\nu_1'^2 - \nu_1^2}{\nu_1^2} = \frac{(606)^2 - (600)^2}{(600)^2} = 0.020
\]

Therefore, increasing the tension by $2\%$ will produce 6 beats per second.

problem: At room temperature, \(\frac{k_{\mathrm{B}} T}{e} = 26 \, \mathrm{mV}\). Calculate the conductivity of this sample.
solution: The conductivity \(\sigma = n e \mu = 1 \times 10^{16} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 10^{2} = 0.16 \, (\Omega \cdot \mathrm{cm})^{-1} = 16 \, (\Omega \cdot \mathrm{m})^{-1}\).

subject: Electrodynamics
topic: Interaction of Electromagnetic Fields with Matter
problem: (b) Using the known characteristic frequency $\omega_{\mathrm{P}}$ and the formula for the refractive index of a dilute plasma $n=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}=\left(1-\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{P}}^{2}}{\omega^{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$, calculate the distance from the Earth to the pulsar. It is known that pulse $f_{2}$ arrives $0.367 \ \mathrm{s}$ after $f_{1}$, with $\omega_{1}=2\pi f_{1}=2563 \ \mathrm{MHz}$ and $\omega_{2}=2\pi f_{2}=3833 \ \mathrm{MHz}$. The electron density is $N=10^{5} \ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$.
solution:
(b) Calculate the distance from the pulsar to Earth. From Question 7.19, we know

$$
L=c \Delta t /\left[\left(1-\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{P}}^{2}}{\omega_{1}^{2}}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}-\left(1-\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{P}}^{2}}{\omega_{2}^{2}}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right]
$$

Substituting the data $\Delta t=0.367 \ \mathrm{s}, \omega_{1}=2.563 \times 10^{9} \ \mathrm{Hz}, \omega_{2}=3.833 \times 10^{9} \ \mathrm{Hz}$ and

$$
\omega_{\mathrm{P}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{\varepsilon_{0}} \cdot \frac{N e^{2}}{m_{e}}} \approx 1.8 \times 10^{4} \ \mathrm{Hz}
$$

Since $\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}$ are much greater than $\omega_{\mathrm{P}}$, we can approximate:

$$
L \approx \frac{2 c \Delta t}{\omega_{\mathrm{P}}^{2}\left(\frac{1}{\omega_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{\omega_{2}^{2}}\right)} \approx 8.6 \times 10^{2} \ \mathrm{(light\ years)}
$$

Thus, the pulsar is approximately 1000 light years away from Earth.

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: Assume a slowly moving antiproton collides with a proton and annihilates into two $\pi^{+}$ and two $\pi^{-}$ ($m_\pi = 140 \, \text{MeV}$). What is the average kinetic energy of each $\pi$ meson (in $\text{MeV}$)?
solution:
The reaction equation is  

$$
\text{p}+\overline{\text{p}} \rightarrow 2 \pi^{+} + 2 \pi^{-}
$$

Since the incoming $\overline{\text{p}}$ is moving slowly, we can assume its $T_{\overline{\text{p}}} = 0$, then the energy of each $\pi$ is  

$$
E_{\pi} \approx \frac{2 m_{\text{p}}}{4} = \frac{m_{\text{p}}}{2}
$$

Therefore, its kinetic energy is  

$$
T_{\pi} \approx E_{\pi} - m_{\pi} = \frac{1}{2} m_{\text{p}} - m_{\pi} \approx \frac{1}{2} \times 938 - 140 = 329 \, \text{MeV}
$$

subject: Solid-State Physics
problem:
Under the action of external force, a simple cubic crystal \((0,0,1)\) plane undergoes relative slip along the \([1,0,0]\) direction. When the slip amount is \(x\), the potential energy function is

\[
U = U_{0} - A \cos \frac{2 \pi x}{a}
\]

Using elastic theory, prove the critical shear stress

\[
\tau_{m} = \frac{G}{2 \pi}
\]

where \(G\) is the shear modulus of the crystal.
solution:
From Figure 1.1.10, we can see that the direction of the closest atomic arrangement on the crystal plane \((0,0,1)\) is \([1,0,0]\). Take \([1,0,0]\) as the \(x\)-axis. When the \((0,0,1)\) plane undergoes relative slip along the \(x\)-direction (minimum slip distance is \(a\)), the restoring force should be

\[
F = \frac{\partial U}{\partial x} = -\frac{2 \pi}{a} A \sin \frac{2 \pi x}{a}
\]

Assume the slip area is \(S\), then the applied shear stress is

\[
\tau = -\frac{F}{S} = \frac{2 \pi}{a S} A \sin \frac{2 \pi x}{a} = \tau_{m} \sin \frac{2 \pi x}{a}
\]

\(\tau_{m}\) is the maximum shear stress, \(\tau_{m} = \frac{2 \pi}{a S} A\). When \(x \ll a\),

\[
\tau = \tau_{m} \sin \frac{2 \pi x}{a} \approx \tau_{m} \cdot 2 \pi \cdot \frac{x}{a}
\]

\(\tau \propto \frac{x}{a}\), stress is proportional to strain, and the crystal undergoes elastic deformation, following Hooke's law. According to elastic theory, the proportionality coefficient is the shear modulus \(G\)

\[
G = \tau_{m} 2 \pi
\]

Thus,

\[
\tau_{m} = \frac{G}{2 \pi}
\]

The maximum shear stress, i.e., the critical shear stress, is reached when the applied shear stress exceeds this value, and the crystal will undergo permanent slip or plastic deformation. Incidentally, from the above theoretical result, \(\frac{\tau_{m}}{G} = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \approx \frac{1}{6}\), but the experimentally measured values of \(\frac{\tau_{m}}{G}\) are listed in Table 1.1.3, showing that the experimental values are smaller than the theoretical prediction of rigid plane slip by 3-4 orders of magnitude. This indicates that the shear stress required for relative slip within a crystal plane is not as large as theoretically predicted. Therefore, Taylor and others proposed a new slip mechanism hypothesis, suggesting that the slip does not involve overall relative movement but is achieved through the movement of dislocations on the slip plane. Compared with the entire crystal plane, the dislocation line involves only a few atoms, which, due to lattice distortion, are in a higher energy state and more prone to relative motion. The movement of dislocations on the slip plane is equivalent to the successive movement of atoms on the slip plane. The critical shear stress calculated according to this model is consistent with the experimental values for actual crystals.

Table 1.1.3

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\hline
\text{Metal} & \frac{\tau_{m}}{G} \\
\hline
\text{Sn} & \frac{1}{1500} \\
\hline
\text{Ag} & \frac{1}{45000} \\
\hline
\text{Al} & \frac{1}{6000} \\
\hline
\end{array}
\]

subject: Thermodynamics

problem: An insulating partition divides an adiabatic container with a volume of \(V\) into two equal parts. The left half of the container holds 1 mole of a Van der Waals gas at a temperature \(T\), with a constant heat capacity at constant volume \(c_v\). The right half is a vacuum. When the partition is removed, the gas expands to fill the entire container. Determine the change in the internal energy \(\Delta U\) of the gas.
solution:
This is a free expansion process of a Van der Waals gas, where \(Q=0\) and \(W=0\). Therefore, the internal energy of the gas remains unchanged, which means

\[
\Delta U=0
\]

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: Given that the wavenumber difference between adjacent lines in the far-infrared pure rotational spectrum of the NaCl molecule is $0.28 \, \text{cm}^{-1}$, find the rotational energy level $\Delta E_1$ for $J = 1$ of the NaCl molecule. It is known that $hc = 1240 \, \text{eV} \cdot \text{nm}$.
solution: For $J = 1$, $\Delta E_1 = hc \Delta \tilde{\nu} = 1240 \times 10^{-7} \times 0.28 = 0.347 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{eV}$.

problem: Consider a crystal prism with an apex angle of $60^{\circ}$, and the optic axis is perpendicular to the principal section of the prism. Sodium yellow light is refracted in the prism at the angle of minimum deviation. Determine the angle of incidence $i_{1o}$ for the ordinary ray (o-ray).

subject: Wave Optics
problem: Using a Michelson interferometer for precise length measurement, the light source is a helium-neon laser with a wavelength of $6328 \, \AA$, and its spectral line width is $10^{3} \, \AA$. The sensitivity of the entire machine (photoelectric conversion) can reach $1/10$ of a fringe. What is the range of a single length measurement?
solution:
The range of a single length measurement $l_{M}$ is determined by the coherence length $l_{0}$, which can be calculated from the spectral line width $\Delta \lambda$:

$$
l_{M} = \frac{1}{2} l_{0} = \frac{1}{2} \frac{\lambda^{2}}{\Delta \lambda} \approx 2 \, \mathrm{m}
$$

subject: Thermodynamics
topic: Second Law of Thermodynamics and Entropy
problem: In an irreversible isothermal expansion process of an ideal gas at a temperature of 300 K, the gas absorbs 100 J of heat from a heat source at the same temperature and performs a certain amount of external work. Assume that the work done by the gas is 10% of the maximum possible work. Calculate the change in entropy of the heat source during this process.
solution:
Since it is an isothermal process, the internal energy of the gas remains unchanged; thus, the work done by the gas equals the heat absorbed:

$$
A=Q=100 \, \mathrm{J}
$$

The change in entropy of the heat source is

$$
\Delta S_{\text{heat source}} = -\frac{Q}{T} = -\frac{100}{300} = -0.33 \, \mathrm{J/K}
$$

problem: A concave mirror converges parallel light perpendicular to its optical axis at a point 20 cm away. Find the focal length $f_0$ of the concave mirror.
solution: According to the properties of a concave mirror, when parallel light perpendicular to the optical axis converges at a point 20 cm from the mirror, the focal length of the concave mirror is $f_0 = 20 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Classical Electromagnetism
problem: An electric dipole with a fixed length has a mass point with mass $m$ at each end. One end has a positive charge $+Q_{2}$, and the other end has a negative charge $-Q_{2}$. It revolves around a fixed point charge $+Q_{1}$ in orbital motion (the two poles of the dipole are constrained within the orbital plane). The dipole moves in a circular orbit around $Q_{1}$, with $\dot{r} \approx \ddot{r} \approx \ddot{\theta} \approx 0$, and $\alpha \ll 1$. Determine the period of small oscillations in the $\alpha$ coordinate.
solution:
Since $\dot{r} \approx \ddot{r} \approx 0$, $r$ is a constant. Also, given $\ddot{\theta}=0$ and $\alpha \ll 1$, implying $\sin \alpha \approx \alpha$, we have

$$
2 m R^{2} \ddot{\alpha}+\frac{Q_{1} Q_{2}}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0}} \cdot \frac{2 R \alpha}{r^{2}}=0
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\omega=\sqrt{\frac{Q_{1} Q_{2}}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0}} \cdot \frac{1}{m R r^{2}}}
$$

The period of small oscillations is

$$
T=\frac{2 \pi}{\omega}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0}}{Q_{1} Q_{2}} \cdot m R r^{2}}
$$

subject: Wave Optics
problem:
The radii of the fifth and fifteenth rings in a Newton's rings experiment are measured to be 0.70 mm and 1.7 mm, respectively. Calculate the radius of curvature of the lens. Assume the wavelength of light is $0.63 \, \mu \mathrm{m}$. The center point of the interference rings may not be in close contact, and a reliable measurement method requires using the following relationship:

$$
R = \frac{r_{k+m}^{2} - r_{k}^{2}}{m \lambda}
$$

where $r_{k+m}$ and $r_{k}$ are the radii of two interference rings, $m$ is the number of rings between them, and $\lambda$ is the wavelength of light.
solution:
According to the given data, take $r_{k+m} = 1.7 \, \mathrm{mm}$, $r_{k} = 0.70 \, \mathrm{mm}$, $m = 15 - 5 = 10$, and $\lambda = 0.63 \, \mu \mathrm{m}$. Substituting these values into the formula yields the radius of curvature of the lens as

$$
R = 381 \, \mathrm{mm}
$$

subject: Statistical Mechanics
problem: The temperature of a surface is $800^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. When chlorine atoms evaporate from the same surface, the number of chlorine atoms outside the surface is a million times the number of chloride ions. Find the electron affinity $V$ of chlorine.
solution:
When an electron leaves the metal and combines with a neutral chlorine atom to form a chloride ion, the increase in energy is $W-e V$, where $V$ is the electron affinity of chlorine. Thus, the energy of the chloride ion is $W-e V$ higher than that of the chlorine atom, hence:

\[
\frac{N\left(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\right)}{N(\mathrm{Cl})}=\exp\left(\frac{e V-W}{k T}\right)=10^{-6}
\]

where $N\left(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\right)$ and $N(\mathrm{Cl})$ are the number of chloride ions and chlorine atoms, respectively. From

\[
\exp\left[\frac{e(V-\Phi)}{k T}\right]=10^{-4}
\]

or

\[
e(V-\Phi)=-9.2 k T
\]

substituting $\Phi=5.1 \mathrm{~V}$, $T=1073 \mathrm{~K}$, $1 \mathrm{eV}=1.60 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}=1.16 \times 10^{4} k \mathrm{~K}$, $k=1.38 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{~J} \cdot \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$ into the equation, we obtain the electron affinity of chlorine:

\[
V=4.25 \mathrm{~V}
\]

subject: Statistical Mechanics
problem:
Consider a two-dimensional classical system with a Hamiltonian given by
$$
H=\frac{1}{2m}\left(P_{1}^{2}+P_{2}^{2}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\mu^{2}\left(x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}\right)-\frac{1}{4}\lambda\left(x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}\right)^{2}
$$
This Hamiltonian describes a potential well containing $N$ particles, each with mass $m$, in thermal equilibrium at temperature $T$. When $T$ is very low, the majority of the particles are in the quadratic part of the potential well, but a few high-energy particles can escape from the well. In the one-dimensional profile of the potential, the edge of the potential well is at $x_{1}=b$. Find $b$.
solution: From the Hamiltonian, we obtain $b=\mu / \sqrt{\lambda}$.

subject: Statistical Mechanics
problem:
In a system following Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics, the equilibrium temperature is $T$. The particle number distribution for non-degenerate energy levels is given below. Determine the system temperature $T$.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{Energy} / \mathrm{eV} & \text{Particle number percentage} \\
30.1 \times 10^{-3} & 3.1 \% \\
21.5 \times 10^{-3} & 8.5 \% \\
12.9 \times 10^{-3} & 23 \% \\
4.3 \times 10^{-3} & 63 \%
\end{array}
$$
solution:
The particle number distribution is given by $\frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}} = \mathrm{e}^{\left(\varepsilon_{1} - \varepsilon_{2}\right) / kT}$, so

$$
T = \frac{\varepsilon_{1} - \varepsilon_{2}}{k} \cdot \frac{1}{\ln \left(N_{2} / N_{1}\right)}
$$

By choosing different $N_{1}$ and $N_{2}$, the corresponding $T$ values obtained are:  
99.2; 99.5; 99.0; 99.5; 100.2; 98.8 (K)

Taking the average, we get  

$$
T = 99.4 \, \text{K}
$$

subject: Electrodynamics
topic: Propagation and Radiation of Electromagnetic Waves
problem: a) Determine the average radiated power of a current element with a moment $I l$. Here $l$ is the length of the current element, which is much smaller than the wavelength of the radiation, and $I$ varies as $\cos \omega t$.
solution:
(a) The current element can be regarded as an electric dipole with frequency $\omega$, and its complex form electric dipole moment is $p=p_{0} \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i} \omega t}$. Since $I=\frac{\mathrm{d} q}{\mathrm{~d} t}$, we know $p_{0}=\frac{I l}{\omega}$. Therefore, the average radiated power is

$$
\bar{P}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0}} \cdot \frac{|\ddot{p}|^{2}}{3 c^{2}}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0}} \cdot \frac{I^{2} l^{2} \omega^{2}}{3 c^{2}}
$$

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: A particle with mass $m$, charge $q$, and initial velocity $v$ undergoes a head-on collision with another identical particle at rest. Find: the closest instant velocities of the two particles.
solution:
When the two particles are closest, their relative velocity is zero, meaning they have the same velocity in the center of mass frame. Let this velocity be $v^{\prime}$, and by the conservation of momentum, we have

$$
2 m v^{\prime} = m v, \quad v^{\prime} = \frac{1}{2} v
$$

subject: Atomic Physics
problem:
When the number of ${ }^{238} \mathrm{Pu}$ nuclei decreases over time, its output power also decreases,

$$
W(t) = W(0) \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}
$$

When $W(t_0) = \frac{W(0)}{8}$, this marks the limit time $t_0$ for using ${ }^{238} \mathrm{Pu}$ as a power source for the instrument,

$$
t_0 = \frac{\ln 8}{\lambda} = \frac{3 \ln 2}{\lambda} = 3 T_{1/2} \approx 270 \text { years }
$$

With 238 grams of ${ }^{238} \mathrm{Pu}$ as the energy source, the instrument can operate for 270 years.
solution: When $W(t_0) = \frac{W(0)}{8}$, the limit time $t_0 \approx 270$ years. 238 grams of ${ }^{238} \mathrm{Pu}$ can provide power for 270 years.

subject: Solid-State Physics
topic: Transport Properties of Electrons and Holes in Solids
problem: If silver is considered as a monovalent metal with a spherical Fermi surface, calculate the radius of the Fermi sphere. The density of silver is \(10.5 \ \mathrm{g/cm^3}\) and the atomic weight is \(107.87\).
solution:
The electron concentration of silver \(n = \frac{10.5}{107.87} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 5.86 \times 10^{22} \ \mathrm{cm}^{-3}\).

The radius of the Fermi sphere \(k_{\mathrm{F}}\) is given by:

\[
k_{\mathrm{F}} = 2 \pi \left(\frac{3}{8 \pi} \cdot n\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} = 2 \pi \left(\frac{3}{8 \pi} \times 5.86 \times 10^{22}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} = 1.2 \times 10^{8} \ \mathrm{cm}^{-1}
\]

subject: Thermodynamics
problem: A tube with a length of \(2 \, \text{m}\) and a cross-sectional area of \(10^{-4} \, \text{m}^{2}\) contains \(\text{CO}_{2}\) gas under standard conditions, with half of the \(\text{CO}_{2}\) molecules containing the radioactive isotope \({ }^{14} \text{C}\). At \(t=0\), the number density of the radioactive gas molecules decreases uniformly from the left end of the tube to zero at the right end. Given that the effective diameter of the \(\text{CO}_{2}\) molecule is \(d=3.67 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{m}\), find the initial density gradient of the radioactive gas.
solution:
Under standard conditions, the number density of \(\text{CO}_{2}\) gas molecules is \(n_{0}=2.69 \times 10^{25} \, \text{/m}^3\).  
Initially, the number density \(n(x)\) of the radioactive \(\text{CO}_{2}\) molecules decreases linearly from \(n_{0}\) at the left end to 0 at the right end, so  

\[ n(x) = n_{0}\left(1-\frac{x}{l}\right) \]  

Therefore, the density gradient of the radioactive \(\text{CO}_{2}\) gas molecules is  

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} x} = \frac{\mu}{N_{\mathrm{A}}} \frac{\mathrm{d} n}{\mathrm{d} x} = -\frac{\mu}{N_{\mathrm{A}}} \frac{n_{0}}{l} = -1.03 \, \text{kg/m}^4 \]  

where \(\mu=46 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{kg/mol}\) is the molar mass of \(\text{CO}_{2}\), and \(N_{\mathrm{A}}=6.02 \times 10^{23} \, /\text{mol}\) is Avogadro's number.

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: The fluid moves steadily along the x-direction, with velocity increasing linearly. It is known that the velocity of the fluid element passing through point B, which is at a distance of $l = 50 \text{ cm}$, is $v_{B} = 6 \, \text{m/s}$. Determine the acceleration of the fluid element as it passes through point B. The velocity increases linearly according to $v = \alpha + \beta x$, with point A being the origin of the x-axis.
solution:
Based on the given conditions, at point B:

$$
x = l = 0.50 \, \text{m}, \quad v = v_{B} = 6 \, \text{m/s}
$$

Given the conditions at point A, $\alpha = 2$ and $\beta = 8$ are established,

$$
v = 2 + 8x
$$

The acceleration is:

$$
a = \frac{\partial v}{\partial t} + v \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} = 16(1 + 4x)
$$

Therefore, at point B, where $x = 0.5 \, \text{m}$:

$$
a_{B} = 48 \, \text{m/s}^{2}
$$

subject: Theoretical Mechanics
problem:
Let $\boldsymbol{A}$ be the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector in the central force motion under the inverse square law of force,

$$
\boldsymbol{A} = \boldsymbol{p} \times \boldsymbol{J} - m^{2} \alpha \frac{\boldsymbol{r}}{r}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{J}$ is the angular momentum with respect to the force center, $\alpha$ is the coefficient of the central force, and $\boldsymbol{F} = -\frac{m \alpha}{r^{2}} \boldsymbol{e}_{r}$. Using the properties of Poisson brackets, find $[A_{y}, H]$ (the subscript $y$ denotes the Cartesian coordinate component) and prove that it is a conserved quantity.
solution:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text{Solution} \quad \boldsymbol{A} = \boldsymbol{p} \times \boldsymbol{J} - m^{2} \alpha \frac{\boldsymbol{r}}{r} \\
& \boldsymbol{p} = p_{x} \boldsymbol{i} + p_{y} \boldsymbol{j}, \quad \boldsymbol{r} = x \boldsymbol{i} + y \boldsymbol{j} \\
& \boldsymbol{J} = \boldsymbol{r} \times \boldsymbol{p} = (x p_{y} - y p_{x}) \boldsymbol{k} \\
& \boldsymbol{A} = (p_{x} \boldsymbol{i} + p_{y} \boldsymbol{j}) \times (x p_{y} - y p_{x}) \boldsymbol{k} - m^{2} \alpha \frac{x \boldsymbol{i} + y \boldsymbol{j}}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}} \\
& = \left[x p_{y}^{2} - y p_{x} p_{y} - m^{2} \alpha \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}\right] \boldsymbol{i} + \left[y p_{x}^{2} - x p_{x} p_{y} - m^{2} \alpha \frac{y}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}\right] \boldsymbol{j} \\
& H = \frac{1}{2 m}(p_{x}^{2} + p_{y}^{2}) - \frac{m \alpha}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}} \\
& [A_{y}, H] = [y p_{x}^{2} - x p_{x} p_{y} - m^{2} \alpha \frac{y}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}, \frac{1}{2 m}(p_{x}^{2} + p_{y}^{2}) - \frac{m \alpha}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}] \\
& = [y p_{x}^{2}, \frac{1}{2 m} p_{y}^{2}] - [x p_{x} p_{y}, \frac{1}{2 m} p_{x}^{2}] + [y p_{x}^{2}, -\frac{m \alpha}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}] \\
& + [x p_{x} p_{y}, \frac{m \alpha}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}] - m^{2} \alpha \left[\frac{y}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}, \frac{1}{2 m}(p_{x}^{2} + p_{y}^{2})\right] \\
& = \frac{1}{2 m} p_{x}^{2}[y, p_{y}^{2}] - \frac{1}{2 m} p_{x} p_{y}[x, p_{x}^{2}] - m \alpha y\left[p_{x}^{2}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}\right] \\
& + x p_{x}\left[p_{y}, \frac{m \alpha}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}\right] + x p_{y}\left[p_{x}, \frac{m \alpha}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}\right] \\
& - \frac{1}{2} m \alpha\left[\frac{y}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}, p_{x}^{2}\right] - \frac{1}{2} m \alpha\left[\frac{y}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}, p_{y}^{2}\right] \\
= & \frac{1}{m} p_{x}^{2} p_{y} - \frac{1}{m} p_{x}^{2} p_{y} - m \alpha y \frac{x}{(x^{2} + y^{2})^{3/2}} \cdot 2 p_{x} \\
& + x p_{x} \cdot m \alpha \frac{y}{(x^{2} + y^{2})^{3/2}} + x p_{y} \cdot m \alpha \cdot \frac{x}{(x^{2} + y^{2})^{3/2}} \\
& - \frac{1}{2} m \alpha\left[-\frac{y x}{(x^{2} + y^{2})^{3/2}}\right] \cdot 2 p_{x} - \frac{1}{2} m \alpha\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}} - \frac{y^{2}}{(x^{2} + y^{2})^{3/2}}\right] 2 p_{y} = 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Through calculation, we find that $[A_{y}, H] = 0$, hence it is a conserved quantity.

subject: Relativity
problem:
After an atomic clock is taken around the Earth on a jet plane and compared with an identical, perfectly synchronized clock that remains stationary, what discrepancy does special relativity predict, given appropriate approximations?

Assume that the plane travels at a speed \( v \) in circular motion around the Earth, with the Earth's radius being \( R = 6400 \times 10^{3} \, \mathrm{m} \), and the plane's speed \( v = 1000 \, \mathrm{m/s} \).
solution:
Consider the reference frame of the plane as \( S^{\prime} \) and the Earth's reference frame as \( S \), with \( S^{\prime} \) also being approximately regarded as an inertial frame. According to the Lorentz transformation formula,

\[ t = \frac{t^{\prime} + \frac{v}{c^{2}} x^{\prime}}{\sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^{2}}} \]

Since \(\Delta x^{\prime} = 0\), we have

\[ \Delta t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^{2}}} \Delta t^{\prime} \]

Because \(\frac{v}{c} \ll 1\), it follows that

\[
\begin{gathered}
\Delta t \approx \left(1 + \frac{v^{2}}{2 c^{2}}\right) \Delta t^{\prime} \\
\Delta t - \Delta t^{\prime} = \frac{v^{2}}{2 c^{2}} \Delta t^{\prime}
\end{gathered}
\]

Assume the time measured by the clock on the plane is \(\Delta t^{\prime} = \frac{2 \pi R}{v}\). As the plane travels around the Earth once, during this period,

\[
\Delta t - \Delta t^{\prime} = \frac{v^{2}}{2 c^{2}} \cdot \frac{2 \pi R}{v} = \frac{\pi R v}{c^{2}}
\]

This is the amount by which the clock on the plane is slower than the stationary clock on Earth. Therefore,

\[
\Delta t - \Delta t^{\prime} = \frac{\pi \cdot 6400 \times 10^{3} \times 1000}{\left(3 \times 10^{8}\right)^{2}} = 2.2 \times 10^{-7} \, \mathrm{s}
\]

subject: Thermodynamics
problem: A tube with a length of \(2 \, \text{m}\) and a cross-sectional area of \(10^{-4} \, \text{m}^{2}\) contains \(\text{CO}_{2}\) gas at standard conditions, with half of the \(\text{CO}_{2}\) gas molecules containing the radioactive isotope \({ }^{14} \text{C}\). At \(t=0\), the number density of the radioactive gas molecules decreases uniformly along the tube from the left end to zero at the right end. It is known that the effective diameter of the \(\text{CO}_{2}\) molecule is \(d=3.67 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{m}\). Determine how many radioactive molecules per second move from left to right through the cross-section at the midpoint of the tube.
solution:
At standard conditions, the number density of \(\text{CO}_{2}\) gas molecules is \(n_{0}=2.69 \times 10^{25} / \text{m}^3\).  
Initially, the number of radioactive molecules passing per second from left to right through the cross-section at the midpoint of the tube is given by

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d} N_{1}}{\mathrm{d} t}=\frac{1}{6} n_{1} \bar{v} \Delta S \]

where \(\bar{\lambda}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2} \pi d^{2} n_{0}}=6.21 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{m}\) is the mean free path of \(\text{CO}_{2}\) molecules, and \(n_{1}\) is the number density of radioactive molecules at \(x=\frac{l}{2}-\bar{\lambda}\), with its value approximately given by

\[ n_{1} \approx \frac{n_{0}}{2}-\left.\bar{\lambda} \frac{\mathrm{d} n}{\mathrm{d} x}\right|_{l / 2}=\frac{n_{0}}{2}\left(1+\frac{2 \bar{\lambda}}{l}\right) \]

Therefore,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} N_{1}}{\mathrm{d} t} & =\frac{n_{0}}{12} \bar{v} \Delta S\left(1+\frac{2 \bar{\lambda}}{l}\right)=\frac{n_{0}}{12} \sqrt{\frac{8 R T}{\pi \mu}} \Delta S\left(1+\frac{2 \bar{\lambda}}{l}\right) \\
& =7.94 \times 10^{22}+4.94 \times 10^{15} \, \text{s}^{-1} \approx 7.94 \times 10^{22} \, \text{s}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\]

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: In a hydrogen atom, calculate the interaction energy of the spherically symmetric \(|\psi(\boldsymbol{r})|^{2}\) and \(\rho(\boldsymbol{r})\), and determine the final energy difference using Fermi's formula. Use the \(s\) state.
solution:
Note: Because \(|\psi(\boldsymbol{r})|^{2}\) is spherically symmetric, we find that \(\phi(\boldsymbol{r})\) is also spherically symmetric, and then assume \(\rho(\boldsymbol{r})\) is also spherically symmetric. Perform the following integral:

\[
\int \mathrm{d}^{3} r \, \rho(r) \frac{\partial^{2} \phi(r)}{\partial x_{i} \partial x_{j}} = \frac{\delta_{ij}}{3} \int \mathrm{d}^{3} r \, \rho(r) \nabla^{2} \phi(r)
\]

Thus,

\[
H = \frac{2}{3} \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{p}} \cdot \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{e}} \int \mathrm{d}^{3} r \, \rho(r) \nabla^{2} \phi(r)
\]

Substituting \(\nabla^{2} \phi(\boldsymbol{r}) = -4 \pi |\psi(\boldsymbol{r})|^{2}\) into the above equation gives

\[
H = -\frac{8 \pi}{3} \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{p}} \cdot \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{e}} \int \mathrm{d}^{3} r \, \rho(r) |\psi(r)|^{2}
\]

Additionally, around the proton \(|\psi(\boldsymbol{r})|^{2}\) varies very slowly, so

\[
H = -\frac{8 \pi}{3} \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{p}} \cdot \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{e}} |\psi(0)|^{2} \quad \text{(Fermi's formula)}
= -\frac{8}{3} \frac{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{p}} \cdot \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{e}}}{\pi a^{3} n^{3}} \boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\mathrm{p}} \cdot \boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\mathrm{e}}
\]

where \(n\) is the principal quantum number, \(a = \frac{\hbar}{m e^{2}}\) is the Bohr radius, and \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{p}} = 2.79 \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{N}}\).

\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\mathrm{p}} \cdot \boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\mathrm{e}}= 
\begin{cases}
+1 & \text{triplet state} \\ 
-3 & \text{singlet state}
\end{cases}
\]

Then the energy difference between the singlet and triplet states is

\[
\Delta E = E_{\mathrm{t}} - E_{\mathrm{s}} = \frac{8 \times 2.79}{3} \left( \frac{m_{\mathrm{e}}}{m_{\mathrm{p}}} \right) \alpha^{4} m_{\mathrm{e}} c^{2} \approx 5.89 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{eV}
\]

where

\[
\alpha = \frac{e^{2}}{\hbar c} = \frac{1}{137}
\]

solution:
The rest energy of an electron is \(m_{\mathrm{e}} c^{2} = 8.187 \times 10^{-14} \mathrm{~J} = 0.5110 \mathrm{~MeV}\). \\
Therefore, the frequency of a photon with energy equal to the rest energy of an electron is

\[
\nu = \frac{m_{\mathrm{e}} c^{2}}{h} = 1.2356 \times 10^{20} \mathrm{~Hz}.
\]

subject: Relativity
problem:
There is a transmitter and a receiver on a spaceship that is moving away from Earth at a constant speed. It sends a signal pulse to Earth, and the spaceship's clock receives the signal, which is reflected back from Earth, after 40 seconds. The frequency of the received signal is half of the transmitted frequency:
(3) When the pulse is received by the spaceship, where is the spaceship located as measured from Earth?
solution:
(3) Let the spaceship's reference frame be the $S$ system, and the Earth's reference frame be the $S^{\prime}$ system. At $t=t^{\prime}=0$, the $x$ and $x^{\prime}$ axes, as well as the $y$ and $y^{\prime}$, and $z$ and $z^{\prime}$ axes, coincide. The velocity of the $S^{\prime}$ system relative to the $S$ system is $\frac{1}{3} c$, in the positive direction along the $x$ or $x^{\prime}$ axis.

Let event $A$ be the emission of the pulse by the spaceship, event $B$ the reception and reflection of the pulse by Earth, and event $C$ the reception of the reflected pulse by the spaceship.

Given: $x_{A}=0, x_{B}^{\prime}=0, x_{C}=0, t_{B}-t_{A}=20 \ \text{seconds}, t_{C}-t_{B}=20 \ \text{seconds}$.

Since
$$
x_{B}-x_{A}=c(t_{B}-t_{A})
$$

Therefore, $x_{B}=20 c$,

$$
\begin{gathered}
x_{B}^{\prime}=\frac{x_{B}-v t_{B}}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^{2}}}, \quad x_{C}^{\prime}=\frac{x_{C}-v t_{C}}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^{2}}} \\
x_{C}^{\prime}=x_{C}^{\prime}-x_{B}^{\prime}=\frac{x_{C}-x_{B}-v(t_{C}-t_{B})}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^{2}}} \\
=\frac{-20 c-\frac{1}{3} c \cdot 20}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2}}}=-\frac{80 \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{\sqrt{8}}=-8.5 \times 10^{9} \ \text{meters}
\end{gathered}
$$

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: For any motion in a gravitational field, prove that its energy depends on $m, g,$ and $h$ in the form $E = K m g \left(\frac{m^{2} g}{h^{2}}\right)^{\alpha}$. Determine $\alpha$.
solution:
For a particle in a gravitational field, the Hamiltonian is

$$
H = -\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}x^{2}} + mgx
$$

From dimensional analysis

$$
[H] = [E] = \left[\frac{\hbar^{2}}{mx^{2}}\right] = [mgx], \quad [x] = \left[\frac{m^{2}g}{h^{2}}\right]^{-1/3}
$$

Therefore

$$
[E] = \left[mg\left(\frac{m^{2}g}{h^{2}}\right)^{-1/3}\right]
$$

Thus, it must be

$$
E = K mg\left(\frac{m^{2}g}{h^{2}}\right)^{-1/3}
$$

where $K$ is a dimensionless constant, which means $\alpha = -\frac{1}{3}$.

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: An accelerator produces a beam of charged $\pi$ mesons with a rest average lifetime of $2.6 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~s}$. After traveling a distance of 10 meters, $10 \%$ of the $\pi$ mesons have decayed. Find the momentum of the $\pi$ mesons.
solution:
Let there initially be $N_{0}$ $\pi$ mesons, with velocity $\beta$ (in units of $c$). The decay constant for moving $\pi$ mesons is $\lambda$. After traveling a distance $l$, the number of $\pi$ mesons is

$$
N(l)=N_{0} \exp \left(-\frac{\lambda l}{\beta c}\right)
$$

The decay constant $\lambda$ is

$$
\lambda =\frac{1}{\tau_{0}}=\frac{\sqrt{1-\beta^{2}}}{\tau_{0}}
$$

Thus,

$$
N(l) =N_{0} \exp \left(-\frac{l \sqrt{1-\beta^{2}}}{\tau_{0} \beta c}\right)
$$

We express $\gamma \beta$ as

$$
\gamma \beta =\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{1-\beta^{2}}}=\frac{l}{\tau_{0} \ln \frac{N_{0}}{N(l)}}
$$

Computing gives

$$
\gamma \beta =\frac{10}{2.6 \times 10^{-8} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8} \times \ln \frac{1}{0.9}}=12.2
$$

The momentum of the $\pi$ mesons is

$$
p=m \gamma \beta=0.14 \times 12.2=1.71\ (\mathrm{GeV}/c)
$$

subject: Statistical Mechanics
problem: Consider a heteronuclear diatomic molecule with a moment of inertia $I$. At high temperatures ($\frac{\beta \hbar^{2}}{2 I} \ll 1$ or $kT \gg \frac{\hbar^{2}}{2 I}$), determine the heat capacity $c(T)$ and establish the temperature range for which this approximation is valid.
solution:
Under the high-temperature approximation, $\frac{\beta \hbar^{2}}{2 I} \ll 1$, i.e., $kT \gg \frac{\hbar^{2}}{2 I}$, the summation can be approximated by an integral.

$$
\begin{gathered}
Z=\int_{0}^{\infty} (2x+1) \exp \left[-\frac{\beta \hbar^{2}}{2 I} x(x+1)\right] \mathrm{d}x=\frac{2 I}{\hbar^{2}} kT, \\
\bar{E}=-\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ln Z = kT.
\end{gathered}
$$

Therefore,

$$
c(T)=k.
$$

subject: Geometrical Optics
problem: Determine the normal magnification of a microscope with a numerical aperture \( NA = 1.5 \), assuming the pupil diameter is 3.0 mm.
solution:
The relationship between the numerical aperture of the microscope, magnification, and the diameter of the exit pupil is given by

\[
D' = 2 S_0 \frac{NA}{|M|}
\]

where \( S_0 \) is the standard vision distance of \( 250 \, \text{mm} \), and \( D' \) is the diameter of the microscope's exit pupil. When the exit pupil is reasonably designed to equal the size of the human pupil, the magnification \( M \) is

\[
M = 2 S_0 \frac{NA}{D_e} = \frac{2 \times 250 \times 1.5}{3.0} = 250 \text{ times}
\]

topic: Orbital and Spin Angular Momentum Problems
problem:
There is a spinless particle with a wave function given by

$$
\psi=K(x+y+2z) \mathrm{e}^{-ar}
$$

where $r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}$ and $K, a$ are real constants. If the $z$-component of the angular momentum $L_{z}$ is measured, what is the probability of measuring $L_{z}=+\hbar$?
solution:
Express the wave function in spherical coordinates

$$
\psi=K r(\cos \phi \sin \theta+\sin \phi \sin \theta+2 \cos \theta) \mathrm{e}^{-ar}
$$

After normalization, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
K^{\prime}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{8 \pi}} \\
\psi(\theta, \phi)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{8 \pi}}\left[-\frac{1}{2}(1-\mathrm{i}) \sqrt{\frac{8 \pi}{3}} Y_{11}+\frac{1}{2}(1+\mathrm{i}) \sqrt{\frac{8 \pi}{3}} Y_{1-1}+2 \sqrt{\frac{4 \pi}{3}} Y_{10}\right]
\end{gathered}
$$

The probability of measuring $L_{z}=+\hbar$ is given by $P\left(\right.$ finding $\left.L_{z}=+\hbar\right)=\left|\left\langle L_{z}=+\hbar \mid \psi(\theta, \phi)\right\rangle\right|^{2}=\frac{1}{8 \pi} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{8 \pi}{3}=\frac{1}{6}$.

Provide the Schrdinger equation with \(T = -\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{~d} y^{2}}\) and \(V = y^{2}\) as the kinetic and potential energy operators, respectively. subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: Consider a particle with the wave function $\psi(r, \theta, \varphi) = A \mathrm{e}^{-r / a_{0}}$, where $A$ and $a_{0}$ are constants. Determine the angular momentum of this state.
solution:
Since $L^{2}, L_{x}, L_{y}, L_{z}$ only depend on $\theta$ and $\varphi$, and $\psi$ does not depend on $\theta$ and $\varphi$, we have

$$
L^{2} \psi = 0, \quad L_{z} \psi = 0, \quad L_{x} \psi = 0, \quad L_{y} \psi = 0
$$

Thus, the angular momentum and each of its components for this state are zero. In fact, $\psi(r, \theta, \varphi) = \sqrt{4 \pi} A \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{r}{a_{0}}} Y_{0,0}(\theta, \varphi)$.

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: The mass of the $J/\psi$ particle is $3.097 \, \text{GeV}/c^{2}$, and it undergoes a complete symmetric decay $J/\psi \rightarrow e^{+} + e^{-}$. Given that the momentum of the $J/\psi$ is $100 \, \text{GeV}/c$ and it decays symmetrically, find the angle between the electron and the $J/\psi$ particle in the laboratory frame.
solution:
Let $\theta$ be the angle between the electron and the $J/\psi$ particle. Momentum conservation requires:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{\mathrm{J}} &= 2p_{\mathrm{e}} \cos \theta \\
\left(\frac{E_{\mathrm{J}}}{2}\right)^{2} &- \left(\frac{p_{\mathrm{J}}}{2\cos \theta}\right)^{2} = E_{\mathrm{e}}^{2} - p_{\mathrm{e}}^{2} = m_{\mathrm{e}}^{2} \\
\cos \theta &= \frac{p_{\mathrm{J}}}{\sqrt{p_{\mathrm{J}}^{2} + m_{\mathrm{J}}^{2} - 4m_{\mathrm{e}}^{2}}} \\
&= \frac{100}{\sqrt{100^{2} + 3.097^{2} + 4 \times (0.511 \times 10^{-3})^{2}}} \\
&= 0.9995
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence:

$$
\theta = 1.77^{\circ}
$$

then

& =\frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0}}\left[-\oint_{L} \mathrm{d}\left(\frac{1}{r}\right)+2 \sqrt{\alpha} \oint_{L} \mathrm{d}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{r}}\right)\right]=0
\end{aligned}

From Coulomb's law $\boldsymbol{F}_{12}=\frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0} r^{2}} \boldsymbol{e}_{r_{12}}$, the electric field of a point charge is

It is clear that

\boldsymbol{E}(r)=\frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0} r^{2}} \boldsymbol{e}_{r}
$$

$$

which is the same as the result obtained for this problem.

subject: Atomic Physics
problem:
Use a gaseous nuclear beam to bombard a thick target of ${ }^{55} \mathrm{Mn}$, producing the radioactive element ${ }^{56} \mathrm{Mn}$, which has a half-life of $T_{1/2}$. The gaseous nuclear beam has a current of $i$, the beam area is $1 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$, the target thickness is $l$, and the reaction cross-section is $\sigma$. Calculate the number of radioactive nuclei ${ }^{56} \mathrm{Mn}$ present after an irradiation time $t$:

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
i=4.8 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~A} & T_{1/2}=2.6 \mathrm{~h} & t=5.2 \mathrm{~h} \\
l=110 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} & \sigma=10^{-25} \mathrm{~cm}^{2} &
\end{array}
$$
solution:
Let the irradiation flux be $\Phi=i / (S e)$, where $e$ is the charge of the gaseous nucleus, and $S$ is the beam area. The half-life of ${ }^{56} \mathrm{Mn}$ is $T_{1/2}$, with $\lambda =\frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$. $N_{56}(t)$ represents the number of ${ }^{56} \mathrm{Mn}$ nuclei after an irradiation time $t$. The gaseous nuclear beam reacts with the target nuclei ${ }^{55} \mathrm{Mn}$ producing ${ }^{56} \mathrm{Mn}$ nuclei within its range in the target. Within the target, the total number of target nuclei ${ }^{55} \mathrm{Mn}$ per unit area is $N_{55}=\frac{N_{0} l}{A}$, where $A$ is the mass number of ${ }^{55} \mathrm{Mn}$. Note the unit of thickness is $\mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$. Initially, consider the effect of target thickness on the beam, where the intensity after passing through the target is $\Phi^{\prime}$, given by:

$$
\Phi^{\prime}=\Phi e^{-\frac{N_{0} l}{A}}=\Phi e^{-\frac{10^{-25} \times 6.023 \times 10^{23} \times 0.11}{55}}=0.99988 \Phi \approx \Phi
$$

Thus, we can neglect the decay of the beam in the target. The production rate of ${ }^{56} \mathrm{Mn}$ nuclei is:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d} N_{56}}{\mathrm{~d} t}=\Phi \sigma \frac{N_{0} l}{A}-\lambda N_{56}=N^{\prime}-\lambda N_{56}
$$

Where $N^{\prime}=\Phi \sigma \frac{N_{0} l}{A}$, let $N_{1}=N_{56}-N^{\prime} / \lambda$, the differential equation becomes:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d} N_{1}}{\mathrm{~d} t}=-\lambda N_{1}
$$

Initial condition: $N_{56}(t=0)=0, N_{1}(0)=-N^{\prime} / \lambda=-\frac{\Phi \sigma N_{0} l}{\lambda A}$. Solving the differential equation gives:

$$
\begin{gathered}
N_{1}(t)=N_{1}(0) e^{-\lambda t}=-\frac{\Phi \sigma N_{0} l}{A \lambda} e^{-\lambda t} \\
N_{56}(t)=\frac{N^{\prime}}{\lambda}+N_{1}=\frac{\Phi \sigma N_{0} l}{A \lambda}\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

With specific numerical values:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Phi=\frac{i}{e}=\frac{4.8 \times 10^{-6}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}=3 \times 10^{13} \, (\mathrm{s}^{-1}) \\
& \frac{N_{0} l}{A}=\frac{6.023 \times 10^{23} \times 0.11}{55}=1.2 \times 10^{21} \, (\mathrm{cm}^{-2}) \\
& \lambda=\frac{\ln 2}{2.6 \times 3600}=7.4 \times 10^{-5} \, (\mathrm{s}^{-1}) \\
& t=5.2 \times 3600=1.87 \times 10^{4} \, (\mathrm{s}) \\
& \sigma=10^{-25} \, \mathrm{cm}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the above expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_{56}(5.2 \, \mathrm{h}) & =\frac{3 \times 10^{13} \times 10^{-25} \times 1.2 \times 10^{21}\left(1-e^{-0.74 \times 1.87}\right)}{7.4 \times 10^{-5}} \\
& =3.65 \times 10^{13}
\end{aligned}
$$

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: Based on the calculation results of the moment of inertia of the HCl molecule, estimate the distance $R$ between the two nuclei in the HCl molecule.
solution:
It is known that $I = \mu R^2, \quad \mu^{-1} = m_{\mathrm{H}}^{-1} + m_{\mathrm{Cl}}^{-1}, R$ is the distance between the two nuclei.

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
R & = \left[\frac{\left(m_{\mathrm{H}} + m_{\mathrm{Cl}}\right) I}{m_{\mathrm{H}} \cdot m_{\mathrm{Cl}}}\right]^{1/2} \\
& = \left[\frac{(1 + 35)}{1 \times 35 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}} \times 2.72 \times 10^{-48}\right]^{1/2} \\
& = 1.30 \times 10^{-10}(\mathrm{m}) = 1.30(\mathrm{\AA})
\end{aligned}
$$
