\]

subject: Wave Optics
problem: Given the following data, calculate the dispersion power of a grating. Grating width \(D=5 \mathrm{~cm}\), line density \(1/d=600\) lines/\(\mathrm{mm}\), and assume \(\lambda=5000 \, \text{}\).
solution:
Typically, when natural light is reflected at the interface of two media, the reflected light is partially polarized. However, when the angle of incidence satisfies

$$
\theta_{B}=\arctan \frac{n_{1}}{n_{0}}
$$

where $n_{0}$ and $n_{1}$ are the refractive indices of the incident medium and the refractive medium respectively, the reflected light is linearly polarized with vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence. This angle $\theta_{B}$ is called the Brewster's angle or the polarization angle.

The calculations for $r, R, \bar{R}$, and $t, T, \bar{T}$ for the $S$ and $P$ components are based on Fresnel's equations. Because the angle of incidence is Brewster's angle, the sum of the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction is $\frac{\pi}{2}$. Intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, while energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam. The reflected light and incident light are in the same medium, with equal cross-sectional areas, while the refracted light and incident light are in different media, with different cross-sectional areas, which is noteworthy.

1. According to Fresnel's equations, the amplitude reflectance $r_{s}$ and amplitude transmittance $t_{s}$ for the $S$ component are

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{s}=\frac{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}-n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}=-\frac{\sin \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\
t_{s}=\frac{2 n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{2 \sin \theta_{2} \cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

The amplitude reflectance $r_{P}$ and amplitude transmittance $t_{P}$ for the $P$ component are

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{P}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}-n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{\tan \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}{\tan \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

where $n_{1}=1$, $n_{2}=n=1.50$, $\theta_{1}$ is the angle of incidence, and $\theta_{2}$ is the angle of refraction. Since the angle of incidence is the Brewster's angle, we have

$$
\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}=\arctan n=\arctan 1.50=56.3^{\circ}
$$

Additionally,

$$
\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}
$$

Substituting into the formulas for $r_{s}$ and $r_{p}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{s}=-\frac{\sin \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}{\sin \left(56.3^{\circ}+33.7^{\circ}\right)}=-0.384 \\
r_{p}=0
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the reflected light and incident light are in the same medium with equal cross-sectional areas, the intensity reflectance $R_{S}$ and $R_{P}$, as well as the energy flow reflectance $\bar{R}_{S}$ and $\bar{R}_{P}$ for the $S$ and $P$ components respectively, are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& R_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad R_{P}=0 \\
& \bar{R}_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad \bar{R}_{P}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

For the refracted light, substituting $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ into $t_{s}$ and $t_{P}$, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
t_{s}=\frac{2 \sin \theta_{2} \cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \sin 33.7^{\circ} \cos 56.3^{\circ}}{\sin \frac{\pi}{2}}=0.616 \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \cos 56.3^{\circ} \sin 33.7^{\circ}}{\cos \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}=0.667
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the refracted light and incident light are in different media with different cross-sectional areas, the intensity transmittance and energy flow transmittance are not simply equal to the square of the amplitude transmittance. The intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, given by

$$
\widetilde{S}=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_{0} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}{\mu_{0} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}}} E^{2}
$$

where $E$ is the amplitude of the electric vector. Since $\mu_{\mathrm{r}} \approx 1$, and the speed of light in vacuum $c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{0}} \mu_{0}}$, and the refractive index $n=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}} \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}$, this can be rewritten as

$$
\bar{S}=\frac{1}{2 c \mu_{0}} n E^{2}
$$

Thus, the intensity is proportional to $n E^{2}$, and the intensity transmittance is

$$
T=\frac{\bar{S}_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1}}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t^{2}
$$

The intensity transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& T_{S}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{S}^{2}=n t_{S}^{2}=0.569 \\
& T_{P}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{P}^{2}=n t_{P}^{2}=0.667
\end{aligned}
$$

The energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam, and the ratio of the cross-sectional areas of the refracted beam to the incident beam is $\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}}$, so the energy flow transmittance is

$$
\bar{T}=\frac{\bar{S}_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}} t^{2}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T
$$

Substituting the values, the energy flow transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{gathered}
\bar{T}_{S}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{S}=0.853 \\
\bar{T}_{P}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{P}=1
\end{gathered}
$$

The fact that the energy flow transmittance $\bar{T}_{P}=1$ for the $P$ component is expected because, when light is incident at the Brewster's angle $\left(\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}\right)$, the reflected light does not contain any $P$ component, meaning the entire energy of the incident $P$ component is transmitted.

problem: A particle moves along a helical path under the force $\boldsymbol{F}=4y \boldsymbol{i} + 2x \boldsymbol{j} + \boldsymbol{k}$, where the parametric equations of the path are $x=4 \cos \theta, y=4 \sin \theta, z=2 \theta$ from $\theta=0$ to $\theta=2\pi$. subject: Solid-State Physics
problem: Given that X-rays produce Bragg reflection on a crystal. The relative error in the measurement of the crystal structure's density and mass is \(3 \times 10^{-4}\). When the angle between the incident and reflected rays and the crystal surface is \(6^{\circ}\), the error is \(3.4^{\prime}\) (in radian units). Determine the relative error of the X-ray wavelength.
solution:
For simplicity, assume the crystal structure's unit cell is a simple cube with a side length of \(d\). (For unit cells of other structures, the difference is just a coefficient close to 1).

From the Bragg reflection formula:

\[
2d \sin \theta = n \lambda
\]

If we take \(n=1\), then

\[
2d \sin \theta = \lambda
\]

Differentiating the above equation gives:

\[
\frac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda} = \frac{\Delta d}{d} + \cot \theta \cdot \Delta \theta
\]

And the volume of the crystal unit cell:

\[
\Omega = d^{3} = \frac{M}{\rho N_{0}}
\]

where: \(M\) is the molar mass, \(\rho\) is the density of the crystal.\\
Differentiating the above equation gives:

\[
\frac{\Delta d}{d} = \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} - \frac{\Delta M}{M}\right)
\]

According to the problem:

\[
\frac{\Delta M}{M} = \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} = 3 \times 10^{-4}
\]

Therefore:

\[
\frac{\Delta d}{d} = 0
\]

Thus, we have:

\[
\frac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda} = \cot \theta \cdot \Delta \theta
\]

Substituting \(\theta = 6^{\circ}\) and \(\Delta \theta = 3.4^{\prime}\) into the equation gives:

\[
\frac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda} \approx 10^{-2}
\]

subject: Classical Electromagnetism
problem: A long thin wire carries a current $I$ and is located at a distance $d$ from a semi-infinite iron block. Assume the permeability of the iron block is infinite. Suppose the magnitude of the image current inside the iron block is $I^{\prime}$, located at $x=-d$. Determine the magnitude and direction of $I^{\prime}$.
solution:
We solve this using the method of images. Let the image current be $I^{\prime}$, located at $x=-d$, with its direction opposite to that of $I$. Its magnitude is given by

$$
I^{\prime}=\frac{\mu-\mu_{0}}{\mu+\mu_{0}} I.
$$

Since $\mu \rightarrow \infty$, it follows that $I^{\prime}=I$.

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: The interaction between an atom and an ion can be described by the potential energy $V(r) = -c r^{-4}$, where $c = \frac{e^{2} p_{a}^{2}}{2}$, $e$ is the ion charge, and $p_{a}$ is the polarizability of the atom. Assuming the ion is much lighter than the atom, find the cross-section $\sigma(v_{0})$ for the ion to hit the atom (that is, to penetrate to $r=0$).
solution:
Assume an ion with energy $E$ and angular momentum $J$ with respect to the center of force is incident towards the atom from infinity,
$$
\frac{1}{2} m \dot{r}^{2} + U(r) = E
$$
At $r = r_{\text{min}}$, $\dot{r} = 0$, so the equation satisfied by $r_{\text{min}}$ is
$$
U(r) = E
$$
which is
$$
\begin{gathered}
-\frac{c}{r^{4}} + \frac{J^{2}}{2 m r^{2}} = E \\
2 m r^{4} E - J^{2} r^{2} + 2 m c = 0 \\
r_{\min}^{2} = \frac{J^{2} \pm \sqrt{J^{4} - 16 m^{2} c E}}{4 m E}
\end{gathered}
$$
When $E = \frac{J^{4}}{16 m^{2} c} = U_{0}$, $r_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{\frac{J^{2}}{4 m \cdot \frac{J^{4}}{16 m^{2} c}}} = \frac{2 \sqrt{m c}}{J}$, which cannot hit the atom;  
When $E < \frac{J^{4}}{16 m^{2} c}$, i.e., $E < U_{0}$, $r_{\min} > \frac{2 \sqrt{m c}}{J}$. This can be derived from the effective potential energy graph. For an ion incident from infinity, the formula for $r_{\text{min}}^{2}$ above can only take $r_{\text{min}}^{2} = \frac{J^{2} + \sqrt{J^{4} - 16 m^{2} c E}}{4 m E}$,  
When $E > \frac{J^{4}}{16 m^{2} c}$, i.e., $E > U_{0}$, $r_{\text{min}}$ is complex. This indicates no $r_{\text{min}}$; from the effective potential energy graph, it is evident that the ion will penetrate to $r = 0$ (when $J = 0$) or $r \rightarrow 0$ (when $J \neq 0$), both cases can be considered as hitting the atom.
$$
J = m \rho v_{0}, \quad \rho = \frac{J}{m v_{0}}
$$
where $\rho$ is the impact parameter of the ion when incident from infinity.
$$
E = \frac{1}{2} m v_{0}^{2}
$$
To hit the atom, $E > U_{0}$, i.e., $E > \frac{J^{4}}{16 m^{2} c}$.  
The maximum impact parameter for an ion incident from infinity at velocity $v_{0}$ to hit the atom is
$$
\begin{aligned}
\rho_{\max}(v_{0}) & = \frac{J_{\max}}{m v_{0}} < \frac{\left(\frac{1}{2} m v_{0}^{2} \cdot 16 m^{2} c\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}}{m v_{0}} = \left(8 m^{-1} c v_{0}^{-2}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}} \\
\sigma(v_{0}) & = \pi \rho_{\max}^{2}(v_{0}) < \pi \left(8 m^{-1} c v_{0}^{-2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{2 \pi}{v_{0}} \sqrt{\frac{2 c}{m}}
\end{aligned}
$$

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: Three identical blocks, each with mass \(m\), are stacked on a horizontal surface. The coefficient of friction between each contact surface is \(\mu\). A horizontal force \(F\) starting from zero is continuously increased and applied to the bottom block. What is the magnitude of \(F\) when the bottom block can begin to move relative to the two blocks above it?
solution:
Assuming that in the critical state where the bottom block is on the verge of moving relative to the two blocks above it, their common acceleration is \(a\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
& 3ma = F - 3\mu mg \\
& ma = F - 3\mu mg - 2\mu mg
\end{aligned}
\]

Eliminating \(a\) yields

\[
F = 6\mu mg
\]

Since there is initially no relative motion, \(F\) must increase from zero to \(6\mu mg\) without causing relative motion. Thus, \(F\) must be slightly greater than \(6\mu mg\) for relative motion to occur.

subject: Semiconductor Physics
problem: Given a single crystal of Ge with an Sb impurity concentration of \(8.4 \times 10^{14} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}\), assuming the impurities are fully ionized and \(\mu_{\mathrm{n}}=0.39 \mathrm{~m}^{2} / \mathrm{V} \cdot \mathrm{s}\), calculate the resistivity of this Ge single crystal.
solution:
Under the assumption of full ionization, \(n = N_{\mathrm{D}}\). Therefore, the resistivity of the material is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\rho & = \frac{1}{\sigma} \approx \frac{1}{n e \mu_{\mathrm{n}} + p e \mu_{\mathrm{p}}} = \frac{1}{n e \mu_{\mathrm{n}}} = \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{D}} e \mu_{\mathrm{n}}} \\
& = \frac{1}{8.4 \times 10^{14} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0.39} = 1.9 \times 10^{-2}(\Omega \mathrm{~m}) = 1.9(\Omega \mathrm{~cm})
\end{aligned}
\]

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: At point $A$, located on the same vertical plane and horizontal line, a small ball is launched at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with an initial speed of $v_{AO} = 9.8 \mathrm{~m/s}$. It is known that when the ball reaches the highest point of its trajectory, another ball launched from point $B$ is intended to meet it at its own highest point. Determine the time $t$ required for the balls to meet.
solution:
According to the kinematics formula, the vertical component of the ball's velocity is zero at the highest point of its trajectory. Therefore, we have:

$$
v_{AO} \sin 30^{\circ} - g t = 0
$$

Solving for the meeting time:

$$
t = \frac{v_{AO} \sin 30^{\circ}}{g} = \frac{9.8 \sin 30^{\circ}}{9.8} = 0.5 \mathrm{~s}
$$

subject: Solid-State Physics
topic: Motion of Electrons in Electromagnetic Fields
problem:
Consider the electron energy band of a one-dimensional crystal, which can be expressed as

\[
E(k)=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{m a^{2}}\left(\frac{7}{8}-\cos k a+\frac{1}{8} \cos 2 k a\right)
\]

where \(a\) is the lattice constant. Calculate the width of the energy band.
solution:
From the condition of extremum,

\[
\frac{d E(k)}{d k}=0
\]

we obtain

\[
\sin k a-\frac{1}{4} \sin 2 k a=\sin k a \left(1-\frac{1}{2} \cos k a\right)=0
\]

For the above equation to equal zero, the only solution is \(\sin k a=0\), corresponding to the two extremum points

\[
k=0, \frac{\pi}{a}
\]

When \(k=0\), \(E(k)\) takes the minimum value, which is the bottom of the energy band:

\[
E(k=0)=E_{\min }=0
\]

When \(k=\frac{\pi}{a}\), \(E(k)\) takes the maximum value, which corresponds to the top of the energy band:

\[
E\left(k=\frac{\pi}{a}\right)=E_{\max }=\frac{2 \hbar^{2}}{m a^{2}}
\]

Thus, the width of the energy band is

\[
\Delta E=E_{\max }-E_{\min }=\frac{2 \hbar^{2}}{m a^{2}}
\]

For the refracted light, substituting $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ into $t_{s}$ and $t_{P}$, we have

\begin{gathered}
t_{s}=\frac{2 \sin \theta_{2} \cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \sin 33.7^{\circ} \cos 56.3^{\circ}}{\sin \frac{\pi}{2}}=0.616 \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \cos 56.3^{\circ} \sin 33.7^{\circ}}{\cos \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}=0.667
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the refracted light and incident light are in different media with different cross-sectional areas, the intensity transmittance and energy flow transmittance are not simply equal to the square of the amplitude transmittance. The intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, given by

$$
\widetilde{S}=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_{0} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}{\mu_{0} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}}} E^{2}
$$

where $E$ is the amplitude of the electric vector. Since $\mu_{\mathrm{r}} \approx 1$, and the speed of light in vacuum $c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{0}} \mu_{0}}$, and the refractive index $n=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}} \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}$, this can be rewritten as

$$
\bar{S}=\frac{1}{2 c \mu_{0}} n E^{2}
$$

Thus, the intensity is proportional to $n E^{2}$, and the intensity transmittance is

$$
T=\frac{\bar{S}_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1}}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t^{2}
$$

The intensity transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& T_{S}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{S}^{2}=n t_{S}^{2}=0.569 \\
& T_{P}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{P}^{2}=n t_{P}^{2}=0.667
\end{aligned}
$$

The energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam, and the ratio of the cross-sectional areas of the refracted beam to the incident beam is $\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}}$, so the energy flow transmittance is

$$
\bar{T}=\frac{\bar{S}_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}} t^{2}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T
$$

Substituting the values, the energy flow transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{gathered}
\bar{T}_{S}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{S}=0.853 \\
\bar{T}_{P}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{P}=1
\end{gathered}
$$

The fact that the energy flow transmittance $\bar{T}_{P}=1$ for the $P$ component is expected because, when light is incident at the Brewster's angle $\left(\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}\right)$, the reflected light does not contain any $P$ component, meaning the entire energy of the incident $P$ component is transmitted.

$$
\theta_{B}=\arctan \frac{n_{1}}{n_{0}}
$$

where $n_{0}$ and $n_{1}$ are the refractive indices of the incident medium and the refractive medium respectively, the reflected light is linearly polarized with vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence. This angle $\theta_{B}$ is called the Brewster's angle or the polarization angle.

The calculations for $r, R, \bar{R}$, and $t, T, \bar{T}$ for the $S$ and $P$ components are based on Fresnel's equations. Because the angle of incidence is Brewster's angle, the sum of the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction is $\frac{\pi}{2}$. Intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, while energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam. The reflected light and incident light are in the same medium, with equal cross-sectional areas, while the refracted light and incident light are in different media, with different cross-sectional areas, which is noteworthy.

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{s}=\frac{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}-n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}=-\frac{\sin \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\

\end{gathered}
$$

The amplitude reflectance $r_{P}$ and amplitude transmittance $t_{P}$ for the $P$ component are

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{P}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}-n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{\tan \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}{\tan \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

where $n_{1}=1$, $n_{2}=n=1.50$, $\theta_{1}$ is the angle of incidence, and $\theta_{2}$ is the angle of refraction. Since the angle of incidence is the Brewster's angle, we have

$$
\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}=\arctan n=\arctan 1.50=56.3^{\circ}
$$

Additionally,

$$
\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}
$$

Substituting into the formulas for $r_{s}$ and $r_{p}$, we obtain

\begin{gathered}

\end{gathered}

$$
\begin{aligned}
& R_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad R_{P}=0 \\
& \bar{R}_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad \bar{R}_{P}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

For the refracted light, substituting $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ into $t_{s}$ and $t_{P}$, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
t_{s}=\frac{2 \sin \theta_{2} \cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \sin 33.7^{\circ} \cos 56.3^{\circ}}{\sin \frac{\pi}{2}}=0.616 \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \cos 56.3^{\circ} \sin 33.7^{\circ}}{\cos \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}=0.667
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the refracted light and incident light are in different media with different cross-sectional areas, the intensity transmittance and energy flow transmittance are not simply equal to the square of the amplitude transmittance. The intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, given by

$$
\widetilde{S}=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_{0} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}{\mu_{0} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}}} E^{2}
$$

where $E$ is the amplitude of the electric vector. Since $\mu_{\mathrm{r}} \approx 1$, and the speed of light in vacuum $c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{0}} \mu_{0}}$, and the refractive index $n=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}} \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}$, this can be rewritten as

$$
\bar{S}=\frac{1}{2 c \mu_{0}} n E^{2}
$$

Thus, the intensity is proportional to $n E^{2}$, and the intensity transmittance is

$$
T=\frac{\bar{S}_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1}}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t^{2}
$$

The intensity transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& T_{S}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{S}^{2}=n t_{S}^{2}=0.569 \\
& T_{P}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{P}^{2}=n t_{P}^{2}=0.667
\end{aligned}
$$

The energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam, and the ratio of the cross-sectional areas of the refracted beam to the incident beam is $\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}}$, so the energy flow transmittance is

$$
\bar{T}=\frac{\bar{S}_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}} t^{2}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T
$$

Substituting the values, the energy flow transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{gathered}
\bar{T}_{S}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{S}=0.853 \\
\bar{T}_{P}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{P}=1
\end{gathered}

The fact that the energy flow transmittance $\bar{T}_{P}=1$ for the $P$ component is expected because, when light is incident at the Brewster's angle $\left(\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}\right)$, the reflected light does not contain any $P$ component, meaning the entire energy of the incident $P$ component is transmitted.

subject: Wave Optics
problem: A monochromatic linearly polarized light is incident perpendicularly on a calcite crystal, with its vibration direction making an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the principal plane. The calcite crystal separates the light into the extraordinary ($e$) ray and the ordinary ($o$) ray. Then, after passing through a Nicol prism located behind the calcite, the principal plane of the prism makes an angle of $50^{\circ}$ with the original incident light's vibration direction. Determine the relative intensity of the two rays.
solution:
As illustrated, after passing through the calcite crystal, the monochromatic linearly polarized light is decomposed into the $e$ ray and the $o$ ray, with their amplitudes given by  

$$
A_{\mathrm{e}} = A \cos \alpha, \quad A_{\mathrm{o}} = A \sin \alpha
$$

After passing through the Nicol prism, their amplitudes become  

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{1} &= A_{\mathrm{e}} \cos (\alpha+\beta) = A \cos (\alpha+\beta) \cdot \cos \alpha, \\
A_{2} &= A_{\mathrm{o}} \sin (\alpha+\beta) = A \sin (\alpha+\beta) \cdot \sin \alpha
\end{aligned}
$$

The intensity ratio of the two beams is  

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{I_{2}}{I_{1}} &= \frac{A_{2}^{2}}{A_{1}^{2}} = \tan^{2}(\alpha+\beta) \cdot \tan^{2} \alpha = \tan^{2}(30^{\circ} + 50^{\circ}) \cdot \tan^{2} 30^{\circ} \\
&= 10.72
\end{aligned}
$$

problem: Given that the two eigen wave functions describing the one-dimensional bound state of a single particle are $\psi_{1}=A \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{1}{2} \alpha^{2} x^{2}}$ and $\psi_{2}=B\left(x^{2}+b x+c\right) \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{1}{2} \alpha^{2} x^{2}}$, where $A, B, b, c$ are all real constants, $-\infty<x<\infty$, please determine the value of $c$.
solution:
By the orthogonal condition $\left\langle\psi_{1} \mid \psi_{2}\right\rangle=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \psi_{1}^{*}(x) \psi_{2}(x) \mathrm{d} x=0$, it can be deduced that $c=-\frac{1}{2 \alpha}$, therefore

$$

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: A thermal neutron beam with a flux of $10^{12} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} \cdot \mathrm{s}$ bombards a gold foil with a thickness of 0.02 cm, resulting in the production of the nuclide ${ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}$, which has a half-life of 2.7 days, through the reaction ${ }^{197} \mathrm{Au}(\mathrm{n}, \gamma){ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}$. The density of gold is $19.3 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$, the reaction cross-section is $97.8 \times 10^{-24} \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$, and the gold content is $100\%$. Calculate the activity of ${ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}$ in the foil after 5 minutes of irradiation.
solution:
Before irradiation, the number of target nuclei of ${ }^{197} \mathrm{Au}$ per unit area is

$$
N_{1}(0)=\frac{0.02 \times 19.3}{197} \times 6.023 \times 10^{23} = 1.18 \times 10^{21} \left(\mathrm{~cm}^{-2}\right)
$$

Let $N_{1}$ and $N_{2}$ be the number of nuclei of ${ }^{197} \mathrm{Au}$ and ${ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}$ at time $t$, respectively; $\sigma$ is the $(\mathrm{n}, \gamma)$ reaction cross-section, $I$ is the flux of the incident neutron beam, and $\lambda$ is the decay constant of ${ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}$.

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{\mathrm{d} N_{1}}{\mathrm{~d} t} = -\sigma I N_{1} \\
\frac{\mathrm{~d} N_{2}}{\mathrm{~d} t} = \sigma I N_{1} - \lambda N_{2} \approx \sigma I N_{1}(0) - \lambda N_{2}
\end{gathered}
$$

After integration, the values of $N_{1}$ and $N_{2}$ at time $t$ are:

$$
\begin{gathered}
N_{1} = N_{1}(0) \mathrm{e}^{-\sigma I t} \\
N_{2} = \frac{\sigma I}{\lambda - \sigma I} N_{1}\left(\mathrm{e}^{-\sigma I t} - \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\right) \\
\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{2.7 \times 24 \times 3600} \approx 2.97 \times 10^{-6} \left(\mathrm{~s}^{-1}\right) \\
\sigma I = 97.8 \times 10^{-24} \times 10^{12} = 9.78 \times 10^{-11} \left(\mathrm{~s}^{-1}\right) \ll \lambda
\end{gathered}
$$

At $t = 300 \mathrm{~s}$, since $\lambda - \sigma I \approx \lambda$ and $\mathrm{e}^{-\sigma I t} \approx 1$, the activity of ${ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}$ is

$$
\begin{gathered}
A(300 \mathrm{~s}) = \lambda N_{2} \approx \sigma I N_{1}(0)\left(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\right) \\
= 9.78 \times 10^{-11} \times 1.18 \times 10^{21} \times \left(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-2.97 \times 10^{-6} \times 300}\right) \\
= 1.03 \times 10^{8} \left(\mathrm{~cm}^{-2} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: An infinite, homogeneous thin plate has a circular hole with a radius of \(a\) cut out, and a homogeneous spherical shell with a radius of \(a\) is placed in the hole, with the center of the circular hole coinciding with the center of the spherical shell. What is the minimum work required to move a particle of mass \(m\) from the center of the hole at point \(O\) to point \(P\) on the line perpendicular to the thin plate passing through \(O\) at a distance \(h\) from \(O\) (where \(h \geq a\))?
solution:
The minimum work \(W\) required in this process must overcome the gravitational work done by both the thin plate and the spherical shell.

$$
W=-\left(W_{1}+W_{2}\right)=2 \pi G m \sigma \left[\left(h^{2}+a^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}+a-\frac{2 a^{2}}{h}\right]
$$

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: The coefficients in the binding energy formula are derived from experimental data. Provide the parameter values given by Weizscker.
solution:
The decay of the charged intermediate boson

\[
\mathrm{W}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{e}^{+} + \nu
\]

The Feynman diagram is shown in Figure 3.20. In the diagram, \(\varepsilon^{\mu}(k)\) is the vector wave function of the \(\mathrm{W}^{+}\) particle, where \(\mu=0,1,2,3\). \(\nu\left(\boldsymbol{p}_{2}\right)\) and \(\overline{\mathrm{u}}\left(\boldsymbol{p}_{1}\right)\) are the Dirac wave functions for the positron and neutrino, respectively. The interaction matrix element and its Hermitian conjugate are:

\[
M_{\mathrm{W} \rightarrow \mathrm{e}^{+}}=\frac{-\mathrm{i}g}{\sqrt{2}} \overline{\mathrm{u}}\left(p_{1}\right) \gamma_{\mu} \cdot \frac{1-\gamma_{5}}{2} \cdot \nu\left(p_{2}\right) \cdot \varepsilon^{\mu}(k)
\]

\[
M_{\mathrm{W} \rightarrow \mathrm{e}^{+}}^{+}=\frac{\mathrm{i} g}{\sqrt{2}} \bar{\nu}\left(p_{2}\right) \gamma_{\nu} \cdot \frac{1-\gamma_{5}}{2} \cdot \mathrm{u}\left(p_{1}\right) \cdot \varepsilon^{\nu}(k)
\]

where \(\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\gamma_{5}\right)\) is the left-handed projection operator. We obtain the square of the decay matrix element:

\[
|M|^{2}=M M^{+}=\frac{g^{2}}{2} \bar{\nu}\left(p_{2}\right) \gamma_{\nu} \cdot \frac{1-\gamma_{5}}{2} \cdot \mathrm{u}\left(p_{1}\right) \overline{\mathrm{u}}\left(p_{1}\right) \gamma_{\mu} \cdot \frac{1-\gamma_{5}}{2} \cdot \nu\left(p_{2}\right) \cdot \varepsilon^{\mu}(k) \cdot \varepsilon^{\nu}(k)
\]

where

\[
\mathrm{u} \overline{\mathrm{u}} = \not{p}_1 + m
\]

\[
\nu \bar{\nu} = \not{p}_2 - m
\]

\[
m_{\nu} \approx m_{\mathrm{e}} \approx 0
\]

When summing over the unpolarized states of \(\mathrm{W}^{+}\), we get:

\[
\sum_{\lambda=1}^{3} \varepsilon_{\lambda}^{\mu}(k) \varepsilon_{\lambda}^{\nu}(k)-\varepsilon_{0}^{\mu}(k) \varepsilon_{0}^{\nu}(k)=-g^{\mu \nu}
\]

Substituting into the above expression:

\[
|M|^{2} =\frac{g^{2}}{2}\left(-g^{\mu \nu}\right) \bar{\nu}\left(p_{2}\right) \gamma_{\nu} \cdot \frac{1-\gamma_{5}}{2} \gamma_{\mu} \cdot \frac{1-\gamma_{5}}{2} \cdot \nu\left(p_{2}\right)
\]

\[
=-\frac{g^{2}}{2} g^{\mu \nu} \bar{\nu}\left(p_{2}\right) \gamma_{\nu \mu_{1}} \gamma_{\mu} \cdot \frac{1-\gamma_{5}}{2} \cdot \nu\left(p_{2}\right)
\]

where \(\bar{\nu} \hat{\theta} \nu\) as a bilinear spinor form is a commutative constant, so we can take the trace of this number:

\[
\left|M\right|^{2} =-\frac{g^{2}}{2} g^{\mu \nu} \operatorname{Tr}\left[\gamma_{\nu \not_{1}} \gamma_{\mu} \cdot \frac{1-\gamma_{5}}{2} \cdot \nu \bar{\nu}\right]
\]

\[
=-\frac{g^{2}}{2} g^{\mu \nu} \operatorname{Tr}\left[\gamma_{\nu \digamma_{1}} \cdot \gamma_{\mu} \cdot \frac{1-\gamma_{5}}{2} p_{2}\right]
\]

\[
=-\frac{g^{2}}{2} g^{\mu \nu} \operatorname{Tr}\left[\gamma_{\nu \mu_{1}} \gamma_{\mu} \gamma_{2} \cdot \frac{1+\gamma_{5}}{2}\right]
\]

\[
=-\frac{g^{2}}{4}\left\{4 g^{\mu \nu}\left[p_{1 \nu} p_{2 \mu}-g_{\mu \nu}\left(p_{1} \cdot p_{2}\right)+p_{1 \mu} p_{2 \nu}\right]+4(-\mathrm{i}) g^{\mu \nu} \varepsilon_{\nu \not 1^{\mu} \not \boldsymbol{p}_{2}}\right\}
\]

Here, \(\not=\gamma_{\mu} p^{\mu}\), in the last term, \(g^{\mu \nu}\) is symmetric, \(\varepsilon_{\nu \mu_{1} \mu_{2}}\) is antisymmetric, so this term is zero. We arrive at a simple relation:

\[
|M|^{2}=-g^{2}\left(2 p_{1} \cdot p_{2}-g^{\mu \nu} g_{\mu \nu} p_{1} \cdot p_{2}\right)
\]

Using the relation:

\[
k = p_{1} + p_{2}
\]

\[
\left(p_{1} + p_{2}\right)^{2} = p_{1}^{2} + p_{2}^{2} + 2 p_{1} p_{2} = 2 p_{1} p_{2} = k^{2} = M_{\mathrm{W}}^{2}
\]

\[
g^{\mu \nu} g_{\mu \nu} = g_{\nu}^{\nu} = \delta_{\nu}^{\nu} = 4
\]

Substituting this into the equation above, we finally obtain the squared decay matrix element:

\[
|M|^{2} = 2 g^{2} p_{1} \cdot p_{2} = g^{2} M_{\mathrm{W}}^{2}
\]

For a two-body decay of \(\mathrm{W}^{+}\), we have

\[
\mathrm{d} \Gamma_{\mathrm{ev}} = \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{W}}} \cdot \frac{1}{32 \pi^{2}} |M|^{2} \cdot \frac{\left|\boldsymbol{p}_{1}\right|}{M_{\mathrm{W}}^{2}} \mathrm{~d} \Omega = \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{32 \pi^{2}} g^{2} M_{\mathrm{W}}^{2} \cdot \frac{\left(\frac{M_{\mathrm{W}}}{2}\right)}{M_{\mathrm{W}}^{2}} \mathrm{~d} \Omega = \frac{g^{2} M_{\mathrm{W}}}{192 \pi^{2}} \mathrm{~d} \Omega
\]

where \(N_{\mathrm{W}}=3\) is the factor for averaging over the initial spin states of \(\mathrm{W}^{+}\). In the rest frame of \(\mathrm{W}^{+}\), we have \(\left|p_{1}\right|=\left|p_{2}\right|=\frac{1}{2} M_{\mathrm{W}}\).

Performing the angular integration gives

\[
\Gamma_{\mathrm{ev}} = \int \mathrm{d} \Gamma_{\mathrm{ev}} = \int_{4 \pi} \frac{g^{2} M_{\mathrm{W}}}{192 \pi^{2}} \mathrm{~d} \Omega = \frac{g^{2} M_{\mathrm{W}}}{48 \pi}
\]

Using the relation

\[
\frac{G_{\mathrm{F}}}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{g^{2}}{8 M_{\mathrm{W}}^{2}} \Rightarrow g^{2}=\frac{8 G_{F} M_{\mathrm{W}}^{2}}{\sqrt{2}}
\]

Finally, the partial width for the decay of the charged intermediate boson \(\mathrm{W}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{e}^{+}+\nu\) is obtained as

\[
\Gamma_{\mathrm{ev}}=\frac{G_{\mathrm{F}} M_{\mathrm{W}}^{3}}{6 \pi \sqrt{2}} \approx \frac{1.17 \times 10^{-5} \times 82^{3}}{6 \pi \sqrt{2}} \approx 0.242 (\mathrm{GeV}) = 242 (\mathrm{MeV})
\]

Of course, we can also roughly estimate the decay width using dimensional analysis from Fermi's theory. The decay width is proportional to the Fermi constant \(G_{\mathrm{F}} \approx 1.17 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{GeV}^{-2}\). At this energy scale, the masses of quarks and leptons can be neglected, leaving the only energy scale as the vector boson's mass \(M_{\mathrm{W}}\). Hence, \(\Gamma \approx G_{\mathrm{F}} M_{\mathrm{W}}^{x}\) with dimensional analysis: \([\Gamma]=\mathrm{M}\), it should have a term proportional to the third power of the vector boson's mass \(M_{\mathrm{W}}\), i.e., \(x=3\),

\[
\Gamma_{\mathrm{W} \rightarrow \mathrm{ev}} \approx G_{\mathrm{F}} M_{\mathrm{W}}^{3} = 1.17 \times 10^{-5} \times 82^{3} \approx 6.45 (\mathrm{GeV})
\]

This is only a rough estimate, which, compared to our calculation above, misses the factor \(6 \pi \sqrt{2} \approx 26.7\).

Experimental value: \(\Gamma=(2.12 \pm 0.05)\) GeV, \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{ev}} / \Gamma=0.107 \pm 0.002\). From this, \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{ev}} \approx 227\) MeV is obtained. The precise calculated value aligns well with current experimental results, while the rough estimate differs significantly from the experimental value.

Neglecting the masses of leptons and quarks, we can derive:

\[
\Gamma_{\mathrm{ud}}=\Gamma_{\mathrm{c} \overline{\mathrm{s}}} \approx 3 \Gamma_{\mathrm{ev}}
\]

where factor 3 is the contribution from quark colors. The total width includes two quark generations and three lepton generations, but the top quark is too heavy for \(\mathrm{W}^{+}\) to decay into. Therefore, considering two quark generations and three lepton generations:

\[
\Gamma=9 \Gamma_{\mathrm{ev}}=9 \times 242=2178 (\mathrm{MeV})
\]

The lifetime of \(\mathrm{W}^{+}\) is given by

\[
\tau = \Gamma^{-1} \approx \frac{1}{2178} = 4.6 \times 10^{-4} (\mathrm{MeV}^{-1}) = 4.6 \times 10^{-4} \times 6.6 \times 10^{-22} = 3.04 \times 10^{-25} (\mathrm{s})
\]

where \( \mathrm{MeV}^{-1} = 6.6 \times 10^{-22} \mathrm{s} \) is used.

subject: Thermodynamics
topic: Thermodynamic State and First Law of Thermodynamics
problem: Using the expression \( p+\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_{T}=T\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial T}\right)_{V} \), find the heat capacity difference \( c_{\mathrm{p}} - c_{\mathrm{v}} \) for a Van der Waals gas given by the equation \( \left(p+\frac{a}{V^{2}}\right)(V-b)=RT \). With the result obtained, prove that under constant pressure \( p \), as \( V \rightarrow \infty \), the heat capacity difference approaches that of an ideal gas.
solution:
For a Van der Waals gas:

\[ 
\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial T}\right)_{V} = \frac{R}{V-b} 
\]

\[ 
\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{p} = \frac{R}{\left(\frac{RT}{V-b}\right) - \left(\frac{2a(V-b)}{V^{3}}\right)} 
\]

Therefore, we have

\[ 
c_{\mathrm{p}} - c_{\mathrm{v}} = \frac{R}{1 - \frac{2a\left(1 - \frac{b}{V}\right)^{2}}{VRT}} 
\]

As \( V \rightarrow \infty \), we find that \( c_{\mathrm{p}} - c_{\mathrm{v}} \rightarrow R \), which is the result for an ideal gas.

problem: In a Michelson interferometer, one arm (mirror) uniformly moves at a speed \( v \). The speed of the moving mirror in a rapid-scan Fourier transform spectrometer falls within this range.

subject: Classical Electromagnetism
problem: There are two coaxial coils with radii $a$ and $b$, separated by a distance $x$, carrying currents $i_{a}$ and $i_{b}$, respectively. Assume $a \gg b$. Calculate the interaction force between the two coils.
solution:
Consider the small coil with radius $b$ as a dipole, with its magnetic moment given by $m_{b}=\pi b^{2} i_{b}$. Therefore, the force on the small coil is

$$
F=m_{b}\left|\frac{\partial B_{a}}{\partial x}\right|=\frac{\pi \mu_{0} a^{2} b^{2} i_{a} i_{b}}{2} \frac{3 x}{\left(a^{2}+x^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}
$$

If the currents in the two coils are in the same direction, the force is attractive; otherwise, it is repulsive.

problem:

The laser frequency is selected so that sodium atoms with a velocity $v_{0}$ can resonantly absorb photons from the laser.

(5) To decelerate atoms with an initial velocity $v_{0}$ moving in a straight line to almost zero velocity in the manner described in part 1, how many absorption events are needed?
solution:
If each absorption event changes the atom's velocity by approximately $\Delta v_{1} \approx -\frac{E}{mc}$, to reduce the velocity from $v_{0}$ to nearly zero requires $N$ absorption events, taking a total time of $\Delta t$. Here,

$$

$$

subject: Semiconductor Physics
topic: Statistical Distribution of Electrons and Holes in Space
problem: If electrons in the valence band of a semiconductor silicon material are considered as free electrons, calculate the width of the valence band in electron volts. (The lattice constant of the silicon crystal \(a=5.4 \, \text{Å}\))
solution:
Treating the valence band electrons in silicon as free electrons, the \(E-k\) relationship is given by

\[
E(k)=\frac{\hbar^{2} k^{2}}{2 m}
\]

Thus, valence band electrons in silicon fill up to higher energy levels according to the above relationship from the \(E(\mathbf{k})=0\) energy level, filling a Fermi sphere with a radius \(k_{\mathrm{F}}\) in \(\mathbf{k}\) space, where the Fermi surface is the top of the valence band (full band). Assume the volume of the silicon crystal as \(V\) and the total number of electrons in the crystal as \(N\), then

\[
2 \cdot \frac{V}{(2 \pi)^{3}} \cdot \frac{4}{3} \pi k_{F}^{3}=N
\]

The electron concentration is \(\frac{N}{V}=n\), leading to

\[
k_{F}=(2 \pi) \cdot n^{\frac{1}{3}} \cdot \left(\frac{3}{8 \pi}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}
\]

A silicon crystal structure is diamond-like with \(a^{3}\) unit cells containing 8 silicon atoms, and each silicon atom contributing 4 valence electrons, so the electron concentration in the crystal

\[
n=\frac{8 \times 4}{a^{3}}
\]

Substituting into the Fermi wave vector equation, we obtain

\[
k_{\mathrm{F}}=(2 \pi) \cdot \left(\frac{12}{\pi}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} \cdot \frac{1}{a}
\]

Therefore, the energy of electrons on the Fermi surface is

\[
E\left(k_{\mathrm{F}}\right)=\frac{\hbar^{2} k_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}}{2 m}=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2 m a^{2}} \cdot (2 \pi)^{2} \times \left(\frac{12}{\pi}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}=\frac{h^{2}}{2 m a^{2}}\left(\frac{12}{\pi}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{\left(6.626 \times 10^{-34}\right)^{2}}{2 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times \left(5.4 \times 10^{-10}\right)^{2}} \times \left(\frac{12}{3.14}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}} \\
& =2.02 \times 10^{-18} \, \text{J} = 12.6 \, \text{eV}
\end{aligned}
\]

So the valence band width of the silicon crystal is approximately 12.6 eV.

subject: Geometrical Optics
problem: An elderly person can see objects clearly from 100 cm to 300 cm. The eye is simplified as a simple lens 2.0 cm away from the retina. What focal length of lens is needed for them to see objects clearly at 25 cm?
solution:
To see an object at \( u = 25 \mathrm{~cm} \) clearly, we have

\[
\Phi = \frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{0.25} + \frac{1}{0.02} = 54 \text{ (diopters)}
\]

And

\[
\Phi_{\text{lens}} = \Phi - \Phi_{\text{eye}} = 54 - \frac{1}{0.0196} = 3 \text{ (diopters)}
\]

Or

\[
f_{\text{lens}} = \frac{1}{\Phi_{\text{lens}}} = \frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~m} = 33 \mathrm{~cm}
\]

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: Consider the situation where the detachment from a circular track occurs at point $A$, and it is necessary to calculate the minimum height $h$ for this to happen. Assume the radius of curvature of the curved section of the track is $R$, and the gravitational acceleration is $g$.
solution:
Now consider the minimum height $h$ required for detachment at point $A$. First, calculate the minimum speed $v$ needed at the point of detachment at $A$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{m v^{2}}{R} = m g \cos 60^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2} m g \\
& v^{2} = \frac{1}{2} g R
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the conservation of mechanical energy,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& m g h = \frac{1}{2} m\left(\frac{1}{2} g R\right) + m g R \sin 30^{\circ} \\
& h = \frac{3}{4} R
\end{aligned}
$$

To surpass the maximum height point $B$ on the track, $h$ must be greater than $R$. Thus, the minimum value of $h$ for detachment is $\frac{3}{4} R$, and the position where detachment begins can only be at point $A$.

problem: If a crystal lattice can act as an excellent diffraction grating, try to estimate the energy of the incident photons. Assume that the order of magnitude of the atomic spacing in the crystal is \(10^{-10} \, \mathrm{m}\) (1 Å). Diffraction can occur when the wavelength of the incident wave is less than this value.

\]

problem:

problem: In the spherical potential well \( V(r) = -\gamma \delta(r-a) \), for a particle with mass \( \mu \) in a bound state, find the value of \(\gamma\) that satisfies the condition \( -k - k \operatorname{coth} ka = -\frac{2 \mu \gamma}{\hbar^{2}} \).
solution:

$$

subject: Wave Optics
problem: Consider a Fabry-Prot cavity with a length of 5 cm and an expanded light source experiment with a wavelength of $0.6 \, \mu\mathrm{m}$. Calculate the angular radius of the interference rings when the angle of the light ray is near $1^{\circ}$. Assume the reflectivity $R = 0.98$.
solution:
Typically, when natural light is reflected at the interface of two media, the reflected light is partially polarized. However, when the angle of incidence satisfies

$$
\theta_{B}=\arctan \frac{n_{1}}{n_{0}}
$$

where $n_{0}$ and $n_{1}$ are the refractive indices of the incident medium and the refractive medium respectively, the reflected light is linearly polarized with vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence. This angle $\theta_{B}$ is called the Brewster's angle or the polarization angle.

The calculations for $r, R, \bar{R}$, and $t, T, \bar{T}$ for the $S$ and $P$ components are based on Fresnel's equations. Because the angle of incidence is Brewster's angle, the sum of the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction is $\frac{\pi}{2}$. Intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, while energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam. The reflected light and incident light are in the same medium, with equal cross-sectional areas, while the refracted light and incident light are in different media, with different cross-sectional areas, which is noteworthy.

1. According to Fresnel's equations, the amplitude reflectance $r_{s}$ and amplitude transmittance $t_{s}$ for the $S$ component are

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{s}=\frac{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}-n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}=-\frac{\sin \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\
t_{s}=\frac{2 n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{2 \sin \theta_{2} \cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

The amplitude reflectance $r_{P}$ and amplitude transmittance $t_{P}$ for the $P$ component are

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{P}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}-n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{\tan \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}{\tan \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

where $n_{1}=1$, $n_{2}=n=1.50$, $\theta_{1}$ is the angle of incidence, and $\theta_{2}$ is the angle of refraction. Since the angle of incidence is the Brewster's angle, we have

$$
\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}=\arctan n=\arctan 1.50=56.3^{\circ}
$$

Additionally,

$$
\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}
$$

Substituting into the formulas for $r_{s}$ and $r_{p}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{s}=-\frac{\sin \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}{\sin \left(56.3^{\circ}+33.7^{\circ}\right)}=-0.384 \\
r_{p}=0
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the reflected light and incident light are in the same medium with equal cross-sectional areas, the intensity reflectance $R_{S}$ and $R_{P}$, as well as the energy flow reflectance $\bar{R}_{S}$ and $\bar{R}_{P}$ for the $S$ and $P$ components respectively, are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& R_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad R_{P}=0 \\
& \bar{R}_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad \bar{R}_{P}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

For the refracted light, substituting $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ into $t_{s}$ and $t_{P}$, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
t_{s}=\frac{2 \sin \theta_{2} \cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \sin 33.7^{\circ} \cos 56.3^{\circ}}{\sin \frac{\pi}{2}}=0.616 \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \cos 56.3^{\circ} \sin 33.7^{\circ}}{\cos \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}=0.667
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the refracted light and incident light are in different media with different cross-sectional areas, the intensity transmittance and energy flow transmittance are not simply equal to the square of the amplitude transmittance. The intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, given by

$$
\widetilde{S}=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_{0} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}{\mu_{0} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}}} E^{2}
$$

where $E$ is the amplitude of the electric vector. Since $\mu_{\mathrm{r}} \approx 1$, and the speed of light in vacuum $c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{0}} \mu_{0}}$, and the refractive index $n=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}} \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}$, this can be rewritten as

$$
\bar{S}=\frac{1}{2 c \mu_{0}} n E^{2}
$$

Thus, the intensity is proportional to $n E^{2}$, and the intensity transmittance is

$$
T=\frac{\bar{S}_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1}}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t^{2}
$$

The intensity transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& T_{S}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{S}^{2}=n t_{S}^{2}=0.569 \\
& T_{P}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{P}^{2}=n t_{P}^{2}=0.667
\end{aligned}
$$

The energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam, and the ratio of the cross-sectional areas of the refracted beam to the incident beam is $\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}}$, so the energy flow transmittance is

$$
\bar{T}=\frac{\bar{S}_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}} t^{2}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T
$$

Substituting the values, the energy flow transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{gathered}
\bar{T}_{S}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{S}=0.853 \\
\bar{T}_{P}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{P}=1
\end{gathered}
$$

The fact that the energy flow transmittance $\bar{T}_{P}=1$ for the $P$ component is expected because, when light is incident at the Brewster's angle $\left(\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}\right)$, the reflected light does not contain any $P$ component, meaning the entire energy of the incident $P$ component is transmitted.

subject: Classical Electromagnetism
problem: Two identical and coaxial superconducting circular coils I and II, each with a radius of \( R \) and self-inductance \( L \), are positioned on a horizontal plane and are very far apart from each other. Each coil carries a current \( j \) in a counterclockwise direction as viewed from above. Now, coil II is moved vertically along its axis by a distance \( R \) and is rotated by an angle of \( \frac{\pi}{2} \) along one of its diameters. Determine the current in each coil at this configuration.
solution:
By symmetry, the magnetic field induced by the current in coil I results in zero magnetic flux through coil II, thus the mutual inductance between the two coils is zero in this configuration. Therefore, using  

\[
\Phi_{1}=L j=L j_{2, \mathrm{I}}, \quad \Phi_{2}=L j=L j_{2, \mathrm{II}}
\]  

we find that the current in both coils I and II is \( j_{2, \mathrm{I}}=j_{2, \mathrm{II}}=j \).

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: Consider the decay $\Lambda^{0} \rightarrow \mathrm{p} + \pi^{-}$ and describe the test for parity conservation in this decay. Assume parity is conserved in the decay of $\Lambda^{0}$ and analyze the parity of the final state system.
solution:
In the decay $\Lambda^{0} \rightarrow \mathrm{p} + \pi^{-}$, both $\mathrm{p}$ and $\Lambda^{0}$ have spin $\frac{1}{2}$ and positive parity, while $\pi^{-}$ has negative parity and spin zero. According to the conservation of total angular momentum, the orbital angular momentum of the two-particle final state system can be 0 or 1.

If $l=0$, the parity of the final state system is $P(\mathrm{p}) P\left(\pi^{-}\right)(-1)^{0}=-1$; \\
If $l=1$, the parity of the final state system is $P(\mathrm{p}) P\left(\pi^{-}\right)(-1)^{1}=+1$. \\
Assuming parity is conserved in the decay of $\Lambda^{0}$, then $l=0$ is forbidden.

subject: Wave Optics
problem: When considering both absorption and scattering of light by a medium, the absorption coefficient is given by $\alpha = \alpha_{0} + \alpha_{s}$, where $\alpha_{0}$ is the true absorption coefficient and $\alpha_{s}$ is the scattering coefficient. According to the Lambert's law, $I = I_{0} \mathrm{e}^{-\left(\alpha_{0} + \alpha_{s}\right) l}$. If, after passing through a certain thickness of the medium, only $20\%$ of the light intensity is transmitted, and it is known that the scattering coefficient $\alpha_{s}$ is half of the true absorption coefficient $\alpha_{0}$, how much does the transmitted light intensity increase if scattering is not considered?
solution:
Using $I = I_{0} e^{-(\alpha_{0} + \alpha_{s}) l}$, we have $I/I_{0} = e^{-(\alpha_{0} + \alpha_{s}) l}$. Substituting $\alpha_{s} = \alpha_{0}/2$ and $I/I_{0} = 0.2$, we get

$$
\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\alpha_{0} + \frac{1}{2} \alpha_{0}\right) l} = \frac{I}{I_{0}} = 0.2
$$

Thus, $\alpha_{0} = \frac{2 \ln 5}{3 l}$. If scattering is eliminated, then $\alpha_{s} = 0$, so

$$
\frac{I'}{I_{0}} = \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha_{0} l} = \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{2}{3} \ln 5} = 0.34 = 34\%
$$

This means the transmitted light intensity increases to $34\%$.

subject: Relativity
problem:
A rocket spaceship is traveling at a speed of $0.8c$ relative to the Earth ($c$ is the speed of light in a vacuum). $O^{\prime}$ and $O$ are observers on the spaceship and Earth, respectively. When $x=x^{\prime}=0$, $t=t^{\prime}=0$. When $O$ observes $O^{\prime}$ through a telescope, his own clock reads 30 s. What is the time reading on $O^{\prime}$'s clock that he sees?

Assume $O^{\prime}$ emits a light signal at event $A$, and $O$ receives this signal and observes $O^{\prime}$'s clock through a telescope at event $B$. Given $x_{B}=0$ and $t_{B}=30 \mathrm{~s}$, find $t_{A}^{\prime}$.
solution:
Using the Lorentz transformation for event $A$,

$$
x_{A}=\frac{x_{A}^{\prime}+v t_{A}^{\prime}}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^{2}}}=\frac{0+0.8 \times 3 \times 10^{8} \cdot t_{A}^{\prime}}{\sqrt{1-(0.8)^{2}}}=4 \times 10^{8} t_{A}^{\prime}
$$

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: Prove that if $(\Delta x)^{2} = \left\langle x^{2} \right\rangle$, $(\Delta p)^{2} = \left\langle p^{2} \right\rangle$, and $\Delta x \Delta p = \frac{\hbar}{2}$, then the minimum energy of a harmonic oscillator is $\frac{\hbar \omega}{2}$.
solution:
For the harmonic oscillator, we have

$$
\langle x \rangle = \langle p \rangle = 0
$$

Therefore,

$$
(\Delta x)^{2} = \left\langle x^{2} \right\rangle, \quad (\Delta p)^{2} = \left\langle p^{2} \right\rangle
$$

The Hamiltonian of the harmonic oscillator is

$$
\begin{gathered}
H = \frac{p^{2}}{2m} + \frac{m \omega^{2}}{2} x^{2} \\
\langle H \rangle = \frac{\left\langle p^{2} \right\rangle}{2m} + \frac{m \omega^{2}}{2} \left\langle x^{2} \right\rangle = \frac{\langle \Delta p \rangle^{2}}{2m} + \frac{m \omega^{2}}{2} \langle \Delta x \rangle^{2}
\end{gathered}
$$

Using $\sqrt{ab} \leq \frac{a+b}{2}$ (where $a, b$ are real numbers), we obtain

$$
\langle H \rangle_{\min} = \sqrt{\langle \Delta p \rangle^{2} \langle \Delta x \rangle^{2}} \omega = \frac{\hbar \omega}{2}
$$

subject: Quantum Mechanics
problem: In the eigenstate of $S_{z}$ being +1, when measuring spin along the direction of $\boldsymbol{n}(\theta, \varphi)$, what are the possible values that can be obtained?
solution:
Express $\boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \boldsymbol{n}$ using the Pauli matrices, obtaining the following representation:

$$
\sigma_{n}=\boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \boldsymbol{n}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\cos \theta & \sin \theta \mathrm{e}^{-i \varphi} \\
\sin \theta \mathrm{e}^{i \varphi} & -\cos \theta
\end{array}\right), \quad \boldsymbol{n}=(\sin \theta \cos \varphi, \sin \theta \sin \varphi, \cos \theta)
$$

Its eigenvalues are $\pm 1$, with corresponding eigenvectors:

$$
\chi_{+}=\binom{\cos \frac{\theta}{2}}{\sin \frac{\theta}{2} \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} \varphi}}, \quad \chi_{-}=\binom{-\sin \frac{\theta}{2} \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i} \varphi}}{\cos \frac{\theta}{2}}
$$

The electron is in the state $\chi_{1 / 2}\left(S_{z}=1\right)=\binom{1}{0}$, so the possible measurement values of $\boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \boldsymbol{n}$ are $\pm 1$.

subject: Thermodynamics
problem:
A resistor of $100 \, \Omega$ at room temperature 300 K carries a current of 10 A for 300 s.  
(2) What is the total change in entropy?
solution:
The heat transferred from the resistor to the surroundings (a constant temperature heat reservoir) is  

$$  
I^{2} R t = 3 \times 10^{6} \, \mathrm{J}  
$$  

The increase in entropy of the constant temperature heat reservoir is $\Delta S_{2} = \frac{3 \times 10^{6}}{300} = 10^{4} \, (\mathrm{J} / \mathrm{K})$. Therefore, the total change in entropy is  

$$  
\Delta S = \Delta S_{1} + \Delta S_{2} = 10^{4} \, \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{K}  
$$

subject: Relativity
problem: A train is moving at a constant speed of \( v = 0.6c \) (where \( c \) is the speed of light in a vacuum), and the time taken to pass two points \( A \) and \( B \) on the ground is 40 minutes (measured by a stationary clock on the train). Determine the distance between points \( A \) and \( B \) as measured by a person on the ground.
solution:
The time experienced by a person on the ground for the train to travel from \( A \) to \( B \) is given by

\[
\Delta t=\frac{\Delta t^{\prime}}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^{2}}}
\]

The distance between points \( A \) and \( B \) is

\[
\Delta L = v \Delta t = 0.6c \cdot \frac{40 \times 60}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{0.6c}{c}\right)^{2}}} = 5.4 \times 10^{11} \, \text{m}
\]

subject: Wave Optics
problem: Based on the following data, calculate the free spectral range of a Fabry-Prot cavity. The length of the Fabry-Prot cavity is \(h=5 \mathrm{~cm}\), with the wavelength around the central region being \(\lambda=5500 \text{ }\), and \(n=1.0\).
solution:
Typically, when natural light is reflected at the interface of two media, the reflected light is partially polarized. However, when the angle of incidence satisfies

$$
\theta_{B}=\arctan \frac{n_{1}}{n_{0}}
$$

where $n_{0}$ and $n_{1}$ are the refractive indices of the incident medium and the refractive medium respectively, the reflected light is linearly polarized with vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence. This angle $\theta_{B}$ is called the Brewster's angle or the polarization angle.

The calculations for $r, R, \bar{R}$, and $t, T, \bar{T}$ for the $S$ and $P$ components are based on Fresnel's equations. Because the angle of incidence is Brewster's angle, the sum of the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction is $\frac{\pi}{2}$. Intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, while energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam. The reflected light and incident light are in the same medium, with equal cross-sectional areas, while the refracted light and incident light are in different media, with different cross-sectional areas, which is noteworthy.

1. According to Fresnel's equations, the amplitude reflectance $r_{s}$ and amplitude transmittance $t_{s}$ for the $S$ component are

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{s}=\frac{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}-n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}=-\frac{\sin \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\
t_{s}=\frac{2 n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{2 \sin \theta_{2} \cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

The amplitude reflectance $r_{P}$ and amplitude transmittance $t_{P}$ for the $P$ component are

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{P}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}-n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{\tan \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}{\tan \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}{n_{2} \cos \theta_{1}+n_{1} \cos \theta_{2}}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

where $n_{1}=1$, $n_{2}=n=1.50$, $\theta_{1}$ is the angle of incidence, and $\theta_{2}$ is the angle of refraction. Since the angle of incidence is the Brewster's angle, we have

$$
\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}=\arctan n=\arctan 1.50=56.3^{\circ}
$$

Additionally,

$$
\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}
$$

Substituting into the formulas for $r_{s}$ and $r_{p}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{s}=-\frac{\sin \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}{\sin \left(56.3^{\circ}+33.7^{\circ}\right)}=-0.384 \\
r_{p}=0
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the reflected light and incident light are in the same medium with equal cross-sectional areas, the intensity reflectance $R_{S}$ and $R_{P}$, as well as the energy flow reflectance $\bar{R}_{S}$ and $\bar{R}_{P}$ for the $S$ and $P$ components respectively, are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& R_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad R_{P}=0 \\
& \bar{R}_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad \bar{R}_{P}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

For the refracted light, substituting $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ into $t_{s}$ and $t_{P}$, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
t_{s}=\frac{2 \sin \theta_{2} \cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \sin 33.7^{\circ} \cos 56.3^{\circ}}{\sin \frac{\pi}{2}}=0.616 \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \cos 56.3^{\circ} \sin 33.7^{\circ}}{\cos \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}=0.667
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the refracted light and incident light are in different media with different cross-sectional areas, the intensity transmittance and energy flow transmittance are not simply equal to the square of the amplitude transmittance. The intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, given by

$$
\widetilde{S}=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_{0} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}{\mu_{0} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}}} E^{2}
$$

where $E$ is the amplitude of the electric vector. Since $\mu_{\mathrm{r}} \approx 1$, and the speed of light in vacuum $c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{0}} \mu_{0}}$, and the refractive index $n=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}} \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}$, this can be rewritten as

$$
\bar{S}=\frac{1}{2 c \mu_{0}} n E^{2}
$$

Thus, the intensity is proportional to $n E^{2}$, and the intensity transmittance is

$$
T=\frac{\bar{S}_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1}}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t^{2}
$$

The intensity transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& T_{S}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{S}^{2}=n t_{S}^{2}=0.569 \\
& T_{P}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{P}^{2}=n t_{P}^{2}=0.667
\end{aligned}
$$

The energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam, and the ratio of the cross-sectional areas of the refracted beam to the incident beam is $\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}}$, so the energy flow transmittance is

$$
\bar{T}=\frac{\bar{S}_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}} t^{2}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T
$$

Substituting the values, the energy flow transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{gathered}
\bar{T}_{S}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{S}=0.853 \\
\bar{T}_{P}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{P}=1
\end{gathered}
$$

The fact that the energy flow transmittance $\bar{T}_{P}=1$ for the $P$ component is expected because, when light is incident at the Brewster's angle $\left(\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}\right)$, the reflected light does not contain any $P$ component, meaning the entire energy of the incident $P$ component is transmitted.

subject: Atomic Physics
problem:
The scattering of high-energy muon neutrinos on nucleons where the number of neutrons and protons in the target are equal. The measured parameter is the ratio of the total cross-section for neutral current to charged current:
$$
R_{\nu} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{NC}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{CC}}} = 0.3
$$
Based on this result, calculate the Weinberg angle. The Weinberg angle provides the relationship between electromagnetic interaction and neutral weak current interaction.

(2) Using this information and the measured value $R_{\nu}$, calculate the Weinberg angle $\theta_{w}$. Assume only two types of quarks and ignore the different momentum distributions among quarks.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c|cc}
\hline
& Left-handed Fermion & Right-handed Fermion \\
\hline
Charged Current & $L_{\mathrm{CC}}=1$ & $R_{\mathrm{CC}}=0$ \\
Neutral Current & $L_{\mathrm{NC}}=I_{3}-Q_{e} \sin^2 \theta_{w}$ & $R_{\mathrm{NC}}=I_{3}-Q_{e} \sin^2 \theta_{w}$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
solution:
(2) First, let us consider the given expression for $\frac{\mathrm{d} \sigma}{\mathrm{d} y}$ within the range $0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1$, the total cross-section is
$$
\sigma_{\mathrm{tot}} = \begin{cases} \frac{G_{\mathrm{F}}^{2} s}{3 \pi} \overline{Q_{\mathrm{W}}^{2}} & \text{Right-handed} \\ \frac{G_{\mathrm{F}}^{2} s}{\pi} \overline{Q_{\mathrm{W}}^{2}} & \text{Left-handed} \end{cases}
$$
Now, consider the charged current scattering, assuming the target is unpolarized, i.e., the left-handed and right-handed quarks are equal. The numbers of protons and neutrons in the target are equal, that is, the number of $u$ and $d$ quarks are equal. Since only $d$ quarks participate in charged current scattering, when averaging the weak current squares over all $u$ and $d$ quarks, we have $\overline{L_{CC}^{2}} = \frac{1}{2}$. The total charged current cross-section averaged over polarizations is
$$
\sigma_{\mathrm{CC}} = \frac{G_{\mathrm{F}}^{2} s}{\pi} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \left( \overline{L_{\mathrm{CC}}^{2}} + \frac{1}{3} \overline{R_{\mathrm{CC}}^{2}} \right) = \frac{G_{\mathrm{F}}^{2} s}{4 \pi}
$$
Next, consider the neutral current. We must note the weak isospin values of particles, for the left-handed component of the spinor fields, $I_{3}$ for $u$ and $d$ quarks are $\frac{1}{2}$ and $-\frac{1}{2}$, respectively; for the right-handed component of the spinor fields, the value of $I_{3}$ is all 0. Although the expressions for $L_{\mathrm{NC}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{NC}}$ are the same, the weak charge values are different. This is a fundamental feature of the Standard Model and also the source of parity violation in weak interactions. The $Q_{e}$ for $u$ and $d$ quarks are $\frac{2}{3}$ and $-\frac{1}{3}$, respectively. For left-, right-handed fermions, the weak charges of $u$ quarks are $L_{\mathrm{NC}} = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{3} \sin^2 \theta_{w}$ and $R_{\mathrm{NC}} = -\frac{2}{3} \sin^2 \theta_{w}$. For left-, right-handed fermions, the weak charges of $d$ quarks are $L_{\mathrm{NC}} = -\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} \sin^2 \theta_{w}$ and $R_{\mathrm{NC}} = \frac{1}{3} \sin^2 \theta_{w}$. Substituting the left, right-handed weak charges and averaging over all quarks in the target nucleus, we get
$$
\overline{L_{\mathrm{NC}}^{2}} = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \left( \frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{3} \sin^2 \theta_{w} \right)^{2} + \left( -\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} \sin^2 \theta_{w} \right)^{2} \right]
$$
$$
\overline{R_{\mathrm{NC}}^{2}} = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \left( \frac{2}{3} \sin^2 \theta_{w} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{1}{3} \sin^2 \theta_{w} \right)^{2} \right]
$$
The total neutral current cross-section is the average of the left, right-handed components, thus
$$
\sigma_{\mathrm{NC}} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{G_{\mathrm{F}}^{2} s}{\pi} \left( \overline{L_{\mathrm{NC}}^{2}} + \frac{1}{3} \overline{R_{\mathrm{NC}}^{2}} \right) = \frac{G_{\mathrm{F}}^{2} s}{4 \pi} \left( \frac{1}{2} - \sin^2 \theta_{w} + \frac{20}{27} \sin^4 \theta_{w} \right)
$$
Experimental measurements give the ratio of the neutral current to the charged current cross-section $R_{\nu}$:
$$
R_{\nu} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{NC}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{CC}}} = \left( \frac{1}{2} - \sin^2 \theta_{w} + \frac{20}{27} \sin^4 \theta_{w} \right) \approx 0.3 
$$
Solving this equation, discarding non-physical solutions greater than 1, gives
$$
\sin^2 \theta_{w} \approx 0.24
$$
This value is close to the current average value of 0.221 obtained from various experiments.

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: A train is traveling directly south at a speed of \(30 \, \mathrm{m/s}\) (relative to the ground) in rain accompanied by a north wind. An observer stationary on the ground measures the path of the raindrops to form a \(25^{\circ}\) angle with the vertical. Meanwhile, an observer on the train sees the traces of the rain on the window glass falling straight down. Find the speed of the raindrops relative to the ground.
solution:
The observer on the train sees the raindrops falling straight down, indicating that the horizontal velocity component of the raindrops relative to the train is zero. Therefore, the horizontal velocity component of the raindrops relative to the ground is equal to the velocity of the train relative to the ground,

\[
v_{\parallel} = 30 \, \mathrm{m/s}
\]

Let \(v\) be the speed of the raindrops relative to the ground; then we have \(v_{\parallel} = v \sin 25^{\circ}\),

\[
v = \frac{v_{\parallel}}{\sin 25^{\circ}} = 71 \, \mathrm{m/s}
\]

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: (1) Use the equivalence principle and the theory of special relativity to calculate the frequency shift of a photon as it falls vertically to the ground from a height \(y\). Calculate to the first order approximation in \(y\) and clearly indicate the sign.
solution:
(1) Let the initial frequency of the photon be \(\nu_{0}\), and its frequency when it falls vertically to the ground from a height \(y\) be \(\nu\). The equivalent mass of the photon is \(\frac{h \nu_{0}}{c^{2}}\) and \(\frac{h \nu}{c^{2}}\) respectively. Let the mass and radius of the Earth be \(M\) and \(R\). Using the conservation of energy, we have:

\[
h \nu_{0} - G \frac{M \cdot \frac{h \nu_{0}}{c^{2}}}{R+y} = h \nu - G \frac{M \cdot \frac{h \nu}{c^{2}}}{R}
\]

For the first order approximation,

\[
\Delta \nu = \nu - \nu_{0} = \frac{g \cdot \frac{\nu_{0}}{c^{2}}}{1 - g \frac{R}{c^{2}}} y
\]

where \(g = \frac{G M}{R^{2}}\) is the local gravitational acceleration. Given \(g R \ll c^{2}\), we have:

\[
\frac{\nu - \nu_{0}}{\nu_{0}} \approx \frac{g}{c^{2}} y = 1.1 \times 10^{-16} y
\]

Let \(y = 20 \, \text{m}\),

\[
\frac{\nu - \nu_{0}}{\nu_{0}} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-15}
\]

subject: Classical Mechanics
problem: A $3:4:5$ inclined plane is fixed on a turntable, and a block is resting on the inclined plane. The coefficient of static friction between the inclined plane and the block is $\mu_{s} = \frac{1}{4}$. Determine the minimum angular velocity $\omega$ required for the block to remain stationary relative to the turntable at a horizontal distance of $40 \text{ cm}$ from the center of the turntable.
solution:
Taking the turntable as the reference frame, the forces acting on the block include gravity $mg$, static friction force $f$, the normal force $N$ from the inclined plane, and the inertial centrifugal force $\boldsymbol{F}$. Consider the critical scenario where there is no relative motion. Given $f = \mu_{s} N$, to find the minimum $\omega$, there is a tendency for the block to slide down, so $\boldsymbol{f}$ is directed up along the inclined plane. The centrifugal force $F = m \omega^{2} r$, where $r$ is the horizontal distance of the block from the center of the turntable, is currently $r = 0.40 \ \text{m}$.

Set up the equilibrium equations along the direction of the inclined plane and perpendicular to it:

$$
\begin{gathered}
mg \sin \theta - m \omega^{2} r \cos \theta - \mu_{s} N = 0 \\
N - mg \cos \theta - m \omega^{2} r \sin \theta = 0
\end{gathered}
$$

From these equations, we can solve for

$$
\omega = \sqrt{\frac{\sin \theta - \mu_{s} \cos \theta}{\cos \theta + \mu_{s} \sin \theta} \cdot \frac{g}{r}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.6 - \frac{1}{4} \times 0.8}{0.8 + \frac{1}{4} \times 0.4} \times \frac{9.8}{0.4}} = 3.3 \ \mathrm{rad/s}
$$

problem: (2) Starting from Newton's laws of motion, analyze the change in a small segment of a string to derive the above relationship.
solution:
Consider the mass element of the string located in the segment $x \sim x+\mathrm{d} x$, as shown in Figure 3.45. The external forces acting on it are $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$, which are the forces exerted by the string to the left of $x$ and to the right of $x+\mathrm{d} x$, respectively. The gravitational force is negligible compared to the resultant force of $\boldsymbol{T}_{1}$ and $\boldsymbol{T}_{2}$.

$$

In the $y$-direction, the net force on the mass element is

\begin{aligned}
T_{2} \sin \theta_{2} - T_{1} \sin \theta_{1} & = T_{2} \cos \theta_{2} \tan \theta_{2} - T_{1} \cos \theta_{1} \tan \theta_{1} \\
& = T_{0} \left( \tan \theta_{2} - \tan \theta_{1} \right) \\
& = T_{0} \left[ \left. \left( \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} \right) \right|_{x+\mathrm{d} x} - \left. \left( \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} \right) \right|_{x} \right] \\
& \approx T_{0} \frac{\partial^{2} y}{\partial x^{2}} \mathrm{~d} x
\end{aligned}
$$

According to Newton's laws of motion,

$$
\begin{gathered}
\eta \mathrm{d} x \frac{\partial^{2} y}{\partial t^{2}} = T_{0} \frac{\partial^{2} y}{\partial x^{2}} \mathrm{~d} x \\
\frac{\partial^{2} y}{\partial t^{2}} - \frac{T_{0}}{\eta} \frac{\partial^{2} y}{\partial x^{2}} = 0

The wave speed of a wave propagating in the string (which can only be a transverse wave) is

The wavelength of the lowest frequency wave (fundamental frequency) propagating in a string of length $l$ is $\lambda = 2 l$,

v = \lambda \nu
$$

Fundamental frequency $\nu = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T_{0}}{\eta}}$, which is the same as $\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\eta}}$ in (1).

\end{gathered}
$$

where $n_{1}=1$, $n_{2}=n=1.50$, $\theta_{1}$ is the angle of incidence, and $\theta_{2}$ is the angle of refraction. Since the angle of incidence is the Brewster's angle, we have

$$
\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}=\arctan n=\arctan 1.50=56.3^{\circ}
$$

Additionally,

$$
\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}
$$

Substituting into the formulas for $r_{s}$ and $r_{p}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{s}=-\frac{\sin \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}{\sin \left(56.3^{\circ}+33.7^{\circ}\right)}=-0.384 \\
r_{p}=0
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the reflected light and incident light are in the same medium with equal cross-sectional areas, the intensity reflectance $R_{S}$ and $R_{P}$, as well as the energy flow reflectance $\bar{R}_{S}$ and $\bar{R}_{P}$ for the $S$ and $P$ components respectively, are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& R_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad R_{P}=0 \\
& \bar{R}_{S}=\left|r_{S}\right|^{2}=0.148, \quad \bar{R}_{P}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

For the refracted light, substituting $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ into $t_{s}$ and $t_{P}$, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
t_{s}=\frac{2 \sin \theta_{2} \cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \sin 33.7^{\circ} \cos 56.3^{\circ}}{\sin \frac{\pi}{2}}=0.616 \\
t_{P}=\frac{2 \cos \theta_{1} \sin \theta_{2}}{\sin \left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) \cos \left(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\right)}=\frac{2 \cos 56.3^{\circ} \sin 33.7^{\circ}}{\cos \left(56.3^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}\right)}=0.667
\end{gathered}
$$

Since the refracted light and incident light are in different media with different cross-sectional areas, the intensity transmittance and energy flow transmittance are not simply equal to the square of the amplitude transmittance. The intensity refers to the average energy flow density, which is the time average of the Poynting vector, given by

$$
\widetilde{S}=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_{0} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}{\mu_{0} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}}} E^{2}
$$

where $E$ is the amplitude of the electric vector. Since $\mu_{\mathrm{r}} \approx 1$, and the speed of light in vacuum $c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{0}} \mu_{0}}$, and the refractive index $n=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}} \mu_{\mathrm{r}}} \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}$, this can be rewritten as

$$
\bar{S}=\frac{1}{2 c \mu_{0}} n E^{2}
$$

Thus, the intensity is proportional to $n E^{2}$, and the intensity transmittance is

$$
T=\frac{\bar{S}_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1}}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t^{2}
$$

The intensity transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& T_{S}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{S}^{2}=n t_{S}^{2}=0.569 \\
& T_{P}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} t_{P}^{2}=n t_{P}^{2}=0.667
\end{aligned}
$$

The energy flow equals the intensity multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the beam, and the ratio of the cross-sectional areas of the refracted beam to the incident beam is $\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}}$, so the energy flow transmittance is

$$
\bar{T}=\frac{\bar{S}_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{\bar{S}_{1} \cos \theta_{1}}=\frac{n_{2} \cos \theta_{2}}{n_{1} \cos \theta_{1}} t^{2}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T
$$

Substituting the values, the energy flow transmittance for the $S$ and $P$ components is

$$
\begin{gathered}
\bar{T}_{S}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{S}=0.853 \\
\bar{T}_{P}=\frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\cos \theta_{1}} T_{P}=1
\end{gathered}
$$

The fact that the energy flow transmittance $\bar{T}_{P}=1$ for the $P$ component is expected because, when light is incident at the Brewster's angle $\left(\theta_{1}=\theta_{B}\right)$, the reflected light does not contain any $P$ component, meaning the entire energy of the incident $P$ component is transmitted.

subject: Wave Optics
problem: Let the refractive indices of dielectric media 1 and 2 be \( n_{1}, n_{2} \left(n_{1} > n_{2}\right) \), and the incident angle \( \theta_{1} \) exceed the critical angle for total internal reflection. Prove that under the condition of total internal reflection, the amplitude reflectivity in Fresnel's equations is a complex number, and provide the phase difference \( \delta \) between the \( S \) and \( P \) components.
solution:
Let the refractive indices of dielectric media 1 and 2 be \( n_{1}, n_{2} \left(n_{1} > n_{2}\right) \), with the incident angle \( \theta_{1} \) greater than the critical angle for total internal reflection, i.e.,

\[
\sin \theta_{1} > \frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} = n
\]

According to Fresnel's equations, the amplitude ratio of the \( S \) and \( P \) components in the reflected light to the corresponding components in the incident light is

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{E_{S_{1}}^{\prime}}{E_{S_{1}}} = \frac{\cos \theta_{1} - \mathrm{i} \sqrt{\sin^{2} \theta_{1} - n^{2}}}{\cos \theta_{1} + \mathrm{i} \sqrt{\sin^{2} \theta_{1} - n^{2}}} \\
& \frac{E_{P_{1}}^{\prime}}{E_{P_{1}}} = \frac{n^{2} \cos \theta_{1} - \mathrm{i} \sqrt{\sin^{2} \theta_{1} - n^{2}}}{n^{2} \cos \theta_{1} + \mathrm{i} \sqrt{\sin^{2} \theta_{1} - n^{2}}}
\end{aligned}
\]

The above equations show that under the condition of total internal reflection, the amplitude reflectivities \(\frac{E_{S_{1}}^{\prime}}{E_{S_{1}}}\) and \(\frac{E_{P_{1}}^{\prime}}{E_{P_{1}}}\) for the \( S \) and \( P \) components are complex numbers. Their magnitudes are both equal to 1, indicating that the amplitudes of the \( S \) and \( P \) components in the reflected light are the same as those in the incident light, meaning that all energy is reflected. Their phase angles are \( -2 \varphi_{S} \) and \( -2 \varphi_{P} \), respectively, indicating different phase changes for the \( S \) and \( P \) components before and after reflection. Since the \( S \) and \( P \) components of the incident light are in phase, the phase difference \( \delta \) between the \( S \) and \( P \) components in the reflected light is

\[
\delta = 2 \left(\varphi_{P} - \varphi_{S}\right) = 2 \arctan \left[\frac{\cos \theta_{1} \sqrt{\sin^{2} \theta_{1} - n^{2}}}{\sin^{2} \theta_{1}}\right]
\]

where \( n = \frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} < 1 \), with light going from a medium with refractive index \( n_{1} \) to a medium with refractive index \( n_{2} \).

subject: Statistical Mechanics
problem: A piece of metal can be considered as an electron source, with a work function of $W = 4 \text{ eV}$. We only consider the ground state of $\mathrm{H}$ (which can accommodate up to two electrons), where the dissociation energy of ground state electrons is $\varepsilon_{1} = 13.6 \text{ eV}$, and the electron affinity is $\varepsilon_{2} = 0.6 \text{ eV}$. When hydrogen atoms and metal reach thermal equilibrium at $T = 300 \text{ K}$, find the probability of finding $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ near the metal.
solution:
Refer to Figure 8.7. We have the equilibrium $\mathrm{e} + \mathrm{H}^{+} \leftrightarrows \mathrm{H}$, where the chemical potential of the electron gas is $\mu_{\mathrm{e}} = -W$. From classical statistics, it is straightforward to derive the concentrations of electrons and hydrogen ions as

$$
\begin{gathered}
[\mathrm{e}] = 2 \mathrm{e}^{\mu_{\mathrm{e}} / k T} \left(\frac{2 \pi m_{\mathrm{e}} k T}{h^{2}}\right)^{3 / 2} \\
[\mathrm{H}^{+}] = 2 \mathrm{e}^{\mu_{\mathrm{H}^{+}} / k T} \left(\frac{2 \pi m_{\mathrm{p}} k T}{h^{2}}\right)^{3 / 2}
\end{gathered}
$$

Here, 2 represents the internal spin degrees of freedom. For the chemical equilibrium condition $\mu_{\mathrm{H}^{0}} = \mu_{\mathrm{e}} + \mu_{\mathrm{H}^{+}}$, we obtain

$$
\frac{[\mathrm{H}^{0}]}{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]} = 2 \exp \left(\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{e}} + \varepsilon_{1}}{k T}\right)
$$

Thus, it is found that the relative probability of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ is

$$
P_{\mathrm{H}^{+}} = 1
$$

subject: Atomic Physics
problem: A particle with mass $m$ has a kinetic energy that is twice its rest energy. This particle collides with another particle of mass $m$ and they combine to form a new particle. Calculate the mass of the new particle.
solution:
Let the mass of the new particle be $M$. The invariant mass squared of the system is given by

$$
S=(E+m)^{2}-p^{2}=M^{2}
$$

Using the energy-momentum relation $E^{2}=p^{2}+m^{2}$, we find the mass of the new particle to be

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M^{2}=2 m^{2}+2 m E=8 m^{2} \\
& M=\sqrt{8} m=2 \sqrt{2} m=2.83 m
\end{aligned}
$$
